lessons.t: The circuit: two pumps, one loop

cards.q: How are the two pumps of the heart arranged in the circulation?
cards.a: In series, in one continuous loop
cards.more: One organ holds both pumps; blood must pass through one to reach the other.

cards.q: What does the right heart do?
cards.a: Takes oxygen-poor blood back from the body → sends it to the lungs

cards.q: What does the left heart do?
cards.a: Takes oxygenated blood back from the lungs → sends it to the rest of the body

cards.q: Why must right and left ventricular output be equal in the steady state?
cards.a: They are in series: whatever the right side pumps, the left side must pump

cards.q: What happens if the right and left heart pump different outputs for more than a few beats?
cards.a: Blood piles up → congestion (as in heart failure)

cards.q: Trace one full lap of the circulation, starting at the right atrium.
cards.a: Right atrium → tricuspid valve → right ventricle → pulmonic valve → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium → mitral valve → left ventricle → aortic valve → aorta → organs → veins → vena cava → right atrium

cards.q: Name the two right-heart valves in the order blood crosses them.
cards.a:
Tricuspid (right atrium → right ventricle)
Pulmonic (right ventricle → pulmonary artery)

cards.q: Name the two left-heart valves in the order blood crosses them.
cards.a:
Mitral (left atrium → left ventricle)
Aortic (left ventricle → aorta)

cards.q: What fraction of the cardiac output passes through each heart chamber and through the lungs every minute?
cards.more: Every drop goes round the one loop, so left ventricular output equals right ventricular output.

cards.q: Typical pulmonary artery pressure?
cards.a: About 25/8 mmHg (mean 15)

cards.q: Typical aortic pressure?
cards.a: About 120/80 mmHg (mean 100)

cards.q: Why does the left ventricle have to generate far more pressure than the right ventricle?
cards.a: Systemic circuit is long and high-resistance; pulmonary circuit is short and low-resistance
cards.more: Picture it: pulmonary circulation is a short garden hose, systemic circulation is a mile of narrow pipe. Same pump rate, wildly different pressure needed.

cards.q: At the same flow, how does left ventricular pressure compare with right ventricular pressure?
cards.a: About 5× the peak pressure; 6–7× the mean

cards.q: Why is the left ventricular wall thick and the right ventricular wall thin?
cards.a: Same flow, but the left must generate about five times the peak pressure
cards.more: The lesson calls the left-high/right-low pressure difference the single most useful fact for the rest of the block.

cards.q: What pressure pattern do both the systemic and pulmonary circuits share?
cards.a: Highest leaving the ventricle → lowest arriving back at an atrium
cards.more: The pulmonary side runs the same pattern at a fraction of the pressure.

cards.q: Mean pressure in the systemic arterioles?
cards.a: 50 mmHg
cards.more: No arteriole value is given for the pulmonary circuit.

cards.q: Mean pressure in the systemic capillaries?
cards.a: 20 mmHg

cards.q: Mean pressure in the pulmonary capillaries?
cards.a: 10 mmHg

cards.q: Mean pressure in the vena cava?
cards.a: 4 mmHg

cards.q: Mean pressure in the pulmonary vein?
cards.a: 8 mmHg

cards.q: Right atrial pressure?
cards.a: 0–2 mmHg

cards.q: Left atrial pressure?
cards.a: 2–5 mmHg
cards.more:
LevelSystemicPulmonary
Main arteryAorta 100 (120/80)Pulmonary artery 15 (25/8)
Arterioles50–
Capillaries2010
Main veinVena cava 4Pulmonary vein 8
Receiving atriumRight atrium 0–2Left atrium 2–5

Mean pressures, mmHg.

cards.q: How is left atrial pressure estimated, since it is hard to measure directly?
cards.a: Pulmonary wedge pressure

cards.q: Why does a catheter wedged in a small pulmonary artery branch read left atrial pressure?
cards.a: It stops flow in that branch, so it senses the left atrium almost directly

cards.q: Rearrange flow = pressure difference ÷ resistance to give resistance.
cards.a: R = ΔP / Q

cards.q: For total peripheral resistance (TPR), what is the pressure difference (ΔP)?
cards.a: Mean arterial pressure (MAP) − right atrial pressure

cards.q: For pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR), what is the pressure difference (ΔP)?
cards.a: Mean pulmonary artery pressure − left atrial pressure

cards.q: Calculate TPR: MAP 96 mmHg, right atrial pressure 2 mmHg, cardiac output 5,229 mL/min.
Calculate PVR: pulmonary artery pressure 15 mmHg, left atrial pressure 5 mmHg, cardiac output 5,229 mL/min.
How does pulmonary vascular resistance compare with total peripheral resistance?
cards.a: PVR ≈ one tenth of TPR
cards.more: Same flow at a fraction of the pressure means a fraction of the resistance.

cards.q: Total flow through all the pulmonary capillaries (or through all the systemic arteries) equals what?
cards.a: The cardiac output

cards.q: What do you need to calculate the resistance of a single organ?
cards.a: That organ's own arterial − venous pressure and its own blood flow

cards.q: Where is most of the blood volume at any moment?
cards.a: In the veins: about two thirds
cards.more: Arteries hold only a small fraction, under high pressure.

cards.q: Which vessels are called the capacitance vessels, and why?
cards.a: Veins: they are the blood reservoir

cards.q: Approximate number of each systemic vessel type: aorta, arteries, arterioles, capillaries?
cards.a:
Aorta 1
Arteries 105
Arterioles 107
Capillaries 1010
cards.more: Each level of branching multiplies the count. Veins and venules together are counted as 1012 in older editions of this figure and 107 in the current one.

cards.q: Which vessels have the largest total cross-sectional area, and about how large?
cards.a: Capillaries: about 2,500 cm² (vs a few cm² for the aorta)
cards.more: A single capillary is tiny, but there are so many that together they have the largest area; that is why blood slows right down in them.

cards.q: How are the systemic organs arranged relative to the aorta, and what follows for their flows?
cards.a: In parallel → their separate flows add up to the whole cardiac output
cards.more: This is Kirchhoff's junction rule.

cards.q: Which organs get the biggest share of cardiac output at rest, and what do they have in common?
cards.a: Liver and gut, kidneys, skeletal muscle, brain → all doing continuous chemical work

cards.q: Resting share of cardiac output: kidneys?
cards.a: About 25%

cards.q: Resting share of cardiac output: liver and gut (gastrointestinal) together?
cards.a: About 25%

cards.q: Resting share of cardiac output: skeletal muscle?
cards.a: About 25%

cards.q: Resting share of cardiac output: brain?
cards.a: About 15%

cards.q: Resting share of cardiac output: coronaries?
cards.a: About 5% (one twentieth)

cards.q: Resting share of cardiac output: skin?
cards.a: About 5%
cards.more:
OrganResting share
Kidneys~25%
Liver + gut~25%
Skeletal muscle~25%
Brain~15%
Coronaries~5%
Skin~5%

cards.q: Which organ has the highest blood flow per gram?
cards.a: Kidney: about half a percent of body weight, a quarter of the output

cards.q: Why do the kidneys take so much of the cardiac output?
cards.a: Their job is filtering, not feeding themselves

cards.q: How do the coronaries combine blood flow and oxygen extraction?
cards.a: Low flow + near-maximal oxygen extraction

cards.q: Why does the heart have almost no oxygen reserve except to dilate its vessels?
cards.a: It already extracts almost all the oxygen from each unit of blood

cards.q: Share of cardiac output vs oxygen extraction: how do resting skeletal muscle and the heart differ?
cards.a:
Resting muscle: big share, extracts little
Heart: small share, extracts almost everything
cards.more: The trap: share of output and oxygen extraction are different things.

cards.q: During exercise, how do the organ shares of cardiac output change?
cards.a:
Skeletal muscle ↑ enormously
Heart ↑ with cardiac output
Gut and kidney ↓

cards.q: What actually drives blood flow?
cards.a: A pressure difference between two points, not pressure itself
cards.more: The lesson flags this as the thing people get wrong most often.

cards.q: Flow in a vessel with 100 mmHg at both ends?
cards.a: Zero

cards.q: Write Ohm's law for blood flow.
cards.a: Q = ΔP / R
cards.more: Q = blood flow, ΔP = pressure gradient, R = resistance. In words: flow = pressure difference ÷ resistance, the same relationship that governs electricity.

cards.q: Ohm's law applied to the whole systemic circulation?
cards.a: MAP = CO × TPR
cards.more: Q becomes the cardiac output (CO), R the total peripheral resistance (TPR), and ΔP the mean arterial pressure (MAP).

cards.q: Why can ΔP for the whole systemic circulation be taken as simply the mean arterial pressure?
cards.a: Right atrial pressure is close to zero

cards.q: Name the three things that set vascular resistance.
cards.a:
Vessel length
Blood viscosity
Vessel radius (dominant)

cards.q: Write the Poiseuille equation for resistance.
cards.a: R = 8ηl / πr<sup>4</sup>
cards.more: η = blood viscosity, l = vessel length, r = radius.

cards.q: Why does vessel width dominate resistance?
cards.a: Resistance depends on radius to the fourth power
cards.more: Nothing else in the system has that kind of leverage.

cards.q: Halve a vessel's radius: what happens to resistance?
cards.a: ↑ 16-fold

cards.q: Halve a vessel's radius at the same pressure gradient: what happens to flow?
cards.a: Falls to one sixteenth

cards.q: What mainly sets blood viscosity?
cards.a: Haematocrit

cards.q: Polycythaemia vs severe anaemia: effect on viscosity and resistance?
cards.a:
Polycythaemia: viscosity ↑ → resistance ↑
Anaemia: viscosity ↓ → resistance ↓
cards.more: A real mechanism for cardiovascular trouble, not a footnote.

cards.q: How does the body control blood flow to a tissue?
cards.a: Almost entirely by changing vessel diameter
cards.more: Because resistance varies with r4, a small change in diameter changes flow enormously.

cards.q: Which vessels are the main resistance vessels?
cards.a: Arterioles: the small muscular vessels just before the capillaries
cards.more: A small squeeze there changes flow enormously.

cards.q: What controls arteriolar diameter, and what decides whether it constricts or dilates?
cards.a: Sympathetic nervous system; the receptor type on the arteriole

cards.q: Alpha-1 receptors on arterioles: effect and location?
cards.a:
Constriction
Skin, gut, kidney, spleen

cards.q: Beta-2 receptors on arterioles: effect and location?
cards.a:
Dilatation
Skeletal muscle

cards.q: What controls coronary arteriolar flow?
cards.a: Local metabolism (very little sympathetic control)

cards.q: What does a surge of adrenaline do to blood distribution?
cards.a: Squeezes blood out of gut and skin → pushes it towards muscle
cards.more: The fight-or-flight redistribution, written in receptor distribution: alpha-1 constricts gut and skin, beta-2 dilates muscle.

cards.q: Which vessels are arranged in series, and how do their resistances combine?
cards.a:
Artery → arteriole → capillary → venule → vein
Rtotal = R1 + R2 + R3 + R4 + R5

cards.q: In vessels in series, how do flow and pressure behave from segment to segment?
cards.a:
Flow: the same at every level
Pressure: falls across each segment

cards.q: Across which series segment does pressure fall most?
cards.a: The arterioles

cards.q: How does total series resistance compare with any single resistance in the series?
cards.a: Bigger than any single one

cards.q: Which vascular beds sit in parallel off the aorta?
cards.a: Cerebral, coronary, renal, gastrointestinal, skeletal muscle, skin

cards.q: How do parallel resistances combine?
cards.a: 1/R<sub>total</sub> = 1/R<sub>1</sub> + 1/R<sub>2</sub> + … + 1/R<sub>6</sub>

cards.q: Four parallel beds, each of resistance 10: what is R<sub>total</sub>?
cards.a: 2.5 (1/R<sub>total</sub> = 4/10)

cards.q: Four parallel beds of resistance 10 (R<sub>total</sub> 2.5): add a fifth, or block one of the four?
cards.a:
Add a fifth → 2
Block one → 3.3

cards.q: How does total parallel resistance compare with the smallest single branch?
cards.a: Smaller than the smallest branch

cards.q: Adding another parallel path does what to total resistance, and why?
cards.a: Always lowers it: blood has another way through

cards.q: Why does the parallel arrangement of the systemic circulation matter?
cards.a: Each organ gets the same driving pressure → controls its own flow independently via its arteriolar diameter

cards.q: Lose a kidney: what happens to total peripheral resistance, and why?
cards.a: Goes up: a parallel channel was removed

cards.q: How does velocity differ from flow?
cards.a: Velocity = distance per minute; flow = volume per minute

cards.q: Formula for velocity of blood flow?
cards.a: v = Q / A
cards.more: A = total cross-sectional area.

cards.q: Cardiac output 5,229 mL/min through an aorta 20 mm across (area 3.14 cm²): velocity?
cards.a: About 1,665 cm/min

cards.q: Cardiac output 5,229 mL/min spread over the capillaries (about 2,500 cm²): velocity?
cards.a: About 2 cm/min

cards.q: Where does blood move slowest, and why?
cards.a: Capillaries: largest total cross-sectional area
cards.more: Flow through every segment in series is the same, so velocity is lowest where total area is greatest.

cards.q: Why is slow capillary velocity useful?
cards.a: Gives time for exchange

cards.q: Where is blood velocity fastest, and why?
cards.a: Aorta: smallest cross-sectional area

cards.q: What is laminar flow?
cards.a: Smooth concentric layers; quiet

cards.q: What makes flow turbulent?
cards.a: Velocity too high, or a vessel narrows abruptly

cards.q: What is a murmur or bruit?
cards.a: The sound of turbulent (disordered) flow

cards.q: Why can you hear Korotkoff sounds when taking blood pressure?
cards.a: The cuff partly occludes the artery → turbulent flow → noise

cards.q: Write the Reynolds number.
cards.a: N<sub>R</sub> = ρdv / η
cards.more: ρ = blood density, d = vessel diameter, v = velocity, η = viscosity.

cards.q: What does a high Reynolds number predict?
cards.a: Turbulence

cards.q: Name the four conditions that favour turbulent flow.
cards.a:
High velocity
Large diameter
High density
Low viscosity

cards.q: Name the two classic settings for flow murmurs.
cards.a:
Anaemia
Narrowed valve or vessel

cards.q: How does anaemia produce a flow murmur?
cards.a: Lowers viscosity → turbulence (not by raising pressure)

cards.q: How does a narrowed valve or vessel produce a murmur?
cards.a: Velocity rises through the narrowing → turbulence

cards.q: Shape of the velocity profile in laminar flow?
cards.a: Parabola: zero at the wall, fastest in the centre

cards.q: Why is velocity zero at the vessel wall in laminar flow?
cards.a: The outermost layer of blood clings to the wall and does not move

cards.q: What happens to the blood streams in turbulent flow, and what does it cost?
cards.a: Break into eddies that mix sideways as well as forward → wasted energy and noise

cards.q: What is shear?
cards.a: Layers of blood sliding past each other at different speeds

cards.q: Where is shear highest and where lowest in a vessel?
cards.a: Highest at the wall; lowest in the centre
cards.more: At the wall, layers slide past the motionless outer layer; in the centre neighbouring layers move at nearly the same speed.

cards.q: How does shear affect blood viscosity, and where is viscosity therefore lowest?
cards.a: Breaks up red-cell clumps → lowers viscosity → lowest near the wall

cards.q: What is compliance?
cards.a: How much a vessel stretches when volume is put into it
cards.more: Also called capacitance.

cards.q: Formula for compliance?
cards.a: C = V / P
cards.more: Millilitres you can add per mmHg of pressure rise.

cards.q: Compliant vessel vs stiff vessel: what happens when you add volume?
cards.a:
Compliant: lots of volume, little pressure rise
Stiff: little volume, pressure jumps

cards.q: How is compliance related to elasticity?
cards.a: Inverse: the stiffer and more elastic the wall, the lower the compliance
cards.more: Elasticity is the stiffness that makes a wall resist stretch and spring back.

cards.q: How much more compliant are veins than arteries?
cards.a: About 20×
cards.more: Veins take roughly twenty times more volume than arteries for the same pressure rise.

cards.q: Why can the veins hold most of the blood at very low pressure?
cards.a: They are highly compliant: they stretch easily
cards.more: Picture it: an artery is a bicycle inner tube (stiff, holds pressure); a vein is a plastic shopping bag (floppy, holds volume at almost no pressure).

cards.q: What happens to arterial compliance with age?
cards.a: Falls: arteries stiffen

cards.q: How does the aorta turn the heart's brief squirt into continuous flow at the tissues?
cards.a: Balloons in systole, storing some stroke volume → recoils in diastole and keeps pushing

cards.q: Without arterial compliance, when would tissues get flow?
cards.a: Only during systole

cards.q: What is systolic pressure?
cards.a: Highest arterial pressure in a cardiac cycle, just after the ventricle ejects

cards.q: What is diastolic pressure?
cards.a: Lowest arterial pressure, while the ventricle relaxes and ejects nothing

cards.q: Formula for pulse pressure?
cards.a: Systolic − diastolic

cards.q: Other things equal, pulse pressure tracks what?
cards.a: Stroke volume

cards.q: Pulse pressure changes whenever which two things change?
cards.a:
Stroke volume
Arterial compliance

cards.q: Formula for mean arterial pressure (MAP)?
cards.a: MAP = diastolic + ⅓ pulse pressure

cards.q: Why does MAP sit closer to diastolic than to systolic?
cards.a: About two thirds of each cycle is spent in diastole

cards.q: Blood pressure 124/82: pulse pressure and MAP?
cards.a:
Pulse pressure 42
MAP 82 + 14 = 96 mmHg

cards.q: Stiff aorta (age or arteriosclerosis): systolic, diastolic and pulse pressure?
cards.a:
Systolic ↑
Diastolic normal or ↓
Pulse pressure wide

cards.q: Why does systolic pressure climb when the aorta stiffens?
cards.a: The aorta cannot absorb the ejected volume

cards.q: Why does diastolic pressure not rise (and often falls) when the aorta stiffens?
cards.a: The aorta cannot recoil to maintain flow in diastole

cards.q: A widening pulse pressure in an older patient usually means what?
cards.a: Arterial stiffness, not a stronger heart

cards.q: Arteriosclerosis: effect on systolic, pulse and mean arterial pressure?
cards.a: All rise
cards.more: Works through reduced compliance; plaque also narrows the arteries, adding resistance.

cards.q: Through what does aortic stenosis change arterial pressure?
cards.a: Stroke volume: the narrowed valve lets less blood out per beat

cards.q: Aortic stenosis: effect on systolic, pulse and mean arterial pressure?
cards.a: All fall

cards.q: Aortic stenosis: effect on the pressure the ventricle must generate?
cards.a: ↑ (higher afterload) to eject through the narrowed valve

cards.q: Aortic regurgitation: what happens to diastolic pressure, and why?
cards.a: Falls: the leaky valve lets ejected blood run back into the relaxed ventricle

cards.q: Aortic regurgitation: what happens to stroke volume and systolic pressure, and why?
cards.a: Both rise: the ventricle re-ejects the regurgitated blood with the next beat

cards.q: Aortic regurgitation: pulse pressure?
cards.a: Wide

cards.q: How does mean pressure behave through the big arteries?
cards.a: Stays high (about 100 mmHg) and barely falls

cards.q: Where does mean pressure drop most steeply along the circulation?
cards.a: Across the arterioles
cards.more: By the capillaries pressure is low and smooth (about 20 mmHg); about 4 mmHg in the vena cava.

cards.q: What does a pressure profile along the vasculature tell you?
cards.a: Where the resistance is: the steep drop marks the resistance vessels

cards.q: What is unstressed volume?
cards.a: Volume sitting in a vessel before pressure starts to rise: held, not pushed

cards.q: What is stressed volume, and why does it matter?
cards.a: Volume above the unstressed volume; only it generates the pressure that drives return to the heart

cards.q: What does sympathetic venoconstriction do to venous blood volume?
cards.a: Converts unstressed volume → stressed volume (creates no blood)
cards.more: Squeezing the reservoir lets the same total volume generate more filling pressure: the body mobilises a transfusion from its own veins in seconds. Expect it as the answer to ‘what raised venous return without adding volume’.

cards.q: Why can the heart beat without any nerve telling it to?
cards.a: It contains cells that depolarise on their own; the fastest sets the rate

cards.q: Where does the cardiac impulse normally start?
cards.a: Sinoatrial (SA) node, in the right atrium

cards.q: What is the normal conduction pathway of the cardiac impulse?
cards.a: SA node → internodal tracts (atria) → atrioventricular (AV) node → bundle of His → right and left bundle branches → Purkinje fibres

cards.q: Which pathway carries the impulse from the right atrium to the left atrium?
cards.a: Bachmann’s bundle

cards.q: Into which fascicles does the left bundle branch split?
cards.a:
Anterior
Posterior
Septal

cards.q: What does the atrioventricular (AV) node deliberately do to the impulse?
cards.a: Slows it down (the AV delay)

cards.q: Why does the AV-node delay matter?
cards.a: Lets the atria finish emptying into the ventricles before the ventricles contract
cards.more: If atria and ventricles contracted together, the atria would squeeze against closed valves and achieve nothing. The AV delay is what makes the atrial kick useful.

cards.q: Why do the Purkinje fibres conduct so fast?
cards.a: So the whole ventricle contracts almost at once, not in a ripple

cards.q: What is conduction velocity?
cards.a: The speed at which the action potential travels

cards.q: Which cardiac tissue conducts fastest, and at what speed?
cards.a: Purkinje fibres: 2–4 m/s

cards.q: Which cardiac tissue conducts slowest, and at what speed?
cards.a: AV node: 0.01–0.03 m/s

cards.q: Rank cardiac conduction velocity, fastest to slowest.
cards.a: Purkinje fibres → atrial and ventricular muscle → AV node
cards.more: Both extremes are deliberate: the slow node buys the atrial kick; the fast Purkinje network makes the ventricle contract as one unit.

cards.q: What two things determine cardiac conduction velocity?
cards.a:
Size of the inward current during the upstroke
Cable properties (membrane and internal resistance)

cards.q: Why does a bigger inward current speed conduction?
cards.a: Steeper upstroke (larger dV/dt) → next patch of membrane reaches threshold sooner

cards.q: Does high or low membrane resistance favour conduction, and why?
cards.a: High: keeps current from leaking out
cards.more: Like the wall of a tunnel.

cards.q: Does high or low internal resistance favour conduction, and why?
cards.a: Low: lets current flow along the fibre
cards.more: Like a road with no traffic.

cards.q: What keeps internal resistance low between cardiac cells?
cards.a: Gap junctions

cards.q: Name the conditions in which cardiac conduction is abnormally fast.
cards.a:
Atrial fibrillation and flutter
Supraventricular tachycardia
Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome

cards.q: What is the defect in Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome?
cards.a: Extra pathway lets the impulse reach the ventricles without the AV-node delay
cards.more: It is a pre-excitation syndrome.

cards.q: What are the two kinds of electrical cell in the heart?
cards.a:
Pacemaker cells (SA and AV node)
Working muscle cells (atrial and ventricular)

cards.q: What makes pacemaker cells automatic?
cards.a: No stable resting potential: they leak slowly up to threshold, fire, and repeat
cards.more: Changing the slope of that leak changes heart rate.

cards.q: In the SA node, phase 4 drifts from what voltage up to what threshold?
cards.a: About −65 mV → threshold about −45 mV

cards.q: What actually sets heart rate at the SA node?
cards.a: How long the cell takes to get from −65 to −45 mV (phase 4)
cards.more: Phase 4 is heart rate.

cards.q: What current drives SA-node phase 4?
cards.a: Funny current, I<sub>f</sub>: an inward sodium current

cards.q: When does the funny current (I<sub>f</sub>) switch on and off?
cards.a: On as the previous beat repolarises; off as the cell nears −45 mV

cards.q: What adds to the funny current late in SA-node phase 4?
cards.a: T-type calcium channels

cards.q: What carries the SA-node upstroke (phase 0)?
cards.a: L-type calcium channels (calcium, not sodium)

cards.q: Why is the nodal upstroke slow, and why does the node conduct slowly?
cards.a: Its upstroke is carried by calcium, not sodium

cards.q: What repolarises the SA node (phase 3)?
cards.a: Potassium current (I<sub>K</sub>): potassium out

cards.q: Which phases does a pacemaker-cell action potential have?
cards.a: Only 4, 0 and 3 (no phase 1 or 2, no plateau, no stable rest)
cards.more:
4Slow drift up: sodium-carrying inward current
0Upstroke: calcium
3Repolarisation: potassium out

cards.q: How does sympathetic stimulation raise heart rate at the SA node?
cards.a: Steepens phase 4 → threshold sooner → rate rises

cards.q: How does vagal stimulation lower heart rate at the SA node?
cards.a: Flattens phase 4 → threshold later → rate falls

cards.q: Besides flattening phase 4, how else does acetylcholine slow the SA node?
cards.a: Raises G<sub>K</sub> → potassium leaves → SA node hyperpolarises → each cycle starts further from threshold
cards.more: Through its G protein, acetylcholine opens a special set of potassium channels.

cards.q: What is the heart’s sympathetic receptor?
cards.a: Beta-1 (norepinephrine, epinephrine)

cards.q: What is the heart’s parasympathetic receptor?
cards.a: Muscarinic M2 (acetylcholine)

cards.q: What does beta-1 stimulation do inside the cardiac cell?
cards.a: Stimulates adenylyl cyclase → cyclic AMP (cAMP) up

cards.q: What does M2 stimulation do inside the cardiac cell?
cards.a: Inhibits adenylyl cyclase → cAMP down

cards.q: How do sympathetic and parasympathetic stimulation change the funny current?
cards.a:
Sympathetic: more If, faster leak
Parasympathetic: less If, slower leak

cards.q: What do chronotropic, dromotropic and inotropic refer to?
cards.a:
Chronotropic: heart rate
Dromotropic: AV conduction
Inotropic: contractility

cards.q: What are the sympathetic effects on heart rate, AV conduction and contractility?
cards.a:
Heart rate up
AV conduction faster
Contractility up
cards.more:
SympatheticParasympathetic
ReceptorBeta-1M2
cAMPUpDown
IfMoreLess
RateUpDown
AV conductionFasterSlower
ContractilityUpDown, atria only

cards.q: What are the parasympathetic effects on heart rate, AV conduction and contractility?
cards.a:
Heart rate down
AV conduction slower
Contractility down, atria only

cards.q: How do AV-nodal cells respond to sympathetic and vagal stimulation?
cards.a: Like the SA node: sympathetic speeds their action potentials, vagal slows them

cards.q: How does the speed of AV conduction show on the electrocardiogram (EKG)?
cards.a:
Faster conduction → shorter PR interval
Slower conduction → longer PR interval

cards.q: Do alpha receptors act on the heart?
cards.a: No: the heart’s sympathetic receptor is beta-1

cards.q: Where does alpha-1 act, and what does it do?
cards.a: On vessels: constricts those of skin, kidney, spleen and gut

cards.q: How does parasympathetic stimulation affect the vessels of skin, kidney, spleen and gut?
cards.a: Dilates them through muscarinic (M2) receptors
cards.more: Textbooks place this receptor on the endothelium as M3, which relaxes the vessel by releasing nitric oxide.

cards.q: How does propranolol change the SA-node action potential?
cards.a: Beta-blocker: flattens phase 4 → rate falls

cards.q: How does atropine change the SA-node action potential?
cards.a: Muscarinic blocker: removes the vagal brake → speeds up (shortens) phase 4

cards.q: Which patient is atropine used to treat?
cards.a: Light-headed, hypotensive patient with sinus bradycardia

cards.q: Why can myasthenia gravis treatment (a cholinesterase inhibitor) cause bradycardia?
cards.a: More acetylcholine on the heart → G<sub>K</sub> up → SA node hyperpolarises → bradycardia

cards.q: What is the resting potential of a working (atrial or ventricular) muscle cell?
cards.a: Stable, about −85 to −90 mV (near the potassium equilibrium potential)

cards.q: Why does a working muscle cell rest near the potassium equilibrium potential?
cards.a: Its resting potassium channels are ungated (always open), so potassium dominates the resting membrane
cards.more: Potassium’s Nernst balance of concentration against charge sets the value.

cards.q: Which cells have the five-phase (fast) action potential?
cards.a: Atrial, ventricular and Purkinje cells

cards.q: Phase 0 of the working-cell action potential: what happens and which current?
cards.a: Upstroke: fast sodium in (I<sub>Na</sub>)

cards.q: How high does the working-cell upstroke peak?
cards.a: About +20 mV

cards.q: Why does the working-cell upstroke stop well short of the sodium equilibrium potential (+65 mV)?
cards.a: Sodium inactivation gates close

cards.q: When is the working-cell upstroke steepest, and why?
cards.a: From a more negative resting potential: more sodium channels are ready to open

cards.q: Phase 1 of the working-cell action potential: what happens?
cards.a: Brief dip: sodium channels inactivate; a little potassium out

cards.q: Phase 2 of the working-cell action potential: what happens and which current?
cards.a: Plateau: calcium in through L-type channels (I<sub>Ca-L</sub>), balanced by potassium out
cards.more: L-type = “long-lasting” calcium channel.

cards.q: What does the calcium entering during the phase 2 plateau do?
cards.a: Triggers contraction

cards.q: Which calcium channel blockers block the plateau current (I<sub>Ca-L</sub>)?
cards.a:
Nifedipine
Diltiazem

cards.q: Phase 3 of the working-cell action potential: what happens and which currents?
cards.a: Repolarisation: calcium channels shut, potassium out wins (I<sub>Ks</sub>, I<sub>Kr</sub>, with I<sub>K1</sub>)
cards.more: IKs and IKr are the slow and rapid delayed-rectifier potassium currents.

cards.q: Phase 4 of the working-cell action potential: what happens and which current?
cards.a: Stable rest near the potassium equilibrium potential; I<sub>K1</sub> (inward rectifier)

cards.q: Which ion carries the upstroke in working cells versus nodal cells?
cards.a:
Working cells: sodium
Nodal cells: calcium
cards.more: One-line version: fast cells upstroke on sodium and plateau on calcium. Nodal cells upstroke on calcium and have no plateau at all.

cards.q: How long do cardiac action potentials last, compared with nerve and skeletal muscle?
cards.a: 150 ms (SA node) to 300 ms (Purkinje fibres), versus 1–2 ms

cards.q: What does the long plateau protect the heart against, and why?
cards.a: Tetany: the cell cannot be re-stimulated until it has relaxed
cards.more: The plateau keeps the cell depolarised and refractory for a long time. A heart that could tetanise would stop pumping.

cards.q: Besides preventing tetany, what two things does the plateau buy time for?
cards.a:
Ventricle to empty
Wave to reach every cell

cards.q: What is excitability?
cards.a: The current needed to reach threshold (how easily the sodium activation gates open)

cards.q: Why is a depolarised cardiac cell refractory?
cards.a: Depolarisation closes the slower sodium inactivation gates; while closed, the cell is refractory

cards.q: What does the absolute refractory period (ARP) span, and when does it end?
cards.a: Upstroke, plateau and most of repolarisation; ends below about −50 mV

cards.q: Why can no stimulus of any size fire the cell during the absolute refractory period?
cards.a: Sodium channels are inactivated and must be reset by repolarisation

cards.q: What is the effective refractory period (ERP)?
cards.a: A little longer than the ARP: no action potential that can propagate can be produced

cards.q: What can fire the cell during the relative refractory period, and why?
cards.a: A stronger-than-normal stimulus: some sodium channels have recovered
cards.more: The result is a smaller, slower action potential.

cards.q: What sets the length of the cardiac refractory period?
cards.a: The plateau
cards.more: Anything that lengthens the plateau lengthens refractoriness and protects against re-entry.

cards.q: What are latent pacemakers?
cards.a: Downstream conduction structures that can fire on their own, slower the further down
cards.more: They are why a heart with a dead SA node still beats, just inadequately.

cards.q: Why does the SA node normally set the heart rate?
cards.a: It fires fastest

cards.q: What takes over if the SA node fails?
cards.a: AV node (slower) → then the ventricle itself (slower still)

cards.q: What is the intrinsic rate of the SA node?
cards.a: 60–100 per minute
cards.more: SA node 60–100 → AV node 40–60 → bundle of His ~40 → Purkinje 20–30. Exact numbers vary; the order never changes.

cards.q: What is the intrinsic rate of the AV node?
cards.a: 40–60 per minute

cards.q: What is the intrinsic rate of the bundle of His?
cards.a: About 40 per minute

cards.q: What is the intrinsic rate of the Purkinje fibres?
cards.a: 20–30 per minute

cards.q: What does the EKG record?
cards.a: The whole heart’s electrical activity from the skin: the sum, not one cell’s action potential

cards.q: What is the difference between an EKG interval and a segment?
cards.a:
Interval includes a wave
Segment is the flat stretch between waves

cards.q: What does the P wave represent?
cards.a: Atrial depolarisation

cards.q: Why is there no EKG wave for atrial repolarisation?
cards.a: It is buried in the QRS

cards.q: What does the PR interval span and contain?
cards.a: Start of P → start of QRS: atrial depolarisation + AV nodal delay (mostly the delay)

cards.q: What is the normal PR interval?
What does the PR segment (end of P to start of QRS) represent?
cards.a: The AV-node delay itself

cards.q: What does the QRS complex represent?
cards.a: Ventricular depolarisation

cards.q: What is the normal QRS duration?
cards.a: Under 0.12 s

cards.q: Why is the QRS narrow normally but wide in some rhythms?
cards.a:
Narrow: travels down the Purkinje system
Wide: spreads muscle-to-muscle instead

cards.q: What is the J point?
cards.a: Where the QRS ends and the ST segment begins

cards.q: What does the ST segment represent?
cards.a: Whole ventricle depolarised at once: the plateau
cards.more: Flat normally; shifts with ischaemia.

cards.q: What does the T wave represent?
cards.a: Ventricular repolarisation

cards.q: What is the small wave that sometimes follows the T wave?
cards.a: U wave

cards.q: What does the QT interval span and contain?
cards.a: Start of QRS → end of T: the entire ventricular action potential
cards.more: Long QT means a long, unstable plateau.

cards.q: Which EKG interval do AV-node problems change?
cards.a: PR interval (it contains the AV node)

cards.q: What do bundle-branch problems do to the EKG?
cards.a: Widen the QRS (it contains the ventricular spread)

cards.q: Which EKG interval do plateau and potassium problems stretch?
cards.a: QT interval (it contains repolarisation)

cards.q: What do rate and rhythm on an EKG strip come from?
cards.a:
Rate: spacing (further apart = slower)
Rhythm: regularity, and whether every P is followed by a QRS

cards.q: How do you get heart rate from large boxes between two R waves?
cards.a: 300 ÷ number of large boxes

cards.q: What heart rates go with 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 large boxes between R waves?
How long is one large EKG box at standard paper speed?
What is heart rate in terms of the R-to-R interval?
cards.a: Rate = 60 ÷ R-to-R interval (s)

cards.q: What are the EKG features of sinus bradycardia?
cards.a: Under 60/min, regular, identical P before every QRS, PR 0.12–0.20 s, QRS under 0.12 s
cards.more: A normal rhythm that is simply slow.

cards.q: In atrial fibrillation, where is the defect?
cards.a: Internodal pathways (SA node and internodal pathways stop working in an orderly way)

cards.q: Who is the classic atrial fibrillation patient?
cards.a: Long-standing hypertension with a cardiomyopathy

cards.q: How fast do the atria fire in atrial fibrillation?
cards.a: 350–650 per minute

cards.q: What are the EKG features of atrial fibrillation?
cards.a: No P waves (fibrillatory baseline), no PR interval, narrow QRS at irregular intervals
cards.more: The ventricular rate can be slow or rapid.

cards.q: In atrial fibrillation with a rapid rate (over 100), where do the drugs act and which drugs?
cards.a: AV node: beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, digoxin
cards.more: All slow AV conduction, so fewer atrial impulses reach the ventricles.

cards.q: What is the fastest way to convert atrial fibrillation to sinus rhythm?
cards.a: Electrical cardioversion (a shock)

cards.q: What are the atrial waves of atrial flutter, and at what rate?
cards.a: Regular sawtooth flutter waves, 220–430 per minute

cards.q: What are the ventricular rate and QRS in atrial flutter?
cards.a: Under 300/min, regular or variable; narrow QRS

cards.q: How is atrial flutter slowed?
cards.a: At the AV node, by beta-1 blockade

cards.q: What are the EKG features of ventricular tachycardia?
cards.a: Fast, regular, wide complexes, no visible P waves

cards.q: Why are the complexes wide in ventricular tachycardia?
cards.a: Beat starts in the ventricle (Purkinje fibres) and spreads slowly muscle cell to muscle cell, outside the fast pathway

cards.q: What are the EKG features of ventricular fibrillation?
cards.a: No countable rate: chaotic waves, no recognisable QRS
cards.more: The ventricles quiver and pump nothing.

cards.q: If the AV delay is long but every beat still gets through, what does the EKG show?
cards.a: Prolonged PR interval

cards.q: If some atrial beats fail to get through the AV node, what does the EKG show?
cards.a: P waves without a following QRS

cards.q: If no atrial beats get through the AV node, what happens?
cards.a: Atria and ventricles beat independently; ventricle falls back on a latent pacemaker (slow but alive)

cards.q: What is re-entry?
cards.a: A region recovers excitability before the wave has finished → wave re-enters tissue it passed → self-sustaining loop
cards.more: The basis of the fast, disorganised rhythms.

cards.q: What defends against re-entry, and what does that mean for anti-arrhythmic drugs?
cards.a: A long refractory period; drugs that lengthen refractoriness are anti-arrhythmic

cards.q: What three things determine stroke volume?
cards.a:
Preload
Afterload
Contractility
cards.more: Every drug and disease in this block acts on one of them. Expect to be given a change and asked which of the three moved.

cards.q: What is preload?
cards.a: How full the ventricle is before it contracts: end-diastolic volume (the stretch)

cards.q: What largely sets preload?
cards.a: Venous return

cards.q: What is afterload?
cards.a: What the ventricle pushes against: arterial pressure (aortic pressure for the left ventricle)

cards.q: What is contractility?
cards.a: How hard the muscle squeezes at any given stretch

cards.q: What sets contractility?
cards.a: Sympathetic drive and calcium handling

cards.q: What is the Frank-Starling mechanism?
cards.a: The more you fill the ventricle, the harder it contracts (bigger end-diastolic volume → bigger stroke volume)
cards.more: Automatic: no nerves or hormones involved.

cards.q: What is the calcium part of the Frank-Starling mechanism?
cards.a: Stretched cell releases more calcium from its internal store per beat, and troponin binds calcium more readily

cards.q: Why is the Frank-Starling mechanism so useful?
cards.a: Keeps the outputs of the two sides of the heart matched automatically
cards.more: If the right ventricle sends more blood to the lungs, more returns to the left, stretching it more, so it ejects more.

cards.q: At what sarcomere length is tension greatest?
cards.a: About 2.2 µm (best actin–myosin overlap)

cards.q: Why does tension fall when the sarcomere is shorter or longer than 2.2 µm?
cards.a:
Shorter: filaments crowd into each other
Longer: they overlap less

cards.q: Where does the normal ventricle work relative to the optimal sarcomere length, and so what does extra filling do?
cards.a: Below it: extra filling stretches sarcomeres toward 2.2 µm → stronger next beat

cards.q: What happens to stroke volume when a dilated, failing ventricle is overstretched?
cards.a: Falls (sarcomeres pushed past the optimum)

cards.q: What is the passive (diastolic) ventricular pressure–volume curve?
cards.a: Pressure from just stretching the relaxed ventricle as it fills

cards.q: What is the active (systolic) ventricular pressure–volume curve?
cards.a: Pressure the ventricle can develop when it contracts from each filling volume
cards.more: It climbs steeply with end-diastolic volume; that climb is the Frank-Starling mechanism.

cards.q: What is the difference between preload and contractility?
cards.a:
Preload: how stretched the muscle is
Contractility: how forcefully it contracts at that stretch

cards.q: What does sympathetic stimulation do to stroke volume at the same filling volume?
cards.a: Raises it (raises contractility)

cards.q: How does digoxin change contractility?
cards.a: Raises it, by raising intracellular calcium

cards.q: On a Frank-Starling graph, what does extra filling do?
cards.a: Moves the heart along one curve

cards.q: On a Frank-Starling graph, what does a change in contractility do?
cards.a: Shifts the whole curve

cards.q: What shifts the Frank-Starling curve up?
cards.a:
Dobutamine
Digoxin
Sympathetic stimulation

cards.q: What shifts the Frank-Starling curve down?
cards.a: Systolic dysfunction (the weak ventricle of congestive heart failure, CHF)

cards.q: How are cardiac muscle cells shaped and joined?
cards.a: Short and branched, joined end to end by intercalated discs

cards.q: What do desmosomes do in the intercalated disc?
cards.a: Hold neighbouring cells together

cards.q: What do gap junctions do in the intercalated disc?
cards.a: Pass the action potential straight from one cell to the next

cards.q: What is the sequence of cardiac excitation-contraction coupling?
cards.a: Action potential → calcium enters during plateau → calcium-induced calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) → calcium binds troponin C → cross-bridge cycling → tension

cards.q: What is the trigger step of cardiac excitation-contraction coupling?
cards.a: Action potential runs down T tubules → opens L-type calcium channels → small calcium entry during the plateau

cards.q: Which drugs act on the L-type calcium channels of the trigger step, and how?
cards.a:
Calcium channel blockers block them
Beta agonists open them further

cards.q: Is the calcium entering during the plateau enough to contract the cell?
cards.a: No: its job is to trigger release of a much larger internal store
cards.more: Calcium amplifying calcium.

cards.q: What is calcium-induced calcium release?
cards.a: Trigger calcium opens the ryanodine receptors of the SR, releasing stored calcium

cards.q: What is a calcium spark?
cards.a: One local SR calcium release; sparks add up to the cell-wide calcium signal

cards.q: What does released calcium bind to cause contraction, and what follows?
cards.a: Troponin C → tropomyosin moves aside → actin and myosin engage

cards.q: When does cardiac relaxation start?
cards.a: When calcium comes off troponin

cards.q: What clears calcium after a beat?
cards.a:
SERCA (SR Ca2+-ATPase): pumps it into the SR
Na+/Ca2+ exchanger: moves it out of the cell
cards.more: The Na+/K+-ATPase maintains the sodium gradient that drives the exchanger.

cards.q: Is cardiac relaxation passive or active?
cards.a: Active: costs ATP
cards.more: Nothing relaxes passively.

cards.q: How long is the cardiac muscle refractory period, and why does that matter?
cards.a: About 250 ms, nearly as long as the contraction, so the cell can’t be re-excited until it is relaxing

cards.q: What does the force of a cardiac beat track?
cards.a: How much calcium reaches troponin
cards.more: Anything that raises it raises contractility; anything that lowers it lowers contractility.

cards.q: What lowers contractility by lowering the calcium reaching troponin?
cards.a:
Ischaemia
Acidosis

cards.q: What is the sympathetic signalling chain that raises contractility?
cards.a: Norepinephrine/epinephrine → β<sub>1</sub> → G<sub>s</sub> → adenylyl cyclase → cAMP → protein kinase A (PKA)

cards.q: Which four targets does protein kinase A phosphorylate in cardiac muscle?
cards.a:
L-type calcium channels
Ryanodine receptors
Phospholamban
Troponin I

cards.q: What does PKA phosphorylation of L-type calcium channels achieve?
cards.a: More trigger calcium enters, so more is released

cards.q: What does phospholamban normally do?
cards.a: Brakes SERCA

cards.q: What does phosphorylating phospholamban achieve?
cards.a: Removes the brake on SERCA → faster SR calcium reuptake (quicker relaxation) + more stored (stronger next beat)

cards.q: What does phosphorylating troponin I achieve?
cards.a: Troponin lets go of calcium sooner → faster relaxation

cards.q: What three changes in the contraction result from sympathetic stimulation?
cards.a:
Faster rate of tension development
Higher peak tension
Faster rate of relaxation

cards.q: Why does quicker relaxation help the heart?
cards.a: Shortens each contraction, leaving more time to fill

cards.q: What is the parasympathetic signalling chain that lowers contractility?
cards.a: Acetylcholine → M<sub>2</sub> → G<sub>i</sub> inhibits adenylyl cyclase → less cAMP

cards.q: What is the parasympathetic effect on contractility, and where?
cards.a: Negative inotropy in the atria: slower tension development, lower peak tension

cards.q: Why are the ventricles barely affected by parasympathetic stimulation?
cards.a: Ventricular muscle gets little vagal innervation

cards.q: What is the positive staircase (Bowditch, treppe) effect?
cards.a: Faster heart rate → tension climbs beat by beat to a stronger new plateau

cards.q: Why does a faster heart beat more strongly?
cards.a: More beats/min → more calcium enters per minute → SR stores more → more to release each beat

cards.q: What is postextrasystolic potentiation?
cards.a: The beat after an extrasystole is stronger than normal

cards.q: Why is the beat after an extrasystole stronger?
cards.a: The extra beat brings in extra calcium that the SR stores

cards.q: How strong is the extrasystole itself?
cards.a: Weaker than normal

cards.q: What drug class is digoxin, and which drugs share it?
cards.a: Cardiac glycosides, with digitoxin and ouabain

cards.q: Where do most cardiac glycosides come from, and since when?
cards.a: Foxglove (Digitalis purpurea, D. lanata); in use since 1785

cards.q: What does digoxin block?
cards.a: The sodium-potassium pump (Na<sup>+</sup>/K<sup>+</sup>-ATPase)

cards.q: How does digoxin raise contractility?
cards.a: Pump blocked → sodium in high → Na<sup>+</sup>/Ca<sup>2+</sup> exchanger stalls → calcium in high → stronger contraction
cards.more: Any question about this drug is a question about one of those four links.

cards.q: Why does high intracellular sodium stall the Na<sup>+</sup>/Ca<sup>2+</sup> exchanger?
cards.a: The exchanger needs a steep sodium gradient to drive calcium out
cards.more: Calcium then builds up in the cell and the SR, and more reaches troponin.

cards.q: What are the uses of digoxin?
cards.a:
Slow heart rate in rapid atrial arrhythmias (atrial fibrillation, flutter, SVT)
CHF still symptomatic after an ACE inhibitor, beta-blocker and spironolactone
cards.more: SVT = supraventricular tachycardia; ACE = angiotensin-converting enzyme.

cards.q: What are the toxic effects of digoxin?
cards.a:
Arrhythmias
Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea
Seizures
Visual disturbances

cards.q: Why does low potassium cause digoxin toxicity?
cards.a: Digoxin binds the pump at its K<sup>+</sup> site; less K<sup>+</sup> competing → more digoxin binds

cards.q: Why does digoxin toxicity cause high potassium?
cards.a: Pump blocked → K<sup>+</sup> not pumped back into cells → builds up in plasma

cards.q: What does a higher afterload do to ejection?
cards.a: The harder the ventricle has to push, the less it ejects

cards.q: What happens to a ventricle facing high afterload over time, and give two causes?
cards.a:
It thickens
Causes: severe hypertension, tight aortic valve

cards.q: What is stroke volume (SV), and its formula?
cards.a: Amount ejected per beat: SV = EDV − ESV
cards.more: EDV = end-diastolic volume; ESV = end-systolic volume.

cards.q: What is ejection fraction (EF), and its formula?
cards.a: Fraction of the filled volume ejected: EF = SV ÷ EDV

cards.q: What is the normal ejection fraction?
cards.a: About 55–70%
cards.more: The standard measure of how well the pump is working.

cards.q: What is the formula for cardiac output (CO)?
cards.a: CO = SV × HR (heart rate)

cards.q: A left ventricle fills to 120 mL and empties to 50 mL: what are SV and EF?
cards.a: SV = 70 mL; EF ≈ 58%

cards.q: In the steady state, what does cardiac output equal, and why?
cards.a: Venous return: the ventricle can only eject what comes back to it

cards.q: What sets heart rate?
cards.a: Autonomic nerves, hormones, and the atrial reflex
cards.more: Atrial reflex: venous return stretching the atria speeds the heart.

cards.q: What sets end-diastolic volume (EDV)?
cards.a: Venous return and filling time (preload)

cards.q: What sets end-systolic volume (ESV)?
cards.a: Contractility (autonomic nerves, hormones) and afterload (vasoconstriction or vasodilation)

cards.q: What does a pressure–volume (PV) loop show?
cards.a: One heartbeat: ventricular volume on the x-axis, pressure on the y-axis

cards.q: Which direction does time run around a pressure–volume loop?
cards.a: Anticlockwise

cards.q: Which four things can you read off a pressure–volume loop at once?
cards.a:
Preload
Afterload
Contractility
Stroke volume

cards.q: Name the four phases of the pressure–volume loop in order, starting with filling.
cards.a: Filling → isovolumetric contraction → ejection → isovolumetric relaxation

cards.q: During ventricular filling, which valve is open, and what happens on the pressure–volume loop?
cards.a: Mitral valve open; volume rises along the bottom at low pressure

cards.q: What event ends ventricular filling (the bottom-right corner of the pressure–volume loop)?
cards.a: End-diastole: ventricle starts to contract → mitral valve closes

cards.q: What is the normal end-diastolic volume (EDV), and which determinant does it represent?
cards.a: About 120 mL; the preload

cards.q: During isovolumetric contraction, what are the valves doing and what happens to pressure and volume?
cards.a: Both valves shut; pressure rises straight up, volume unchanged
cards.more: The ventricle squeezes but nothing can leave. This is the vertical right-hand side of the loop.

cards.q: What ends isovolumetric contraction, and at about what pressure?
cards.a: Left ventricular pressure exceeds aortic pressure (about 80 mm Hg) → aortic valve opens

cards.q: During ejection, what happens on the pressure–volume loop?
cards.a: Aortic valve open; volume falls as blood leaves

cards.q: What ends ejection, and at about what pressure?
cards.a: End-systole (about 120 mm Hg): aortic pressure exceeds ventricular pressure → aortic valve closes

cards.q: What is the normal end-systolic volume (ESV)?
cards.a: About 50 mL

cards.q: During isovolumetric relaxation, what are the valves doing and what happens to pressure and volume?
cards.a: Both valves shut; pressure drops straight down at constant volume

cards.q: What ends isovolumetric relaxation and starts filling again?
cards.a: Ventricular pressure falls below left atrial pressure → mitral valve opens

cards.q: On an unfamiliar pressure–volume loop, what do the two vertical sides (no volume change) tell you?
cards.a: Both valves are closed
cards.more: Whenever volume is not changing, both valves are shut: the quickest way to orient yourself on a loop.

cards.q: Which dimension of the pressure–volume loop is the stroke volume?
cards.a: The width (end-diastolic − end-systolic volume)
cards.more: Anything that makes the loop wider has increased stroke volume.

cards.q: Calculate the stroke volume when end-diastolic volume is 120 mL and end-systolic volume is 50 mL.
cards.a: 120 − 50 = 70 mL
cards.more: Costanzo’s loop uses 140 and 70 mL: the stroke volume is the same 70 mL.

cards.q: How is ejection fraction (EF) defined?
cards.a: Stroke volume ÷ end-diastolic volume
cards.more: Stroke volume as a proportion of the volume the beat started with. A normal heart ejects rather more than half of what it filled with.

cards.q: Calculate the ejection fraction for a stroke volume of 70 mL and an end-diastolic volume of 120 mL. What is normal?
cards.a:
70/120 = 58%
Normal 55–70%

cards.q: With a stroke volume of 70 mL at 70–80 beats per minute, what is the cardiac output?
cards.a: 4,900–5,600 mL/min

cards.q: How does increased preload change the pressure–volume loop?
cards.a: Right-hand edge moves right (more filling) → wider loop

cards.q: How does increased afterload change the pressure–volume loop, and why?
cards.a: Taller and narrower: higher pressure needed before ejecting → less ejected

cards.q: How does increased contractility change the pressure–volume loop?
cards.a: Left-hand edge moves left (empties further) → wider loop

cards.q: Which line on the pressure–volume loop reflects contractility, and how is it read?
cards.a: End-systolic pressure–volume relationship (ESPVR), through the top-left corner; steeper = stronger ventricle

cards.q: What is the physical rule of thumb for how preload, afterload and contractility change the loop?
cards.a:
More filling → wider
Harder to push against → narrower
Stronger squeeze → empties further

cards.q: A loop is wider than normal. How do you tell whether preload or contractility caused it?
cards.a: Position: shifted left = contractility (emptied better); shifted right = preload (filled more)

cards.q: What is the formula for left ventricular stroke work?
cards.a: Stroke volume × aortic pressure

cards.q: Which part of the pressure–volume loop represents the work done on the blood that beat?
cards.a: The area enclosed by the loop

cards.q: If blood pressure stays the same, how does more preload change cardiac work?
cards.a: More preload → more stroke volume → more output → more work

cards.q: Trace the chain from more cardiac work to clinical harm.
cards.a: More work → more myocardial O<sub>2</sub> consumption → more ischemia → more arrhythmia and death

cards.q: Which costs more O<sub>2</sub>: pressure work or volume work?
cards.a: Pressure work
cards.more: Ejecting the same 70 mL against a higher pressure is the expensive kind of work, like a small heavy box being harder to carry than a big empty one.

cards.q: Why is increased afterload “more work for less reward”?
cards.a: Taller loop (more pressure work) with a smaller stroke volume

cards.q: Why is angina the number-one symptom of aortic stenosis?
cards.a: Ventricle must generate very high pressures → O<sub>2</sub> demand outruns supply
cards.more: Aortic stenosis is the extreme case of pressure (afterload) work.

cards.q: Why does afterload reduction (vasodilation) help in congestive heart failure (CHF)?
cards.a: Less work → less O<sub>2</sub> consumed
cards.more: The same reasoning explains why high blood pressure harms.

cards.q: Which drug class lowers afterload and lowers mortality in congestive heart failure?
cards.a: Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors

cards.q: Does digoxin lower afterload or mortality in congestive heart failure?
cards.a: Neither; it raises contractility

cards.q: State the law of Laplace for ventricular wall tension.
cards.a:
T = P × r
T = (P × r) ÷ wall thickness
cards.more: T = wall tension, P = pressure, r = radius.

cards.q: Why does a dilated ventricle have more wall tension at the same pressure?
cards.a: Larger radius; tension rises with radius

cards.q: How does lowering ventricular pressure affect a dilated ventricle?
cards.a: Lowers wall tension → further dilation less likely

cards.q: What happens to wall tension when wall thickness doubles?
cards.a: It halves

cards.q: Why does a ventricle pumping against high pressure hypertrophy?
cards.a: A thicker wall lowers wall tension

cards.q: How does Costanzo write the law of Laplace for a sphere?
cards.a: P = 2HT/r (H = wall thickness)
cards.more: Same relationships as T = P × r ÷ thickness, plus a factor of 2.

cards.q: State the Fick principle for cardiac output (CO).
cards.a: CO = O<sub>2</sub> consumption ÷ ([O<sub>2</sub>]<sub>pulmonary vein</sub> − [O<sub>2</sub>]<sub>pulmonary artery</sub>)

cards.q: In the Fick calculation, which blood has the lowest O<sub>2</sub> saturation, and why?
cards.a: Pulmonary artery blood: it is mixed venous blood

cards.q: In the Fick calculation, which blood has the highest O<sub>2</sub> saturation?
cards.a: Pulmonary vein blood

cards.q: Which blood has even lower O<sub>2</sub> than pulmonary artery blood?
cards.a: Coronary sinus blood (drains the heart muscle)

cards.q: How much O<sub>2</sub> does each gram of hemoglobin carry?
cards.a: 1.34 mL O<sub>2</sub>

cards.q: What is the O<sub>2</sub> content of fully saturated blood with 15 g hemoglobin per 100 mL?
cards.a: About 20 mL O<sub>2</sub> per 100 mL
cards.more: Fully saturated = all four binding sites filled.

cards.q: What are the saturation and O<sub>2</sub> content of venous blood?
cards.a: About 75% (three of four sites); about 15 mL O<sub>2</sub> per 100 mL

cards.q: Calculate cardiac output: O<sub>2</sub> consumption 250 mL/min, arterial 20 and venous 15 mL O<sub>2</sub> per 100 mL.
cards.a: 250 ÷ (0.20 − 0.15) = 5,000 mL/min

cards.q: What is the Wiggers diagram?
cards.a: The cardiac cycle against time: pressures, ventricular volume, heart sounds, venous pulse and ECG stacked
cards.more: The same beat as the pressure–volume loop, drawn against time instead of volume. ECG = electrocardiogram.

cards.q: On the Wiggers diagram, what do you use as the clock?
cards.a: The electrocardiogram (ECG): P wave (atria depolarize) → QRS (ventricles)

cards.q: List the seven phases of the cardiac cycle in order.
cards.a: Atrial systole → isovolumetric contraction → rapid ejection → reduced ejection → isovolumetric relaxation → rapid filling → reduced filling (diastasis)
cards.more:
PhaseValves/soundsMarkers
Atrial systoleS4 if stiff ventricleAfter P; a wave
Isovol. contractionAV valves close: S1With QRS; c wave
Rapid, reduced ejectionAortic valve opensVolume falls; T wave in reduced
Isovol. relaxationSemilunar close: S2; dicrotic notchAfter T
Rapid fillingMitral opens; S3v wave peaks
Diastasis—Longest; shortens first

cards.q: Atrial systole: which heart sound (if present) and which venous pulse wave?
cards.a: S4 (if the ventricle is stiff); a wave (after the P wave)

cards.q: Isovolumetric contraction: which valves close, which sound, and which markers?
cards.a: Atrioventricular (AV) valves close → S1; starts with the QRS; c wave

cards.q: During ejection, which valve opens, and where does the T wave fall?
cards.a: Aortic valve opens; T wave during reduced ejection
cards.more: Ventricular volume falls through rapid, then reduced, ejection.

cards.q: Isovolumetric relaxation: which valves close, which sound, and what aortic pressure marker?
cards.a: Semilunar valves close → S2; dicrotic notch on the aortic trace (after the T wave)

cards.q: Rapid filling: which valve opens, which sound (if present), and which venous wave peaks?
cards.a: Mitral valve opens; S3; v wave peaks as the mitral valve opens

cards.q: Which phase of the cardiac cycle is longest and is the first to shorten when heart rate rises?
cards.a: Reduced filling (diastasis)

cards.q: What does S3 represent, and what does it mean in an adult?
cards.a: Rapid ventricular filling; pathologic sign of congestive heart failure (volume overload)
cards.more: It usually means more treatment is needed.

cards.q: What does S4 represent?
cards.a: Atrial systole pushing blood into a stiff, non-compliant ventricle

cards.q: What does S4 point to, and does it need extra therapy?
cards.a: Left ventricular hypertrophy or hypertension; no extra therapy by itself

cards.q: How does aortic stenosis change the pressure–volume loop, and why?
cards.a: Tall and narrower: much higher pressure needed to eject through a narrow opening
cards.more: A pure afterload problem.

cards.q: How does aortic regurgitation change the pressure–volume loop?
cards.a: Wide and shifted right
cards.more: Blood flows back into the ventricle during diastole on top of normal filling, so the ventricle takes a very large volume and ejects a very large stroke volume.

cards.q: Why is there no true isovolumetric relaxation in aortic regurgitation?
cards.a: The aortic valve is leaking throughout

cards.q: How does mitral stenosis change the pressure–volume loop?
cards.a: Small and shifted left: reduced preload, reduced stroke volume
cards.more: Filling is obstructed, so the ventricle cannot take a normal volume.

cards.q: Why is there no true isovolumetric contraction in mitral regurgitation?
cards.a: Blood escapes back into the atrium as soon as the ventricle squeezes → volume falls immediately

cards.q: Why does a leaking valve destroy a vertical side of the pressure–volume loop?
cards.a: The vertical sides exist only because all four valves are shut

cards.q: A pressure–volume loop has lost its vertical contraction side. Which valve is incompetent?
cards.a: Mitral valve

cards.q: A pressure–volume loop has lost its vertical relaxation side. Which valve is incompetent?
cards.a: Aortic valve

cards.q: Which variable do the cardiac function curve and the vascular function curve share on their x-axis?
cards.a: Right atrial pressure (effectively the heart’s filling pressure)

cards.q: Trace the chain from venous return to cardiac output.
cards.a: Venous return → right atrial pressure → left ventricular filling (end-diastolic volume) → stroke volume → × heart rate = cardiac output

cards.q: In the steady state, how does venous return relate to cardiac output?
cards.a: They are equal
cards.more: The heart can only eject what comes back.

cards.q: What does the cardiac function curve show?
cards.a: The more filled the heart (higher right atrial pressure), the more it pumps: Frank-Starling as a graph

cards.q: At about what right atrial pressure does the cardiac function curve level off, and at what maximum output?
cards.a: About 4 mm Hg; about 9 L/min

cards.q: What happens when right atrial pressure rises beyond the cardiac function curve’s plateau?
cards.a: No added output; it only pushes back against venous return

cards.q: What does the vascular function curve show, and which way does it slope?
cards.a: Higher right atrial pressure → less venous return; slopes downward
cards.more: A high back-pressure in the right atrium opposes venous return.

cards.q: Why does the vascular function curve go flat at its left end?
cards.a: Right atrial pressure below zero → veins collapse → no further gain

cards.q: What does the crossing point of the cardiac and vascular function curves represent?
cards.a: The operating point: the heart pumps exactly what the body returns

cards.q: What is the mean systemic filling pressure?
cards.a: The pressure in the circulation with the heart stopped and pressure equalised everywhere
cards.more: Blood is still under pressure because the vessels are elastic and stretched around it.

cards.q: What does mean systemic filling pressure do for venous return?
cards.a: Drives blood back towards the heart

cards.q: Where is mean systemic filling pressure on the vascular function curve?
cards.a: The x-axis intercept

cards.q: What are the only two things that change mean systemic filling pressure?
cards.a:
Blood volume
Venous tone (how tightly the veins hold the blood)

cards.q: How do transfusion, haemorrhage, venoconstriction and venodilatation change mean systemic filling pressure?
cards.a:
Transfusion ↑
Haemorrhage ↓
Venoconstriction ↑
Venodilatation ↓

cards.q: Do heart rate and contractility change mean systemic filling pressure?
cards.a: No; it is a property of the vasculature, not the pump

cards.q: Which kind of change moves the cardiac function curve?
cards.a: A change in the heart’s strength (contractility)
cards.more: The vascular curve stays put.

cards.q: More contractility (e.g. sympathetic drive): what happens to the curves and the new operating point?
cards.a: Cardiac curve shifts up → higher cardiac output, lower right atrial pressure
cards.more: The stronger heart empties the atrium better.

cards.q: Heart failure or a negative inotrope: what happens to the curves and the new operating point?
cards.a: Cardiac curve drops → lower cardiac output, higher right atrial pressure

cards.q: Which kind of change moves the vascular function curve?
cards.a: Blood volume or venous tone

cards.q: Which way do transfusion, haemorrhage and venoconstriction shift the vascular function curve?
cards.a:
Transfusion/fluid overload → right
Haemorrhage → left
Venoconstriction → right

cards.q: Why does venoconstriction shift the vascular function curve to the right?
cards.a: Squeezing the venous reservoir pushes blood towards the heart

cards.q: More blood volume or venoconstriction: what is the new operating point?
cards.a: Higher cardiac output and higher right atrial pressure

cards.q: Haemorrhage or venodilation: what is the new operating point?
cards.a: Lower cardiac output and lower right atrial pressure

cards.q: What is the unstressed volume?
cards.a: Blood that only fills the vessels and produces no pressure; mostly venous
cards.more: Like the water that fills the pipes before any comes out of the tap.

cards.q: Roughly how large is the unstressed volume?
cards.a: About the first 4 L of blood

cards.q: What proportion of blood volume do the veins hold?
cards.a: About 60%

cards.q: What is the stressed volume?
cards.a: Volume above the unstressed volume; mostly arterial; it produces blood pressure

cards.q: How does venoconstriction raise blood pressure?
cards.a: Lowers venous compliance → shifts blood into the stressed volume

cards.q: What does venodilation do to unstressed volume, stressed volume and venous return?
cards.a: Blood pools in veins → unstressed volume ↑ → stressed volume and venous return ↓

cards.q: Name the venodilators.
cards.a:
Nitrates (nitroglycerin, amyl nitrite)
Morphine
Furosemide
Sildenafil
Prostacyclin
cards.more: Sildenafil boosts the nitric oxide pathway.

cards.q: What are the features of acute pulmonary edema?
cards.a:
Sudden breathlessness
Rales
Edema
S3 gallop

cards.q: In acute pulmonary edema, what do a venodilator and a diuretic each do?
cards.a: Venodilator parks blood in the unstressed volume; diuretic removes it
cards.more: The goal is to move volume out of the lungs fast.

cards.q: Which drug works fastest in acute pulmonary edema and raises unstressed volume the most?
cards.a: Nitroglycerin
cards.more: It raises unstressed volume more than an arteriolar dilator (hydralazine), an angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor, an angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB) or a β-blocker.

cards.q: Why does a recruit standing still at attention for an hour become lightheaded and tachycardic?
cards.a: No leg-muscle pump → blood pools in leg veins → venous return and output fall → reflex tachycardia

cards.q: What does raising arteriolar resistance do to cardiac output and venous return?
cards.a: Lowers both: less blood gets round the circuit per minute

cards.q: Which variable moves both the cardiac and vascular function curves, and what mainly sets it?
cards.a: Total peripheral resistance (TPR); set mainly by the arterioles

cards.q: How does higher total peripheral resistance affect the cardiac function curve?
cards.a: Raises afterload → lowers the cardiac curve

cards.q: How does higher total peripheral resistance affect the vascular function curve?
cards.a: Rotates it down around an unchanged x-axis intercept (mean systemic filling pressure)

cards.q: What does lower total peripheral resistance do to the curves and cardiac output?
cards.a: Both curves move up → higher cardiac output

cards.q: What does a diuretic do to the curves and the operating point?
cards.a: Less blood volume → return curve shifts left → lower output, lower right atrial pressure
cards.more:
DiureticVolume ↓ → return curve left → output ↓, right atrial pressure ↓
ACE inhibitor, ARBTPR ↓ → both curves up → output ↑
Digoxin, dobutaminePositive inotropes → cardiac curve up → output ↑, right atrial pressure ↓

cards.q: What do ACE inhibitors and ARBs do to the curves and cardiac output?
cards.a: Lower TPR (arteriolar dilation) → both curves move up → higher output

cards.q: What do digoxin and dobutamine do to the curves and the operating point?
cards.a: Positive inotropes → cardiac curve shifts up → higher output, lower right atrial pressure

cards.q: In congestive heart failure, why can the β<sub>1</sub>-blocker metoprolol raise cardiac output despite slowing the heart?
cards.a: Larger stroke volume more than offsets the slower rate
cards.more: Part of the reason: a slower heart has longer diastoles to fill.

cards.q: What is the conservation logic behind measuring cardiac output from oxygen (Fick)?
cards.a: Cardiac output = O<sub>2</sub> consumed per minute ÷ arteriovenous O<sub>2</sub> content difference
cards.more: All the oxygen consumed must have been carried there by blood, so dividing the consumption by how much each unit of blood gave up gives how much blood went round per minute.

cards.q: What does a wide arteriovenous O<sub>2</sub> difference indicate?
cards.a: Low cardiac output
cards.more: Tissues extracting more O2 per unit of blood, for the same O2 consumption, means less blood flowed.

cards.q: Which pressure does the body defend minute to minute?
cards.a: Mean arterial pressure (MAP)

cards.q: What are the body’s fast and slow systems for holding blood pressure steady?
cards.a:
Fast: baroreceptor reflex (seconds)
Slow: renin-angiotensin-aldosterone (hours to days)

cards.q: Give the equation for mean arterial pressure in terms of cardiac output and resistance.
cards.a: MAP = cardiac output (CO) × total peripheral resistance (TPR)

cards.q: Give the equation for mean arterial pressure from systolic and diastolic pressure.
cards.a: MAP = diastolic + ⅓ pulse pressure (systolic − diastolic)

cards.q: Why does doubling cardiac output not double mean arterial pressure?
cards.a: CO and TPR are not independent: when one changes, the other tends to move the opposite way

cards.q: How does a saline bolus raise pressure in a hypotensive septic patient?
cards.a: ↑ Venous return → ↑ cardiac output → ↑ MAP
cards.more: Volume acts through the cardiac output term.

cards.q: Where are the arterial baroreceptors?
cards.a:
Carotid sinus
Aortic arch
cards.more: They watch the pressure in the vessels feeding the brain.

cards.q: What is the carotid sinus?
cards.a: The dilated bulb at the carotid bifurcation

cards.q: How does baroreceptor firing change with arterial pressure?
cards.a:
Pressure ↑ → more stretch → more firing
Pressure ↓ → less firing

cards.q: Which nerves carry carotid sinus baroreceptor signals to the medulla?
cards.a: Carotid sinus nerve (Hering’s nerve) → glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX)

cards.q: Which nerve carries aortic arch baroreceptor signals?
cards.a: Vagus nerve (CN X)

cards.q: Which medullary nucleus receives baroreceptor input?
cards.a: Nucleus of the solitary tract (nucleus tractus solitarius)
cards.more: It reads the firing rate and responds.

cards.q: Besides baroreceptor input, what does the nucleus tractus solitarius receive from the facial nerve (CN VII)?
cards.a: Taste

cards.q: Name the three medullary centres of the baroreceptor reflex and their outflow.
cards.a:
Cardiac decelerator (cardioinhibitory) → vagus to heart
Cardiac accelerator → sympathetic
Vasoconstrictor (C1) → sympathetic

cards.q: When arterial pressure falls, how does the medulla change autonomic outflow?
cards.a: Receptors fire less → ↑ sympathetic outflow, vagal tone withdrawn

cards.q: Name the four effector responses to a fall in arterial pressure, with their receptors.
cards.a:
Heart rate ↑ (β1)
Contractility ↑ (β1)
Arterioles and veins constrict (α1)
Renin ↑ (β1)

cards.q: What does the baroreceptor reflex do when arterial pressure rises?
cards.a: Receptors fire more → ↑ vagal, ↓ sympathetic → heart rate and contractility ↓; arterioles and veins dilate

cards.q: What do baroreceptors actually sense?
cards.a: Stretch, not pressure directly; change more than absolute level

cards.q: What happens to baroreceptors in chronic hypertension?
cards.a: They reset to defend the new, higher pressure
cards.more: Because they respond to change more than to absolute level, they adapt.

cards.q: Why does standing up not normally make you faint?
cards.a: Blood pools in legs → venous return and pressure dip → baroreceptors fire the sympathetic response within a beat or two

cards.q: What causes orthostatic hypotension?
cards.a: A broken baroreflex arc: autonomic neuropathy, or a drug blocking the vessels’ ability to respond

cards.q: What is the Valsalva manoeuvre?
cards.a: Breathing out hard against a closed glottis, as when bearing down

cards.q: Trace the Valsalva manoeuvre from intrathoracic pressure to heart rate.
cards.a: ↑ Intrathoracic pressure → great veins compressed → venous return ↓ → cardiac output and arterial pressure ↓ → carotid baroreceptors → tachycardia

cards.q: What does the Valsalva manoeuvre do to most murmurs?
cards.a: Makes them quieter (less blood moving through the heart)

cards.q: How does carotid sinus massage slow the heart?
cards.a: Stretches the sinus (mimics a pressure rise) → ↑ CN IX firing → reflex vagal slowing

cards.q: Carotid sinus massage is a first treatment for which arrhythmia?
cards.a: Supraventricular tachycardia

cards.q: How does the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) mainly raise blood pressure?
cards.a: By controlling volume (over hours to days)

cards.q: Which cells release renin?
cards.a: Juxtaglomerular cells

cards.q: What are the three triggers for renin release?
cards.a:
Low renal perfusion (less afferent arteriole stretch)
Low Na+ reaching the macula densa
β1 sympathetic stimulation

cards.q: What does renin do?
cards.a: Converts angiotensinogen → angiotensin I
cards.more: Renin is an enzyme.

cards.q: Where is angiotensinogen made?
cards.a: The liver

cards.q: How active is angiotensin I by itself?
cards.a: Does almost nothing

cards.q: What converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II, and where mainly?
cards.a: Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE), mainly in the lungs

cards.q: What does aldosterone do, and why is it the slow arm?
cards.a: Kidney retains Na<sup>+</sup> and therefore water; slow because it works by making new proteins (hours to days)

cards.q: Put the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone cascade in order, from low pressure to restored pressure.
cards.a: ↓ Renal perfusion → renin: angiotensinogen → angiotensin I → (ACE) angiotensin II → vasoconstriction + aldosterone → Na<sup>+</sup> and water retained → ↑ volume → ↑ pressure

cards.q: Name the five actions of angiotensin II, plus its growth effect.
cards.a:
Arteriolar vasoconstriction
Aldosterone release (adrenal cortex)
↑ Na+ reabsorption in proximal tubule
Antidiuretic hormone (ADH) release from pituitary
Thirst
+ Cardiac and vascular hypertrophy

cards.q: Which renal action of angiotensin II is fast?
cards.a: Direct ↑ Na<sup>+</sup> reabsorption in the proximal tubule

cards.q: Why does angiotensin II’s release of antidiuretic hormone and thirst raise volume?
cards.a: ADH → more water reabsorbed; thirst → more water drunk

cards.q: Why does blocking the renin-angiotensin system help in congestive heart failure (CHF)?
cards.a: Blocks angiotensin II-driven cardiac and vascular hypertrophy

cards.q: Which transporter mediates angiotensin II’s proximal tubule effect?
cards.a: Na<sup>+</sup>/H<sup>+</sup> exchanger: Na<sup>+</sup> into the cell, H<sup>+</sup> into the lumen

cards.q: In the proximal tubule, what happens to the H<sup>+</sup> secreted by the Na<sup>+</sup>/H<sup>+</sup> exchanger?
cards.a: H<sup>+</sup> + filtered HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> → CO<sub>2</sub> + water → CO<sub>2</sub> enters cell → H<sup>+</sup> + HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> → HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> into blood

cards.q: What is the net effect of angiotensin II on the proximal tubule?
cards.a: Na<sup>+</sup> and HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> reabsorbed; no net change in H<sup>+</sup>

cards.q: What is contraction alkalosis, and why does it happen?
cards.a: Low volume → high angiotensin II → bicarbonate retained → metabolic alkalosis
cards.more: Classic case: a marathon runner who has sweated all day in the sun turns up with a metabolic alkalosis.

cards.q: Which drug blocks renin?
cards.a: Aliskiren

cards.q: Where in the cascade do ACE inhibitors act?
cards.a: Block conversion of angiotensin I → angiotensin II

cards.q: Where do angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs, “-sartans”) act?
cards.a: Block angiotensin II at its receptor

cards.q: Which drugs block aldosterone?
cards.a:
Spironolactone
Eplerenone

cards.q: Which renin-angiotensin-aldosterone blockers lower mortality in congestive heart failure?
cards.a:
ACE inhibitors
ARBs
Aldosterone blockers
(not renin inhibition)

cards.q: How do the baroreceptor reflex and RAAS differ in timescale and mechanism?
cards.a:
Baroreceptors: seconds, change tone
RAAS: days, change volume

cards.q: In the first minutes of heavy bleeding, what keeps the brain perfused?
cards.a: Reflex vasoconstriction (baroreceptor reflex)
cards.more: The hormones build up too slowly to be the answer.

cards.q: How do chemoreceptors differ from baroreceptors in what they watch?
cards.a: Chemoreceptors watch blood chemistry; baroreceptors watch pressure

cards.q: Where are the peripheral chemoreceptors?
cards.a: Carotid bodies and near the aortic arch (in the bloodstream)

cards.q: What do peripheral chemoreceptors respond to?
cards.a: Fall in O<sub>2</sub>; also rising CO<sub>2</sub> and falling pH

cards.q: Why are peripheral chemoreceptors a late warning rather than a fine control?
cards.a: They only fire strongly once O<sub>2</sub> has fallen a good way

cards.q: Where are the central chemoreceptors, and what bathes them?
cards.a: Brainstem; cerebrospinal fluid (not blood)

cards.q: What do central chemoreceptors respond to?
cards.a: CO<sub>2</sub>: strictly the pH change it causes after crossing into cerebrospinal fluid
cards.more: They are much less sensitive to O2.

cards.q: Which chemoreceptors are the dominant minute-to-minute controllers of breathing?
cards.a: Central chemoreceptors

cards.q: Which chemoreceptors mediate hypoxic drive?
cards.a: Peripheral chemoreceptors only
cards.more: Central = the CO2 sensor that barely sees O2; peripheral = the O2 sensor that can also see CO2.

cards.q: What vital-sign combination is the signature of raised intracranial pressure?
cards.a: High blood pressure with a slow pulse
cards.more: The one place where hypertension and bradycardia belong together.

cards.q: Why does raised intracranial pressure cause hypertension with bradycardia?
cards.a: Compressed cerebral vessels → brain ischemia → sympathetic surge → high arterial pressure → baroreceptors slow the heart

cards.q: Where are the low-pressure stretch receptors, and what do they report?
cards.a: Atria and great veins; filling, not arterial pressure

cards.q: What do the atria do when stretched by a volume load?
