cards.a: Release a peptide → salt and water loss + vessel relaxation

cards.q: How does the atrial stretch response relate to the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system?
cards.a: Opposes it: RAAS retains volume when pressure falls; atrial peptide dumps volume when filling rises

cards.q: Why are capillaries ideal for exchange?
cards.a: One cell thick + enormously numerous → huge surface area and very slow flow
cards.more: Capillaries are where the circulation justifies itself: everything else exists to get blood here.

cards.q: What property of a substance decides how it crosses the capillary wall?
cards.a: Whether it dissolves in lipid

cards.q: How do oxygen and carbon dioxide cross the capillary wall?
cards.a: Diffuse straight through the endothelial cells (lipid-soluble) — fast

cards.q: What sets the rate at which oxygen and carbon dioxide diffuse across capillaries?
cards.a:
Partial-pressure difference
Surface area of open capillaries

cards.q: How do water-soluble substances (water, ions, glucose, amino acids) cross the capillary wall?
cards.a: Between the cells, through water-filled clefts — more slowly
cards.more: They cannot cross cell membranes, so they must go between the endothelial cells.

cards.q: How many pressures govern fluid movement across the capillary wall, and how do they split?
cards.a: Four: two favour filtration, two favour reabsorption
cards.more: Only two really matter day to day: capillary hydrostatic and plasma oncotic pressure.

cards.q: What is capillary hydrostatic pressure, and which way does it move fluid?
cards.a: Blood pressure inside the capillary → pushes fluid out

cards.q: What is plasma oncotic pressure, and which way does it move fluid?
cards.a: Pull of plasma proteins (mainly albumin) → draws fluid back in
cards.more: The proteins are too big to leak out, so they stay in the capillary and pull.

cards.q: Which way does interstitial hydrostatic pressure move fluid across the capillary wall?
cards.a: Pushes it back into the capillary

cards.q: Which way does interstitial oncotic pressure move fluid across the capillary wall?
cards.a: Pulls it out of the capillary

cards.q: Name the two Starling pressures that favour filtration.
cards.a:
Capillary hydrostatic (Pc)
Interstitial oncotic (πi)

cards.q: Name the two Starling pressures that favour reabsorption.
cards.a:
Plasma (capillary) oncotic (πc)
Interstitial hydrostatic (Pi)

cards.q: What happens to fluid at the arterial end of a capillary, and why?
cards.a: Filters out into the tissue — hydrostatic pressure wins

cards.q: What happens to fluid at the venous end of a capillary, and why?
cards.a: Most is reabsorbed — hydrostatic pressure has fallen, oncotic pressure has not
cards.more: Hydrostatic pressure falls along the length of the capillary while oncotic pressure barely changes, so the arteriolar end usually filters and the venular end usually reabsorbs.

cards.q: What happens to the small fluid surplus left in the tissue after each capillary pass?
cards.a: Lymphatics collect it → return it to the circulation

cards.q: Write the Starling equation for fluid movement across a capillary.
cards.a: J<sub>v</sub> = K<sub>f</sub> [(P<sub>c</sub> − P<sub>i</sub>) − (π<sub>c</sub> − π<sub>i</sub>)]
cards.more: Jv = fluid movement; Kf = filtration coefficient; Pc/Pi = capillary/interstitial hydrostatic; πc/πi = capillary/interstitial oncotic pressure.

cards.q: In the Starling equation, what is K<sub>f</sub>?
cards.a: Filtration coefficient (hydraulic conductance) — how leaky the wall is
cards.more: Same driving pressure, leakier capillary → more fluid moves.

cards.q: In the Starling equation, what are P<sub>c</sub> and P<sub>i</sub>?
cards.a: Capillary and interstitial hydrostatic pressure
cards.more: The printed key under Costanzo fig 4.34 calls Pi oncotic — that is a mistake.

cards.q: In the Starling equation, what are π<sub>c</sub> and π<sub>i</sub>?
cards.a: Capillary (plasma) and interstitial oncotic pressure

cards.q: In the Starling equation, what does a positive vs a negative result mean?
cards.a:
Positive → filtration
Negative → reabsorption

cards.q: Net Starling pressure if P<sub>c</sub> 30, P<sub>i</sub> 1, π<sub>c</sub> 26, π<sub>i</sub> 3 mmHg?
cards.a: (30 − 1) − (26 − 3) = +6 mmHg → net filtration
cards.more: Net pressure = (out-pushers) − (in-pullers). Decide which way each pressure points before adding.

cards.q: Net Starling pressure is +6 mmHg and K<sub>f</sub> is 0.5 mL/min per mmHg. How much fluid filters?
cards.a: 3 mL/min

cards.q: Write the net driving force (NDF) form of the Starling equation.
cards.a: NDF = (P<sub>c</sub> − P<sub>i</sub>) − σ(π<sub>c</sub> − π<sub>i</sub>)

cards.q: What is σ, the reflection coefficient?
cards.a: How completely the capillary wall holds protein back

cards.q: What does a reflection coefficient (σ) of 1 mean?
cards.a: Protein cannot cross → exerts its full oncotic pull

cards.q: How does capillary hydrostatic pressure change along a typical capillary?
cards.a: ~35 mmHg (arteriolar end) → ~15 mmHg (venular end)

cards.q: What is plasma oncotic pressure along a typical capillary?
cards.a: Stays near 25 mmHg

cards.q: On the idealised profile (hydrostatic 35 → 15 mmHg, oncotic 25 mmHg), what is the net fluid change?
cards.a: None — loss from plasma = gain back to plasma
cards.more: The real balance leaves a small surplus, which becomes lymph.

cards.q: Where do lymphatic capillaries lie?
cards.a: In the interstitium, beside the blood capillaries

cards.q: What do the one-way flap valves of lymphatic capillaries let in?
cards.a: Interstitial fluid and protein — in, but not back out

cards.q: Where does lymph re-enter the circulation?
cards.a: Lymphatics merge → thoracic duct → large veins

cards.q: What propels lymph along the lymphatic vessels?
cards.a:
The vessels' own smooth muscle
Surrounding skeletal muscle squeezing them

cards.q: What is oedema, in terms of Starling forces?
cards.a: The capillary balance tipping outward — surplus outgrows what lymphatics can carry

cards.q: Name the four mechanisms of oedema.
cards.a:
Hydrostatic pressure too high
Oncotic pressure too low
Capillary too leaky
Lymphatics blocked
cards.more: Any oedema question is asking which one. Four different terms, one equation.

cards.q: Causes of oedema from capillary hydrostatic pressure too high?
cards.a:
Heart failure
Venous obstruction
Arteriolar dilation
Extracellular fluid volume expansion
Standing (blood pools in leg veins)

cards.q: Causes of oedema from plasma oncotic pressure too low?
cards.a:
Liver failure
Nephrotic syndrome
Malnutrition
cards.more: All mean not enough albumin.

cards.q: Urine protein loss that defines nephrotic syndrome?
cards.a: More than 3.5 g/day

cards.q: How do inflammation and burns cause oedema?
cards.a: Capillary too leaky → protein escapes, dragging water with it
cards.more: Inflammation hits two terms at once: it raises permeability and lets protein leak out.

cards.q: Causes of oedema from blocked lymphatics?
cards.a:
Lymph node removal or irradiation (classic)
Filariasis (parasitic infection of the nodes)

cards.q: Which Starling pressure does lymphatic obstruction change?
cards.a: None — pressures stay normal; the drain is removed

cards.q: What role do chemoreceptors play in blood-pressure control?
cards.a: Backup/emergency system to the baroreceptors
cards.more: They matter little for ordinary pressure control, but when pressure falls far enough that tissues are short of oxygen, they fire hard and drive a powerful sympathetic response.

cards.q: What do the peripheral chemoreceptors monitor?
cards.a:
Oxygen
Carbon dioxide
pH

cards.q: Where are the peripheral chemoreceptors?
cards.a:
Carotid body (glomus caroticum), at the carotid bifurcation
Aortic bodies, on the arch
cards.more: They sit right beside the baroreceptor areas (carotid sinus, aortic arch).

cards.q: What nerves carry peripheral chemoreceptor signals, and to where?
cards.a: Cranial nerves IX and X → nucleus tractus solitarius (medulla)
cards.more: The same route as the baroreceptors.

cards.q: What is the main stimulus for the peripheral chemoreceptors?
cards.a: Hypoxia
cards.more: High carbon dioxide or low pH makes them more sensitive to hypoxia.

cards.q: What three responses follow hypoxia sensed by the peripheral chemoreceptors?
cards.a:
Arteriolar vasoconstriction
Transient fall in heart rate
Hyperventilation

cards.q: Why is the heart-rate fall from peripheral chemoreceptor stimulation only transient?
cards.a: The extra breathing itself speeds the heart back up

cards.q: What do the central chemoreceptors in the medulla respond to?
cards.a: Rising carbon dioxide and falling pH
cards.more: They are much less sensitive to hypoxia.

cards.q: Classic trigger and response of the central chemoreceptors?
cards.a: Brain short of blood → local CO<sub>2</sub> rises → big sympathetic rise + peripheral vasoconstriction → blood shunted to brain

cards.q: What is the Cushing reflex?
cards.a: Raised intracranial pressure → hypertension with bradycardia
cards.more: The central chemoreceptor response when the cause of brain ischaemia is raised intracranial pressure.

cards.q: Why can 100% oxygen make a carbon-dioxide-retaining COPD patient worse?
cards.a: Removes the hypoxic drive → breathing falls off
cards.more: Example: chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) with pH 7.22, PCO2 70 mmHg, PO2 55 mmHg — the patient depends on hypoxic drive to keep breathing.

cards.q: Two triggers for antidiuretic hormone (ADH, vasopressin) release?
cards.a:
Osmolality rises
Pressure or volume falls

cards.q: How much must osmolality rise to release ADH, and what receptor/effect follows?
cards.a: ~1% → V2 (kidney): water reabsorption
cards.more:
TriggerChangeReceptor, effect
Osmolality ↑~1%V2: water reabsorption
Pressure/volume ↓~10%V1: vasoconstriction

cards.q: How much must pressure or volume fall to release ADH, and what receptor/effect follows?
cards.a: ~10% → V1 (vascular smooth muscle): vasoconstriction

cards.q: Which ADH trigger is more sensitive?
cards.a: Osmolality — by far

cards.q: Why is vasopressin helpful in septic shock unresponsive to several litres of saline?
cards.a: V1 action constricts arterioles directly

cards.q: Where are the cardiopulmonary (low-pressure) baroreceptors?
cards.a: Veins, atria, pulmonary artery
cards.more: Where most of the blood volume sits.

cards.q: What do the cardiopulmonary (low-pressure) baroreceptors sense?
cards.a: Fullness (volume), not arterial pressure

cards.q: Four responses of the low-pressure baroreceptors to a rise in volume?
cards.a:
↑ Atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP)
↓ ADH (hypothalamus inhibited)
Renal vasodilation → kidney excretes the extra volume
↑ Heart rate (Bainbridge reflex)

cards.q: What is the Bainbridge reflex?
cards.a: ↑ Venous filling → ↑ heart rate, passing the extra venous volume forward
cards.more: Contrast: a rise in arterial pressure slows the heart, but a rise in venous filling speeds it.

cards.q: What does atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) do?
cards.a:
Relaxes vascular smooth muscle → ↓ TPR
Kidney loses salt and water
cards.more: It empties the volume side.

cards.q: What is BNP, and what is it used for clinically?
cards.a: B-type natriuretic peptide (mainly from stretched ventricles) — blood test showing unexplained breathlessness is congestive heart failure

lessons.t: Special circulations, and the body under stress

cards.q: What share of resting cardiac output goes to skeletal muscle, gut and kidneys?
cards.a: About a quarter each

cards.q: What share of resting cardiac output goes to the brain, heart and skin?
cards.a:
Brain ~15%
Heart ~5%
Skin ~5%

cards.q: How does exercise shift the shares of cardiac output?
cards.a: More to muscle; less to gut and skin

cards.q: Which structures receive all of the cardiac output every minute?
cards.a: Each heart chamber and the lungs

cards.q: Two directions from which organ blood flow is controlled?
cards.a:
Local: tissue metabolites act on its arterioles
Neural and hormonal: sympathetic nerves + circulating vasoactive substances

cards.q: What is autoregulation?
cards.a: An organ keeping its own blood flow nearly constant despite changing arterial pressure, by adjusting its arterioles

cards.q: Two mechanisms of autoregulation?
cards.a:
Myogenic
Metabolic

cards.q: What is the myogenic mechanism?
cards.a: A stretched arteriole constricts by itself — no nerve involved

cards.q: What is the metabolic mechanism of autoregulation?
cards.a: Local waste products (adenosine, CO<sub>2</sub>, K<sup>+</sup>) dilate arterioles when flow falls short of need

cards.q: Where is autoregulation strongest, and where weakest?
cards.a:
Strongest: heart, brain, kidney
Weakest: skin, bone

cards.q: State the law of Laplace for a vessel wall.
cards.a: Tension = pressure × radius

cards.q: How does the law of Laplace explain the myogenic response?
cards.a: Pressure ↑ → arteriole narrows → wall tension steady; extra resistance holds flow constant
cards.more: When pressure falls, the arteriole widens.

cards.q: What is active hyperaemia?
cards.a: Flow rising while demand rises (e.g. exercising muscle)

cards.q: What is reactive hyperaemia?
cards.a: Flow rising afterwards (after exertion or a brief blockage) to repay the oxygen debt
cards.more: The coronary bed is the classic example.

cards.q: Name the dilating metabolites produced by working tissue.
cards.a:
Lactate
H+
CO2
K+
Adenosine
Inorganic phosphate
cards.more: Work makes tissue hypoxic, and hypoxia generates lactate and acid; work also releases CO2, potassium, adenosine and phosphate. All dilate most vascular beds.

cards.q: How is adenosine produced in working tissue?
cards.a: Hypoxic tissue breaks down ATP (and cAMP)

cards.q: Why does a small rise in ATP turnover cause a big proportional rise in adenosine?
cards.a: Cells hold ~1000× more ATP than adenosine

cards.q: What is an adenosine thallium (nuclear) stress test?
cards.a: Adenosine dilates coronaries strongly, standing in for exercise → detects ischaemia in a patient who cannot exercise

cards.q: How does a raised extracellular K<sup>+</sup> dilate vessels?
cards.a: Hyperpolarizes vascular smooth muscle → cannot depolarize to contract → relaxes
cards.more: Potassium leaks out of contracting muscle.

cards.q: Where does phosphate come from in working muscle, and what does it do?
cards.a: Piles up as ATP is spent → dilates skeletal-muscle vessels

cards.q: What mainly controls coronary blood flow?
cards.a: Local metabolites (almost entirely metabolic) — not nerves

cards.q: Strongest coronary vasodilators?
cards.a:
Hypoxia
Adenosine

cards.q: Why can the heart get more oxygen only by getting more flow?
cards.a: It already extracts nearly all the oxygen offered at rest

cards.q: When does the left coronary artery fill, and why?
cards.a: Diastole — in systole the contracting muscle squeezes its own vessels shut

cards.q: Where is the blood with the lowest oxygen saturation in the body?
cards.a: Coronary sinus
cards.more: Because the heart extracts so much oxygen.

cards.q: What is cerebral blood flow most sensitive to?
cards.a: CO<sub>2</sub> (plus tight autoregulation)
cards.more: Oxygen matters much less until it is very low.

cards.q: Effect of raised vs lowered arterial CO<sub>2</sub> on cerebral vessels?
cards.a:
↑ CO2 → dilate, flow ↑
Hyperventilation (↓ CO2) → constrict, flow ↓

cards.q: Effect of acid (H<sup>+</sup>) on cerebral vessels?
cards.a: Dilates them

cards.q: Why is a patient with brain herniation from a haematoma hyperventilated?
cards.a: Low CO<sub>2</sub> constricts cerebral vessels → intracranial pressure falls quickly
cards.more: A holding measure while drainage is arranged.

cards.q: Why does rising intracranial pressure reduce cerebral blood flow?
cards.a: Rigid skull: intracranial pressure directly opposes the pressure driving blood in

cards.q: Effect of low alveolar oxygen on pulmonary vessels?
cards.a: Constriction (hypoxia dilates everywhere else)
cards.more: The pulmonary exception is the single most tested item in this lesson.

cards.q: Why is hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction useful?
cards.a: Diverts blood from badly ventilated areas → well ventilated ones

cards.q: What happens with widespread lung hypoxia, as in emphysema?
cards.a: Widespread vasoconstriction → pulmonary hypertension

cards.q: What treatment lowers mortality in hypoxic pulmonary hypertension from emphysema?
cards.a: Home oxygen

cards.q: What is skin blood flow controlled for?
cards.a: Temperature, not the skin's own needs — the body's radiator
cards.more: Blood is shunted to the surface to lose heat and away to conserve it, so skin flow swings over an enormous range.

cards.q: Through which receptor does sympathetic tone control skin vessels?
cards.a: Alpha-1 (entirely)

cards.q: Why is skin the first bed clamped down when blood pressure falls?
cards.a: Almost purely sympathetically driven → cold, pale skin of a bleeding patient

cards.q: What controls skeletal-muscle blood flow at rest?
cards.a: Central sympathetic control: alpha-1 constriction

cards.q: What controls skeletal-muscle blood flow during running?
cards.a: Autoregulation: lactate (most), K<sup>+</sup>, adenosine + circulating epinephrine's beta-2 dilation

cards.q: How is renal blood flow autoregulated?
cards.a: Myogenic response + tubuloglomerular feedback

cards.q: Which vascular beds have dense sympathetic supply, and which have very little?
cards.a:
Dense: skin, skeletal muscle
Very little: coronary, pulmonary, cerebral

cards.q: Effect of histamine and bradykinin on the microcirculation?
cards.a: Dilate arterioles, constrict venules → capillary pressure ↑ → fluid leaks out

cards.q: Vascular effect of serotonin?
cards.a: Constricts

cards.q: Vascular effect of prostaglandins?
cards.a: Variable, mostly dilate; prostacyclin dilates pulmonary vessels

cards.q: Major vascular difference between epinephrine and norepinephrine?
cards.a: Beta-2: epinephrine adds beta-2 dilation of muscle vessels; norepinephrine (little beta-2) constricts via alpha-1

cards.q: Where are epinephrine and norepinephrine made?
cards.a:
Epinephrine: only adrenal medulla
Norepinephrine: adrenal medulla, sympathetic nerve endings, brain

cards.q: Where is the body's thermostat, and how does it work?
cards.a: Hypothalamus, by negative feedback; skin is its main tool

cards.q: Responses to warming vs cooling?
cards.a:
Warming → skin vasodilation + sweating
Cooling → skin vasoconstriction + shivering

cards.q: Normal core body temperature?
cards.a: 37 °C (98.6 °F); more exactly 36.8 ± 0.4 °C
cards.more: Wunderlich's norm from a million readings. Normal range about 35.6–38.5 °C.

cards.q: When in the day is body temperature lowest and highest?
cards.a:
Lowest ~6 am
Highest ~6 pm

cards.q: How do rectal temperature readings differ?
cards.a: About 0.6 °C (1 °F) higher

cards.q: How does body temperature relate to ovulation?
cards.a: Cooler before ovulation than after

cards.q: Three ways the body makes heat?
cards.a:
Thyroid hormone
Sympathetic system
Shivering

cards.q: How does thyroid hormone generate heat?
cards.a: T4 → T3 (more active) → speeds Na<sup>+</sup>/K<sup>+</sup>-ATPase → ↑ oxygen consumption and metabolic rate

cards.q: Temperature intolerance in hypothyroidism vs hyperthyroidism?
cards.a:
Hypothyroid: cannot tolerate cold
Hyperthyroid: cannot tolerate heat

cards.q: What switches on sympathetic heat production, and which hormones join it?
cards.a: Cold, directly; with cortisol, growth hormone, glucagon

cards.q: How do catecholamines generate and keep heat?
cards.a: Burn brown fat (beta-1 receptors); alpha-1 skin vasoconstriction keeps heat in
cards.more: Costanzo says only "beta receptors"; many texts name beta-3. Thyroid hormone is permissive for the catecholamine effect.

cards.q: Mechanism of shivering?
cards.a: Cold → hypothalamus readjusts alpha and gamma motor neurons → rhythmic skeletal-muscle contraction

cards.q: Which part of the hypothalamus controls heat loss?
cards.a: Anterior hypothalamus

cards.q: How does the skin lose heat?
cards.a: ↓ Sympathetic outflow → skin vessels dilate → blood shunted to surface veins → red, warm skin

cards.q: What drives sweating?
cards.a: Sympathetic cholinergic fibres (sympathetic nerves releasing acetylcholine)

cards.q: Pathway of fever?
cards.a: Pyrogens → interleukin-1 → hypothalamus → prostaglandin E2 → raised set point

cards.q: How do aspirin, other NSAIDs and acetaminophen lower fever?
cards.a: Inhibit cyclooxygenase → no prostaglandin E2
cards.more: NSAIDs = non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs.

cards.q: How much does each 1 °C of fever raise fluid and calorie needs?
cards.a: About 13%

cards.q: Heat cramps: temperature, mental state and clues?
cards.a: Both normal; painful leg, arm or abdominal muscles; creatine kinase (CK) normal

cards.q: Heat exhaustion: mental state and clues?
cards.a: Normal, or mild confusion clearing within 30 min of cooling; sweating, nausea, vomiting, headache, weakness, dizziness, severe thirst; BP normal
cards.more: Mild–moderate dehydration. May faint but recovers promptly.

cards.q: Why may a patient with heat exhaustion faint (Costanzo)?
cards.a: Heavy sweating shrinks blood volume → arterial pressure falls

cards.q: Heat stroke: temperature, mental state and clues?
cards.a: Above 40 °C; altered mental status; dry skin; CK often raised

cards.q: Treatment of heat stroke?
cards.a: Evaporative cooling + intravenous fluids

cards.q: What is malignant hyperthermia, and its findings?
cards.a: Probably inherited reaction to anaesthetics (enflurane, sevoflurane): masseter and general rigidity, high CK and arterial CO<sub>2</sub>

cards.q: Treatment of malignant hyperthermia?
cards.a: Dantrolene

cards.q: Overall cardiovascular response to exercise?
cards.a: Metabolites dilate muscle; sympathetic ↑ rate and contractility; venous return ↑; cardiac output ↑ several-fold

cards.q: In exercise, why does mean pressure rise only modestly, and what happens to pulse pressure?
cards.a:
Overall resistance falls (much muscle dilated)
Pulse pressure widens

cards.q: Where does the cardiovascular drive in exercise start?
cards.a:
Central command (brain)
Mechano- and chemoreceptors in working muscle

cards.q: What do central command and muscle receptors do to autonomic outflow in exercise?
cards.a: ↑ Sympathetic outflow; vagal tone withdrawn from the heart

cards.q: How does venous return keep pace in exercise?
cards.a: Veins constrict + muscle pump squeezes them (one-way valves → towards heart)

cards.q: Which beds constrict in exercise?
cards.a: Skin, spleen, gut, kidney, inactive muscle

cards.q: Which beds dilate in exercise?
cards.a: Working muscle (metabolites + beta-2), coronary, cerebral

cards.q: Costanzo's two refinements to the exercise response?
cards.a:
Brain flow held steady, not increased
Skin constriction reverses as body temperature climbs → skin flushes

cards.q: Why do heat and exercise together cause collapse?
cards.a: Muscle and skin both want flow; not enough cardiac output for both

cards.q: Initial haemodynamic chain in haemorrhage?
cards.a: Volume ↓ → venous return ↓ → cardiac output ↓ → pressure ↓

cards.q: Immediate reflex response to haemorrhage?
cards.a: Baroreceptors (carotid sinus IX, aortic arch X) → medulla: ↑ sympathetic, ↓ parasympathetic → tachycardia, ↑ contractility, venoconstriction, arteriolar constriction

cards.q: Which beds are constricted in haemorrhage, and why?
cards.a: Skin, gut, kidney → protect brain and heart

cards.q: Why does fluid shift in from the tissues after haemorrhage?
cards.a: Constricted arterioles ↓ capillary hydrostatic pressure → Starling balance tips to reabsorption

cards.q: Why is renin released in haemorrhage?
cards.a: ↓ Renal perfusion and ↓ afferent arteriole stretch → juxtaglomerular cells release renin
cards.more: ADH also rises. A fall in volume of about 10% releases enough ADH to act on V1 receptors (arteriolar constriction), on top of its V2 effect (the kidney holds on to water).

cards.q: What does angiotensin II do in haemorrhage?
cards.a:
Constricts arterioles
Releases aldosterone → sodium and water retained
cards.more: RAAS = renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system.

cards.q: How do chemoreceptors add to the haemorrhage response?
cards.a: Hypoxia → peripheral chemoreceptors push sympathetic outflow higher; brain ischaemia → central chemoreceptors do the same

cards.q: Subarachnoid haemorrhage with new, deep T-wave inversions: what do they reflect?
cards.a: Increased sympathetic outflow — not a coronary clot

cards.q: Reflex chain on standing up?
cards.a: Blood pools in legs → venous return ↓ → pressure ↓ → carotid baroreceptors → medulla → beta-1 tachycardia + alpha-1 vasoconstriction
cards.more: Corrects pressure within seconds. Same arc as haemorrhage; only the trigger changes.

cards.q: Why do the ankles swell after long standing?
cards.a: Pooling ↑ capillary hydrostatic pressure in the legs → more filtration

cards.q: Normal pulse and systolic changes on standing?
cards.a:
Pulse rises < 10 beats/min
Systolic falls < 20 mmHg

cards.q: What is a positive orthostatic test, and what does it mean?
cards.a: Pulse ↑ 10, systolic ↓ 20, diastolic ↓ 10 → ~15–20% of blood volume lost

cards.q: In a gastrointestinal bleed, what do orthostatics vs endoscopy tell you?
cards.a:
Orthostatics: how severe (volume lost)
Endoscopy: where it is bleeding

cards.q: Systolic < 100 or pulse > 100 in a bleed: how much is lost and what do you do?
cards.a: ~30% lost → skip orthostatics, give 1 L normal saline

cards.q: Why give normal saline rather than 5% dextrose in water for blood loss?
cards.a: Dextrose water spreads through all body water instead of staying in the circulation

cards.q: Pressure stays low (e.g. 70/40 after 4 L saline): what next?
cards.a: Add a vasopressor: norepinephrine (or dopamine, vasopressin, phenylephrine)

cards.q: What is a Swan–Ganz catheter?
cards.a: Balloon-tipped catheter floated through right atrium and ventricle into a pulmonary artery (right-heart catheterization)

cards.q: What does the right atrial pressure on a Swan–Ganz catheter reflect?
cards.a: Filling (preload)

cards.q: What does the Swan–Ganz wedge pressure equal?
cards.a: Left atrial pressure
cards.more: Read with the balloon wedged in a small pulmonary artery branch.

cards.q: How is systemic vascular resistance (SVR) obtained from a Swan–Ganz catheter?
cards.a: Calculated from the cardiac output it measures

cards.q: Septic shock: SVR, cardiac output, wedge?
cards.a:
SVR ↓
CO ↑
Wedge ↓
cards.more: Endotoxin dilates vessels → resistance and wedge fall; baroreceptor reflex drives output up.

cards.q: Cardiac failure: SVR, cardiac output, wedge?
cards.a:
SVR ↑
CO ↓
Wedge ↑
cards.more: Weak ventricle can't keep output up; blood backs into the left atrium → wedge rises; reflex vasoconstriction raises resistance.

cards.q: Hypovolaemia: SVR, cardiac output, wedge?
cards.a:
SVR ↑
CO ↓
Wedge ↓
cards.more:
Too little venous return lowers output and wedge together; reflex vasoconstriction raises resistance.

SVRCOWedge
Sepsis↓↑↓
Cardiac failure↑↓↑
Hypovolaemia↑↓↓

lessons.t: Drugs that act on the heart and vessels

cards.q: What equation do you read every cardiovascular drug off?
cards.a: BP = CO × TPR
cards.more: Blood pressure = cardiac output × total peripheral resistance.

cards.q: A drug can change BP only through which two things?
cards.a:
CO (acting on the heart)
TPR (acting on the arterioles)

cards.q: Three steps of any drug's blood-pressure tracing?
cards.a: Direct effect → change in pressure → baroreceptor reflex (if anything is left to carry it)

cards.q: Effect of α<sub>1</sub> receptor activation?
cards.a: Arterioles and veins constrict → TPR ↑

cards.q: Effect of β<sub>1</sub> receptor activation?
cards.a: Heart beats faster and harder → CO ↑

cards.q: Effect of β<sub>2</sub> receptor activation on vessels?
cards.a: Skeletal-muscle arterioles dilate → TPR ↓

cards.q: Effect of M<sub>2</sub> receptor activation?
cards.a: Heart (vagus) slows → CO ↓

cards.q: Effect of M<sub>3</sub> receptor activation on vessels?
cards.a: Endothelium releases nitric oxide (NO) → vessels dilate

cards.q: Where are N<sub>N</sub> receptors?
cards.a: Every autonomic ganglion, sympathetic and parasympathetic

cards.q: What does α<sub>2</sub> do?
cards.a: Brake on norepinephrine release from the nerve ending; in the brainstem ↓ sympathetic outflow

cards.q: Reflex response to a rise in BP?
cards.a: Vagal (M<sub>2</sub>) reflex → slows the heart

cards.q: Reflex response to a fall in BP?
cards.a: Sympathetic (β<sub>1</sub>) reflex → speeds the heart

cards.q: Why does blocking autonomic ganglia silence every reflex?
cards.a: Both reflex arms run through autonomic ganglia

cards.q: Tracing for phenylephrine (pure α<sub>1</sub> agonist)?
cards.a: TPR ↑ → BP ↑ → vagal reflex slows heart → CO ↓

cards.q: Tracing for a vasodilator?
cards.a: TPR ↓ → BP ↓ → reflex tachycardia → CO ↑

cards.q: Three kinds of drug that give the vasodilator tracing?
cards.a:
β2 agonist (albuterol)
Any arteriolar dilator
α1 blocker (prazosin)

cards.q: Size of prazosin's BP fall, and its use?
cards.a: Mild (e.g. 140/100 → 130/90) — antihypertensive

cards.q: Why does phentolamine cause a bigger reflex tachycardia than prazosin?
cards.a: Also blocks α<sub>2</sub> → brake removed → more norepinephrine reaches the heart

cards.q: Effect of a drug that raises stroke volume alone (β<sub>1</sub>: dobutamine or dopamine, cardiotonic use)?
cards.a: CO ↑ → BP ↑

cards.q: Phenylephrine after prazosin (α<sub>1</sub> blocker)?
cards.a: Little or no rise — receptor occupied

cards.q: Phenylephrine after atropine (M<sub>2</sub> blocker)?
cards.a: Bigger rise — vagal reflex can no longer slow the heart

cards.q: Phenylephrine after mecamylamine (ganglion blocker)?
cards.a: Rise with no reflex at all — every reflex must pass through a ganglion

cards.q: Phenylephrine after physostigmine (anticholinesterase)?
cards.a: Acetylcholine lingers → vagal reflex potentiated → heart slows so much that pressure drops back sharply

cards.q: Receptors and BP effect of norepinephrine?
cards.a: α<sub>1</sub>, β<sub>1</sub>: TPR and CO ↑ together → BP climbs steeply

cards.q: Why does norepinephrine show no reflex slowing of the heart?
cards.a: A vagal reflex is triggered, but the direct β<sub>1</sub> push covers it
cards.more: Many pharmacology texts describe the reflex winning instead, with heart rate falling slightly.

cards.q: Receptors and BP effect of epinephrine?
cards.a: α<sub>1</sub>, β<sub>1</sub>, β<sub>2</sub>: CO and BP ↑, no visible reflex

cards.q: Why does diastolic pressure rise less with epinephrine than norepinephrine?
cards.a: β<sub>2</sub> dilation of muscle vessels opposes the α<sub>1</sub> constriction

cards.q: Receptors and BP effect of isoproterenol?
cards.a: β<sub>1</sub>, β<sub>2</sub> (no α<sub>1</sub>): TPR ↓ → mean and diastolic ↓; CO ↑, pulse pressure widens
cards.more: The direct β1 effect also hides any reflex.

cards.q: Norepinephrine after phentolamine?
cards.a: Only β<sub>1</sub> left → BP still rises, on output alone

cards.q: Epinephrine after phentolamine?
cards.a: β2 dilation wins → TPR ↓ → BP falls (epinephrine reversal)
cards.more: Also called Dale's vasomotor reversal.

cards.q: Norepinephrine after a β blocker?
cards.a: Only α<sub>1</sub> left → behaves like phenylephrine

cards.q: Isoproterenol after a blocker of both β<sub>1</sub> and β<sub>2</sub>?
cards.a: Response abolished

cards.q: Isoproterenol after metoprolol (β<sub>1</sub>-selective)?
cards.a: β<sub>2</sub> still lowers TPR and BP — no direct CO rise and no β<sub>1</sub> reflex to offset it

cards.q: Terbutaline (β<sub>2</sub> agonist) after metoprolol?
cards.a: Same as isoproterenol: TPR and BP fall with no β<sub>1</sub> offset

cards.q: Effect of vagal stimulation (M<sub>2</sub>)?
cards.a: Heart slows or stops → pressure plunges

cards.q: What happens during and after prolonged vagal stimulation?
cards.a: Heart escapes and beats again (β<sub>1</sub> drive helping); when stimulation stops, sympathetic reflex (α<sub>1</sub>, β<sub>1</sub>) leaves pressure above baseline

cards.q: Vagal stimulation after atropine?
cards.a: Nothing happens

cards.q: Carotid occlusion tracing?
cards.a: ↓ Pressure at carotid sinus → baroreceptors report a fall → sympathetic (α<sub>1</sub>, β<sub>1</sub>) pressor rise → opposed by vagal (M<sub>2</sub>) reflex

cards.q: How does acetylcholine (ACh) lower BP?
cards.a: Mainly vasodilation via M<sub>3</sub> → nitric oxide

cards.q: ACh after neostigmine (anticholinesterase)?
cards.a: Deeper, longer fall — both M<sub>2</sub> and M<sub>3</sub>/NO actions potentiated

cards.q: Nicotine tracing?
cards.a: N<sub>N</sub> in every ganglion → small vagal dip, then larger sympathetic rise

cards.q: Nicotine after neostigmine vs after atropine?
cards.a:
Neostigmine: vagal dip potentiated
Atropine: vagal dip gone, only pressor rise

cards.q: Why do drugs that remove sympathetic tone lower BP with no reflex?
cards.a: They remove the pathway the reflex would use

cards.q: Clonidine: mechanism?
cards.a: Central α<sub>2</sub> agonist → cuts sympathetic outflow at the vasomotor centre

cards.q: Mecamylamine: mechanism?
cards.a: Blocks autonomic ganglia (N<sub>N</sub>)

cards.q: Metyrosine: mechanism?
cards.a: Stops norepinephrine and epinephrine being made

cards.q: Reserpine: mechanism?
cards.a: Empties nerve endings of norepinephrine

cards.q: Atenolol (β<sub>1</sub> blocker): effect, and why no reflex?
cards.a: CO ↓ → BP ↓; no reflex because β<sub>1</sub> is blocked

cards.q: Labetalol (β + α<sub>1</sub> blocker): effect, and why no reflex?
cards.a: CO and TPR ↓ → BP ↓; no reflex because β<sub>1</sub> is blocked

cards.q: Venodilators and diuretics: how do they lower BP?
cards.a: ↓ Venous return → CO and BP ↓; reflex ↑ heart rate, but output stays low

cards.q: Name the drugs that lower BP with no reflex tachycardia.
cards.a:
Atenolol
Labetalol
Clonidine
Mecamylamine
Metyrosine
Reserpine
cards.more:

NorepinephrineCO ↑, reflex masked↑

cards.q: What are the two parts of the circulatory system?
cards.a:
Cardiovascular (blood vascular) system
Lymphatic vascular system

cards.q: Which side of the heart drives each circulation, and at what pressure?
cards.a:
Right heart → low-pressure pulmonary circulation (lungs)
Left heart → high-pressure systemic circulation (body)

cards.q: In what order does blood pass through the vessels after leaving the heart?
cards.a: Elastic arteries → muscular arteries → small arteries → arterioles → capillaries → venules → small → medium → large veins

cards.q: What is the difference between an afferent and an efferent vessel?
cards.a:
Afferent arrives at a structure
Efferent carries blood away from it

cards.q: Name the three tunics of every blood vessel wall, from inside out.
cards.a: Tunica intima → tunica media → tunica adventitia
cards.more: Almost every histology question about vessels is really asking which layer is emphasised.

cards.q: What makes up the tunica intima?
cards.a: Endothelium + a little connective tissue
cards.more: The innermost tunic.

cards.q: Which tunic does every vessel have, right down to a capillary?
cards.a: Tunica intima

cards.q: In arteries, what marks the outer border of the intima?
cards.a: Internal elastic lamina — a wavy sheet of elastin

cards.q: What makes up the tunica media?
cards.a: Smooth muscle + elastic tissue

cards.q: Which tunic varies most between vessels and is usually the thickest, most prominent tunic of an artery?
cards.a: Tunica media

cards.q: In arteries, what may mark the outer edge of the media?
cards.a: External elastic lamina

cards.q: What is the tunica adventitia, and what does it do?
cards.a: Outer connective tissue that anchors the vessel

cards.q: In big vessels, what extra structure does the adventitia carry?
cards.a: Its own blood supply, the vasa vasorum

cards.q: What is the structure of endothelium?
cards.a: One layer of flat cells on a basal lamina, held together by junctional complexes

cards.q: What is endothelium's basic role as a lining?
cards.a: Interface between blood and organs — the selective barrier for everything exchanged with the tissues
cards.more: Far from passive: healthy endothelium also keeps four pairs of opposing signals in balance (tone, growth, clotting, inflammation).

cards.q: Which endothelial signals dilate vessels, and which constricts them?
cards.a:
Dilate: nitric oxide, prostacyclin
Constrict: endothelin-1

cards.q: What opposing pair does endothelium balance for vessel-wall growth?
cards.a: Growth inhibition vs growth promotion (growth factors)

cards.q: What are endothelium's antithrombotic features?
cards.a:
Non-clotting surface
Heparin
Tissue plasminogen activator

cards.q: What is endothelium's main prothrombotic factor?
cards.a: von Willebrand factor

cards.q: What pair does endothelium balance for inflammation?
cards.a: Anti-inflammation vs proinflammation (letting white cells stick and leave)

cards.q: When endothelium is damaged or dysfunctional, which way does the balance tip, and what does that start?
cards.a: Toward constriction, growth, prothrombosis, proinflammation → thrombosis and atherosclerosis
cards.more:
JobOne sideOther side
ToneDilatation (NO, prostacyclin)Constriction (endothelin-1)
GrowthInhibitionPromotion (growth factors)
ClottingAntithrombosis (surface, heparin, tPA)Prothrombosis (vWF)
InflammationAnti-Pro- (white cells stick, leave)

Damage tips toward the right-hand column.

cards.q: Which vessels are the elastic arteries, and what is their functional name?
cards.a: Aorta and its big branches — low-resistance conducting vessels

cards.q: What fills the media of an elastic artery?
cards.a: Concentric, fenestrated elastic lamellae alternating with smooth-muscle layers
cards.more: On a slide the media looks layered and wavy.

cards.q: Why are elastic arteries built of elastin?
cards.a: They take each ejection's full force, balloon out, then recoil in diastole to keep blood moving
cards.more: Structure matches function: they must stretch and spring back.

cards.q: Why do elastic arteries need vasa vasorum?
cards.a: Walls too thick to be fed by diffusion from the lumen
cards.more: The vasa vasorum (“vessels of the vessels”) are arterioles, capillaries and venules in the adventitia and outer media.

cards.q: What is the functional name of muscular arteries, and what do they do?
cards.a: Distributing vessels — carry blood to individual organs

cards.q: What makes up the media of a muscular artery, and why?
cards.a: Mostly smooth muscle — to change diameter, direct flow and help regulate blood pressure

cards.q: What is the classic slide giveaway of a muscular artery?
cards.a: Prominent internal elastic lamina — a crisp wavy line at the inner edge of the media

cards.q: On a slide, how do you tell an elastic artery from a muscular artery?
cards.a:
Wavy elastic sheets through the whole media → elastic
One crisp wavy line at the inner border, muscle behind → muscular
cards.more: Both have three tunics; what differs is what the media is made of, and it follows from the job: recoil (elastin) vs changing diameter (muscle).

cards.q: What is the functional name of arterioles?
cards.a: Resistance vessels

cards.q: What does the wall of an arteriole consist of?
cards.a: 1–3 layers of smooth muscle; intima of endothelium alone; very thin adventitia
cards.more: A small artery has more smooth-muscle layers.

cards.q: Why do arterioles, with only a few muscle layers, control flow through the entire circulation?
cards.a: Resistance depends very steeply on radius

cards.q: What is the functional name of capillaries?
cards.a: Exchange vessels

cards.q: What does a capillary wall consist of?
cards.a: Endothelium + basement membrane + scattered pericytes; no media or adventitia

cards.q: Why is a capillary wall only one cell thick?
cards.a: Anything thicker would obstruct exchange

cards.q: What are pericytes, and which vessels do they wrap?
cards.a: Small cells whose long processes wrap the endothelium of capillaries and postcapillary venules
cards.more: As close as a capillary gets to a media.

cards.q: What basal lamina surrounds a pericyte?
cards.a: Its own, fused with the endothelial basal lamina

cards.q: What do pericytes contain, and what do they do?
cards.a: Contractile proteins — help regulate flow

cards.q: How are the three capillary types told apart?
cards.a: Electron microscope: how continuous the endothelium and basement membrane are
cards.more: Under the light microscope they look alike. Each type sits where its leakiness suits the organ.

cards.q: Describe the wall of a continuous capillary.
cards.a: Unbroken endothelium sealed by tight junctions, marginal folds, many pinocytotic vesicles (caveolae); continuous basement membrane
cards.more: The most common and narrowest type.

cards.q: Where are continuous capillaries found?
cards.a: Muscle, brain, connective tissue, lung, thymus

cards.q: Why do continuous capillaries give the tightest control, and what do they make possible in the brain?
cards.a: Tight junctions pass only water and small solutes; in brain they seal clefts completely → blood–brain barrier

cards.q: Describe the wall of a fenestrated capillary.
cards.a: Tight junctions; thin cytoplasm pierced by pores (fenestrae), many closed by a diaphragm; continuous basement membrane

cards.q: Where are fenestrated capillaries found, and why there?
cards.a: Endocrine glands, pancreas, intestinal villi — fast exchange of small molecules (hormones out, nutrients in)

cards.q: Describe the wall of a sinusoidal (discontinuous) capillary.
cards.a: Gaps between endothelial cells as well as pores; discontinuous basement membrane; wide, irregular lumen

cards.q: Where are sinusoidal capillaries found?
cards.a: Bone marrow, liver, spleen, lymph nodes, some endocrine glands
cards.more: Textbooks usually list sinusoids only in marrow, liver, spleen and some endocrine organs, not lymph nodes.

cards.q: What can cross a sinusoidal capillary wall, and what example uses this?
cards.a: Large molecules and whole cells — new blood cells leave the bone marrow this way

cards.q: In the liver, what do sinusoid pores cluster into?
cards.a: Sieve plates

cards.q: On an electron micrograph, how do you name the capillary type from its wall?
cards.a:
Unbroken cytoplasm + tight junctions → continuous
Thin cytoplasm with pores, intact basement membrane → fenestrated
Gaps between cells, broken basement membrane, wide lumen → sinusoid
cards.more:
TypeWallWhere
ContinuousTight junctions, caveolae, continuous BMMuscle, brain, CT, lung, thymus
FenestratedPores (often diaphragm), continuous BMEndocrine, pancreas, villi
SinusoidalGaps + pores, discontinuous BMMarrow, liver, spleen

cards.q: What vessel often feeds a capillary bed from an arteriole, and what rings it?
cards.a: Metarteriole — ringed by scattered smooth muscle cells acting as precapillary sphincters

cards.q: What happens in a capillary bed when the precapillary sphincters relax?
cards.a: Blood spreads through the true capillaries → bed is perfused

cards.q: What happens when the precapillary sphincters contract?
cards.a: Blood bypasses the bed via a thoroughfare channel → straight into the postcapillary venule

cards.q: What is the simple pathway linking capillary beds?
cards.a: Arteriole → capillaries → venule

cards.q: What is an arteriovenous shunt, and where is it used?
cards.a: Arterial side joined directly to venous side, skipping capillaries — skin uses them to vary blood flow

cards.q: What is a portal system, and where are there examples?
cards.a: Two capillary beds in series joined by a portal vein — liver, anterior pituitary

cards.q: On a slide, how do you tell an artery from its companion vein?
cards.a:
Artery: thick muscular wall, round open lumen
Vein: thin wall, large, often collapsed or irregular lumen
cards.more: The comparison most likely to be tested. Companion vessels on one slide: the round thick-walled one is the artery.

cards.q: In a neurovascular bundle, how is the nerve told apart from the artery and vein?
cards.a: Solid — no lumen

cards.q: Which is the thickest layer of a vein?
cards.a: Tunica adventitia
cards.more: Veins have all three tunics but a thin media.

cards.q: What are venous valves made of?
cards.a: Folds of intima and its subendothelial connective tissue, endothelium on both faces

cards.q: Where are venous valves common and where absent, and why?
cards.a: Common in legs; absent in great veins of thorax — they matter only where blood moves against gravity

cards.q: What are the size grades of veins?
cards.a:
Venules ~10–100 µm
Small veins <1 mm
Medium veins 1–10 mm
Large veins >10 mm

cards.q: What does the wall of a postcapillary venule consist of?
cards.a: Endothelium + pericytes

cards.q: Where do white blood cells mainly stick to the vessel wall and leave the circulation in infection or tissue damage?
cards.a: Postcapillary venules

cards.q: Next to an arteriole, how does a venule look?
cards.a: Wider lumen, thinner wall

cards.q: What size rules hold for every vein?
cards.a: Lumen wider than wall is thick; adventitia thickens as the vein gets bigger

cards.q: Describe the wall of the vena cava.
cards.a: Thin intima; media of a few circular smooth-muscle layers; adventitia by far thickest, with longitudinal smooth-muscle bundles and vasa vasorum

cards.q: What is the thickest layer of the aorta, and what is it made of?
cards.a: Media — wavy fenestrated elastic membranes (black in an elastic stain)

cards.q: What is the simple thickest-layer rule for artery vs vein?
cards.a:
Thickest layer media → artery
Thickest layer adventitia → vein

cards.q: What makes a leg vein varicose?
cards.a: Incompetent valves or a dilated vein wall → enlarged, tortuous veins (painful knots under the skin)
cards.more: Commoner in people who stand for long periods.

cards.q: How do varicose veins damage the skin?
cards.a: Slow, turbulent flow → upstream capillary beds engorge → fluid leaks into skin → stasis dermatitis, venous ulcers

cards.q: In a varicose-vein biopsy, how do the valves appear?
cards.a: Thin flaps of intima inside a dilated lumen

cards.q: What is deep vein thrombosis, and what is its main danger?
cards.a: Clot on the wall of a deep leg vein → can break free → pulmonary embolus

cards.q: What do lymphatic vessels do?
cards.a: Collect excess interstitial fluid left by capillaries and return it to the blood as lymph

cards.q: Describe the structure of a lymphatic capillary.
cards.a: Blind-ended, very thin endothelial tube; no tight junctions; incomplete basal lamina

cards.q: How does fluid enter a lymphatic capillary?
cards.a: Through openings between the endothelial cells

cards.q: What are anchoring filaments in lymphatic capillaries?
cards.a: Collagen and elastin tying the endothelial cells to surrounding tissue, holding the openings open

cards.q: What stops lymph flowing back out of a lymphatic capillary?
cards.a: Overlapping edges of endothelial cells acting as flaps

cards.q: Trace lymph from the tissues back to the blood.
cards.a: Lymphatic capillaries → larger lymphatic vessels → lymph nodes → thoracic duct or right lymphatic duct → great veins at the root of the neck
cards.more: In the lymph nodes the lymph is filtered and immune responses start.

cards.q: How does a lymphatic vessel wall compare with a vein of the same size?
cards.a: Thinner, with layers hard to make out

cards.q: What are lymphatic valves, and what pushes lymph along?
cards.a: Paired folds of intima covered by endothelium; outside pressure such as skeletal-muscle contraction

cards.q: What is a lacteal?
cards.a: The lymphatic capillary in the clear core of an intestinal villus

cards.q: On a slide, what is the quickest way to tell a lymphatic from a venule or small vein?
cards.a: No red blood cells in the lumen
cards.more: A lymphatic also has a very thin wall with indistinct layers, may show valves, and holds pale, protein-rich lymph and a few white cells.

cards.q: What is lymphoedema?
cards.a: Fluid trapped in tissue because lymphatics are blocked

cards.q: What causes elephantiasis in lymphatic filariasis?
cards.a: Parasitic roundworms obstruct lymphatic vessels → massive swelling of a leg or the scrotum

lessons.t: The heart wall and its valves

cards.q: Name the three layers of the heart wall, from inside out.
cards.a: Endocardium → myocardium → epicardium
cards.more: The heart is a vessel wall rearranged: its three layers map onto the vessel's three tunics.

cards.q: The endocardium is continuous with which layer of the great vessels?
cards.a: Tunica intima

cards.q: What makes up the endocardium?
cards.a: Endothelium on thin connective tissue with some smooth muscle → deeper subendocardial layer

cards.q: What conducting fibres run in the subendocardial layer?
cards.a: Purkinje fibres

cards.q: What is the myocardium, and which vessel tunic does it correspond to?
cards.a: Thick cardiac-muscle middle layer, by far the bulkiest — equivalent of the media

cards.q: What is the epicardium, and what does it carry?
cards.a: Visceral layer of the serous pericardium — carries coronary vessels and fat
cards.more: On the surface, epicardial fat fills the anterior interventricular sulcus around the coronary branch running in it.

cards.q: List the layers of the pericardium, from outside in.
cards.a: Fibrous pericardium → parietal serous layer → pericardial cavity → visceral serous layer (epicardium)

cards.q: What does the fibrous pericardium do, and what is its key mechanical property?
cards.a: Tough outer sac anchoring the heart; cannot stretch acutely

cards.q: Where is the pericardial cavity, and what does it hold?
cards.a: Between parietal and visceral serous layers; a small volume of lubricating fluid

cards.q: What is the mechanism of cardiac tamponade?
cards.a: Blood fills pericardial cavity → inextensible fibrous pericardium → heart squeezed from outside, cannot fill
cards.more: Example cause: a myocardial wall rupture. The mechanism is purely the inextensibility of the outer layer.

cards.q: What is the difference between a pericardial effusion and tamponade?
cards.a:
Effusion: fluid in the sac
Tamponade: fluid compresses the heart enough to stop it filling

cards.q: What is constrictive pericarditis?
cards.a: Scarred pericardium, thickened by connective tissue to >5 mm, inelastic → restricts venous inflow (no fluid needed)

cards.q: What treats constrictive pericarditis?
cards.a: Pericardiectomy (removing the pericardium)

cards.q: In section, what are the layers of the parietal pericardium, outside in?
cards.a: Dense fibrous layer → areolar tissue → mesothelium facing the cavity

cards.q: In section, what does the epicardium consist of?
cards.a: Mesothelium over loose connective tissue holding fat, nerves and coronary vessels

cards.q: What secretes pericardial fluid, and why is it needed?
cards.a: Mesothelium — stops the two layers rubbing

cards.q: Mesothelium vs endothelium: what do they share, and how do they differ?
cards.a:
Both simple squamous
Mesothelium lines a body cavity (pericardial sac)
Endothelium lines heart and vessels

cards.q: How is the myocardium arranged?
cards.a: Concentric, spiral layers around each chamber; connective-tissue septa (with vessels, nerves) group fibres into fascicles

cards.q: Why is the left ventricular wall much thicker than the right?
cards.a: It pumps into the high-pressure systemic circulation
cards.more: In cross-section the left ventricle is a thick ring; the right is a thinner crescent wrapped against the interventricular septum.

cards.q: Which are thicker, atrial or ventricular muscle cells?
cards.a: Ventricular

cards.q: What do atrial muscle cells store in small secretory granules?
cards.a: Atrial natriuretic factor (ANF)

cards.q: What does atrial natriuretic factor do?
cards.a: Makes the kidney excrete more sodium and water
cards.more: So the atria double as an endocrine organ.

cards.q: What is the cardiac conduction system made of?
cards.a: Modified cardiac muscle cells, specialised for conduction rather than contraction

cards.q: Trace the cardiac conduction pathway.
cards.a: SA node → AV node → AV bundle (of His) → right and left bundle branches → Purkinje fibres

cards.q: Where is the sinoatrial (SA) node, and what is its role?
cards.a: Wall of the right atrium — pacemaker

cards.q: Where is the atrioventricular (AV) node?
cards.a: Floor of the right atrium, at the atria–ventricle junction

cards.q: Why is the delay at the AV node useful?
cards.a: Lets the atria finish emptying before the ventricles contract

cards.q: What course does the AV bundle (of His) take?
cards.a: Through an opening in the cardiac skeleton → interventricular septum → splits into right and left bundle branches

cards.q: What do Purkinje fibres do?
cards.a: Carry the signal rapidly to both ventricles, ending on contractile muscle → ventricles contract together
cards.more: They are the subendocardial network the bundle branches break up into.

cards.q: What does an electrocardiogram (ECG) record?
cards.a: Spread of the impulse through the heart, from skin electrodes

cards.q: What three features together identify cardiac muscle on a slide?
cards.a:
Striated
Central nucleus
Intercalated discs
cards.more: The histology clickers lean on these three features to tell cardiac from skeletal and smooth muscle.

cards.q: Cardiac vs skeletal muscle: how do the nuclei differ?
cards.a:
Cardiac: usually one, central
Skeletal: many, at the periphery

cards.q: Cardiac vs skeletal muscle: how do the cell shapes differ?
cards.a:
Cardiac: short, branching
Skeletal: long fibres

cards.q: How do intercalated discs look on a slide?
cards.a: Dark cross-lines joining cells end to end — unique to cardiac muscle

cards.q: What three junctions does an intercalated disc contain?
cards.a:
Fascia adherens
Desmosomes
Gap junctions

cards.q: What do the fascia adherens and desmosomes of the intercalated disc do?
cards.a: Hold cells together against the pull of contraction

cards.q: What do the gap junctions of the intercalated disc do?
cards.a: Let the signal spread cell to cell → the heart works as one electrical unit

cards.q: Where do Purkinje fibres sit on a heart slide?
cards.a: Subendocardial layer — the deepest part of the endocardium

cards.q: What do Purkinje fibres look like, compared with ordinary cardiac muscle?
cards.a: Larger and paler — abundant glycogen, few myofibrils
cards.more: The pallor is the giveaway: pale, fat cells in the subendocardium are Purkinje fibres.

cards.q: Why do Purkinje fibres look pale on a slide?
cards.a: Glycogen washes out in processing → clear cytoplasm around a central nucleus, myofibrils pushed to the edge

cards.q: How do Purkinje fibre intercalated discs differ from typical ones?
cards.a: Desmosomes and gap junctions present; fasciae adherentes poorly developed

cards.q: What are heart valves made of?
cards.a: Fold of dense connective tissue covered by endothelium — not muscular
cards.more: A passive flap that opens and closes with the pressure across it.

cards.q: Which heart-wall layer do the valves belong to?
cards.a: Endocardium (folds of the lining); core continuous with the cardiac skeleton

cards.q: Name the atrioventricular valves.
cards.a:
Right: tricuspid
Left: bicuspid (mitral)

cards.q: What stops the AV valve cusps turning inside out into the atria?
cards.a: Papillary muscles contract → tense the chordae tendineae
cards.more: Rising ventricular pressure pushes the cusps shut.

cards.q: Name the semilunar valves and where each sits.
cards.a:
Pulmonary: right ventricle → pulmonary trunk
Aortic: left ventricle → aorta

cards.q: With no muscular support, how do semilunar valves stay shut?
cards.a: Their three cusps brace against one another like a tripod

cards.q: Name the parts of a semilunar cusp and what lies behind it.
cards.a:
Nodule at middle of free edge; lunule on either side
Sinus: bulge of vessel wall behind each cusp

cards.q: What tissue forms the cardiac skeleton?
cards.a: Dense irregular connective tissue

cards.q: How is the cardiac skeleton arranged?
cards.a: Four fibrous rings (annuli) around the four valves, joined by the left and right fibrous trigones

cards.q: Into which structures does the cardiac skeleton extend?
cards.a:
Valve cusps
Chordae tendineae
Membranous part of the interventricular septum

cards.q: What are the jobs of the cardiac skeleton?
cards.a:
Anchors the valves
Insertion for atrial and ventricular muscle
Electrically insulates atria from ventricles

cards.q: What is the only electrical path from atria to ventricles?
cards.a: AV bundle (of His), which pierces the cardiac skeleton
cards.more: The insulating skeleton forces the signal through the AV node.

cards.q: Where do the right and left coronary arteries arise?
cards.a: Aortic sinuses, just above the aortic valve

cards.q: When do the coronary arteries fill, and what drives it?
cards.a: Between contractions — the stretched elastic aortic wall recoils and pushes blood in

cards.q: What are the main branches of the left coronary artery?
cards.a:
Anterior interventricular
Circumflex

cards.q: What are the main branches of the right coronary artery?
cards.a:
Right marginal
Usually the posterior interventricular

cards.q: What is a myocardial infarction?
cards.a: Coronary thrombosis (clot) kills the muscle that artery supplies

lessons.t: The airway, from nose to bronchiole

cards.q: Anatomically, what makes up the upper and lower respiratory tract?
cards.a:
Upper: nasal cavity, sinuses, pharynx
Lower: larynx, trachea, bronchi, lungs

cards.q: What is the conducting portion of the respiratory tract, and what does it do?
cards.a: Nasal cavity → terminal bronchioles; only conditions and carries air

cards.q: What is the respiratory portion, and what does it do?
cards.a: Respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, alveoli — exchanges gas

cards.q: What is the last conducting segment of the airway?
cards.a: Terminal bronchiole

cards.q: What lines the nasal vestibule?
cards.a: Keratinized stratified squamous epithelium (skin) with sweat and sebaceous glands and vibrissae

cards.q: What are vibrissae?
cards.a: Coarse filtering hairs of the nasal vestibule

cards.q: What happens to the vestibule epithelium further into the nose?
cards.a: Loses its keratin in a transition zone

cards.q: Which nasal surfaces carry olfactory epithelium, and which carry respiratory epithelium?
cards.a:
Olfactory: superior concha and roof
Respiratory: middle and inferior conchae

cards.q: How does the nasal cavity condition inhaled air?
cards.a:
Secretions humidify
Capillary loops + large venous plexus warm
Mucus traps particles
Plasma cells add immunoglobulin A (IgA)

cards.q: What type of epithelium is respiratory epithelium, and on what?
cards.a: Pseudostratified ciliated columnar, on a thick basement membrane

cards.q: Why is respiratory epithelium called pseudostratified?
cards.a: All cells touch the basement membrane, but nuclei sit at different heights

cards.q: Name the five cell types of respiratory epithelium.
cards.a:
Ciliated columnar
Goblet
Basal
Brush
Small granule (Kulchitsky)

cards.q: What are the approximate proportions of the respiratory epithelial cells?
cards.a:
Ciliated, goblet, basal: ~30% each
Small granule: ~3%
Brush: few

cards.q: Which is the most numerous cell of respiratory epithelium?
cards.a: Ciliated columnar cell

cards.q: How many cilia does each ciliated cell have, and what do they do?
cards.a: 250–300 motile cilia — sweep mucus toward the pharynx

cards.q: What makes the dark line under the cilia of respiratory epithelium?
cards.a: Basal bodies

cards.q: How do goblet cells look?
cards.a: Basal nucleus; apex full of mucin granules

cards.q: What is the role of the basal cells of respiratory epithelium?
cards.a: Stem cells

cards.q: Describe the brush cell of respiratory epithelium.
cards.a: Thick, blunt microvilli; chemosensory, in synaptic contact with afferent nerve endings

cards.q: Small granule (Kulchitsky) cells belong to which system, and what do they contain?
cards.a: Diffuse neuroendocrine system (DNES) — dense-core granules of peptide hormone (calcitonin-like in bronchi)

cards.q: What stain marks small granule (Kulchitsky) cells?
cards.a: Peptide-hormone immunostain

cards.q: Which lung cancer arises from small granule (Kulchitsky) cells?
cards.a: Small cell lung cancer

cards.q: How does olfactory epithelium differ from respiratory epithelium?
cards.a: Taller pseudostratified; thin basement membrane; no goblet cells

cards.q: What cell perceives smell, and where are its nuclei in the epithelium?
cards.a: Bipolar olfactory neuron — nuclei form a middle row

cards.q: What does the dendrite of an olfactory neuron end in?
cards.a: Knob of long non-motile cilia (“olfactory hairs”) carrying the receptors

cards.q: Where do olfactory neuron axons go?
cards.a: Through the cribriform plate as the olfactory nerve

cards.q: Describe the supporting (sustentacular) cells of olfactory epithelium.
cards.a: Microvilli and ion channels; nuclei nearest the surface

cards.q: Why does smell lost in a cold come back?
cards.a: Basal stem cells on the basement membrane regenerate the olfactory neurons

cards.q: What is the giveaway of olfactory mucosa in the lamina propria?
cards.a: Serous Bowman's glands
cards.more: The lamina propria also holds nerve bundles and vessels.

cards.q: Is olfactory epithelium ciliated?
cards.a: Only non-motile neuronal cilia; no motile ciliated cells
cards.more: Some tables call it “ciliated” because of those neuronal cilia.

cards.q: How does the lining of the sinuses and nasopharynx differ from nasal respiratory epithelium?
cards.a: Thinner, with few goblet cells and few, small glands

cards.q: What muscle and structures are found in the pharynx and nasopharynx?
cards.a:
Pharynx: skeletal muscle
Nasopharynx: pharyngeal tonsil, auditory tube opening

cards.q: What goes wrong in primary ciliary dyskinesia?
cards.a: Deformed cilia fail to beat together → mucus, dirt and bacteria build up

cards.q: Where does mucus build up in primary ciliary dyskinesia, and what else is affected?
cards.a: Nasal cavity, sinuses, middle ear, trachea, bronchi, lungs; fertility impaired in both sexes

cards.q: Which laryngeal surfaces have non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium, and why?
cards.a: Lingual surface of epiglottis + vocal folds — they take friction

cards.q: What lines the rest of the larynx, including the vestibular (false) folds?
cards.a: Respiratory epithelium (starting on the laryngeal surface of the epiglottis)

cards.q: What cartilage is the epiglottis, and what else does it contain?
cards.a: Elastic cartilage — with perichondrium, seromucous glands, taste buds

cards.q: What cartilage are the thyroid and cricoid?
cards.a: Hyaline (may contain bone in adults)

cards.q: What is in the laryngeal lamina propria?
cards.a: Mixed seromucous glands, areolar tissue, mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT)

cards.q: What does each true vocal fold contain?
cards.a: Elastic vocal ligament (top edge of conus elasticus) over the striated vocalis muscle

cards.q: What separates the true vocal fold from the vestibular fold above?
cards.a: The ventricle (rising into a small saccule)

cards.q: What is a singer's nodule?
cards.a: Callus-like growth at the midpoint of the vocal fold from voice overuse, covered by stratified squamous epithelium

cards.q: List the layers of the tracheal wall, inside out.
cards.a: Mucosa → submucosa → hyaline cartilage → adventitia

cards.q: What is the tracheal mucosa made of?
cards.a: Respiratory mucosa with lymphoid tissue, edged by an elastic membrane

cards.q: What glands are in the tracheal submucosa, and what do they make?
cards.a: Seromucous glands (some in lamina propria too) — watery mucus

cards.q: What is the tracheal cartilage like, and what does it do?
cards.a: C-shaped hyaline rings with perichondrium (may contain bone in adults) — hold the lumen open

cards.q: What bridges the posterior gap of the tracheal cartilage rings?
cards.a: Trachealis muscle (smooth)

cards.q: What is in the tracheal adventitia?
cards.a: Vessels, nerves, lymphatics, fat

cards.q: Name the bronchi in order from the carina.
cards.a: Primary (main) → secondary (lobar) → tertiary (segmental)

cards.q: What cartilage do primary bronchi have?
cards.a: Trachea-like rings (complete in some sources, C-shaped in others)

cards.q: What are the wall features of intrapulmonary bronchi?
cards.a:
Folded respiratory epithelium, few goblet cells
Spiral smooth muscle in lamina propria
Serous and mucous glands
MALT
Isolated hyaline cartilage plates

cards.q: What form does the cartilage take in intrapulmonary bronchi?
cards.a: Isolated plates of hyaline cartilage

cards.q: What lies against the adventitia of an intrapulmonary bronchus?
cards.a: Lung tissue and a branch of the pulmonary artery

cards.q: How does the bronchial wall change distally?
cards.a: Epithelium shortens; glands and goblet cells thin out

cards.q: What size are bronchioles, and what do they lack?
cards.a: <1 mm across — no cartilage, no glands

cards.q: What does a bronchiole wall have instead of cartilage?
cards.a: Folded mucosa with well-developed smooth muscle

cards.q: How does the epithelium change along the bronchioles?
cards.a: Ciliated low columnar → non-ciliated cuboidal; club cells take over

cards.q: What epithelium lines the terminal bronchiole?
cards.a: Simple cuboidal (some atlases say low columnar)

cards.q: Which cells make up the terminal bronchiole epithelium?
cards.a: Mostly club cells; some ciliated cells; a few brush and granule cells

cards.q: What surrounds the terminal bronchiole epithelium, and what is missing from its wall?
cards.a: 1–2 layers of smooth muscle with elastic fibres; no alveoli opening from the wall

cards.q: Where are club (Clara) cells, and how do they look?
cards.a: Terminal and respiratory bronchioles — non-ciliated cuboidal, dome-shaped apices full of granules

cards.q: What do club cells secrete?
cards.a: Surfactant-like phospholipids and mucins

cards.q: How do club cells detoxify inhaled chemicals?
cards.a: Abundant smooth endoplasmic reticulum (SER)

cards.q: What immune defences do club cells add?
cards.a: IgA secretory component, antimicrobial peptides, cytokines

cards.q: Besides secretion and defence, what other role do some club cells have?
cards.a: Stem cells

cards.q: Hyaline cartilage: last seen where, and gone by where?
cards.a: Last in bronchi (rings, then plates) → gone by bronchioles
cards.more:
FeatureLast seenGone by
CartilageBronchiBronchioles
GlandsBronchiBronchioles
Goblet cellsLarger bronchiolesTerminal bronchioles
CiliaRespiratory bronchiolesAlveolar ducts
Smooth muscleAlveolar ductsAlveolar wall
Elastic fibresAlveoliPresent throughout

cards.q: Glands: last seen where, and gone by where?
cards.a: Last in bronchi → gone by bronchioles

cards.q: Goblet cells: last seen where, and gone by where?
cards.a: Last in larger bronchioles → gone by terminal bronchioles

cards.q: Cilia: last seen where, and gone by where?
cards.a: Last in respiratory bronchioles (a few) → gone by alveolar ducts

cards.q: Smooth muscle: last seen where, and gone by where?
cards.a: Last in alveolar ducts (ringing alveolar openings) → gone by the alveolar wall

cards.q: Which airway wall component is present all the way to the alveoli?
cards.a: Elastic fibres

cards.q: What is asthma, and which cells are involved?
cards.a: Chronic inflammation of the bronchial tree — mast cells, eosinophils, T lymphocytes

cards.q: What is the sequence of an acute asthmatic bronchospasm?
cards.a: Antigen → mast cells degranulate → bronchiolar smooth muscle contracts suddenly

cards.q: Why do bronchioles suffer most in asthma?
cards.a: Proportionally thickest muscle layer and no cartilage to hold them open

cards.q: What chronic wall changes does asthma cause?
cards.a:
Smooth-muscle hypertrophy
Thickened basement membrane
More goblet and basal cells
Mucus plugs
Squamous metaplasia

cards.q: How do epinephrine and other sympathomimetics help in asthma?
cards.a: Relax bronchiolar smooth muscle → widen bronchioles

cards.q: What happens to the bronchial lining of a chronic smoker?
cards.a: Ciliated columnar → stratified squamous (squamous metaplasia) → can progress to precancerous dysplasia

cards.q: Why does squamous metaplasia in smokers impair clearance?
cards.a: Squamous cells withstand smoke but have no cilia, so mucus is not cleared

lessons.t: Where gas is exchanged: bronchioles to alveoli

cards.q: What is the first segment of the respiratory portion, and where does it come from?
cards.a: Respiratory bronchiole — branches from the terminal bronchiole

cards.q: What lines a respiratory bronchiole?
cards.a: Small cuboidal cells and club cells over some smooth muscle (like the terminal bronchiole)

cards.q: What is the main difference between a respiratory and a terminal bronchiole?
cards.a: Alveoli open from the respiratory bronchiole's wall
cards.more: Gas exchange begins the moment alveoli appear in the airway wall, so the openings are what you look for.

cards.q: What vessel runs alongside a respiratory bronchiole?
cards.a: A branch of the pulmonary artery

cards.q: What makes up the wall of an alveolar duct?
cards.a: Almost entirely alveolar openings, each ringed by a little smooth muscle (pink knob between alveoli)

cards.q: What is an alveolar sac?
cards.a: A cluster of alveoli around a shared space, at the end of an alveolar duct

cards.q: From the alveolar ducts on, what is the lining and supporting matrix?
cards.a: Simple squamous lining; elastic and collagen (reticular) fibres

cards.q: Where is smooth muscle found in the alveolar region?
cards.a: Only at the alveolar openings

cards.q: What do the elastic fibres around alveoli do?
cards.a: Let alveoli stretch on inspiration and recoil passively on expiration

cards.q: Describe the type I pneumocyte.
cards.a: Squamous, extremely thin, joined by occluding (tight) junctions
cards.more: On a slide you see only a flat, dark nucleus against the wall.

cards.q: What is the role of type I pneumocytes?
cards.a: Line almost the entire alveolar surface; gas crosses them

cards.q: What are the other names for the type II pneumocyte?
cards.a: Septal cell; great alveolar cell

cards.q: Describe the type II pneumocyte on a slide.
cards.a: Cuboidal, rounded, bulging into the alveolus, often where septa meet; pale vesicular cytoplasm

cards.q: On TEM, what organelle identifies a type II pneumocyte, and what does it store?
cards.a: Lamellar bodies (granules of stacked membranes) → store surfactant

cards.q: What happens to type II pneumocytes after alveolar damage?
cards.a: They divide to replace both type I and type II cells (stem cell of the lining)

cards.q: What is the physical structure of surfactant?
cards.a: Film of phospholipids and lipoproteins over a thin layer of water

cards.q: What are the components of surfactant?
cards.a:
Dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine (DPPC)
Cholesterol
Surfactant proteins A, B, C, D

cards.q: How does surfactant work, and what does it achieve?
cards.a: Lowers surface tension → alveoli don't collapse at end-expiration, inflate with less force → less work of breathing

cards.q: Type II pneumocytes share surfactant production and other functions with which airway cell?
cards.a: Club cells

cards.q: What are alveolar macrophages also called, where do they come from, and where do they sit?
cards.a: Dust cells — from blood monocytes; in the alveoli or septa

cards.q: What do alveolar macrophages phagocytose?
cards.a: Inhaled particles and red cells that escape the capillaries

cards.q: How do alveolar macrophages leave the lung?
cards.a: Mucociliary clearance or the lymphatics

cards.q: What are heart failure cells?
cards.a: Alveolar macrophages full of brown haemosiderin from red cells leaking into congested alveoli in congestive heart failure

cards.q: What is anthracosis, and where do the cells collect?
cards.a: Carbon-laden macrophages (coal miners, city dwellers, smokers) — in connective tissue beside lymphatics, lymphoid tissue along bronchi, at the hilum
cards.more: Large black-pigmented cells in alveoli and septa are macrophages.

cards.q: What does the interalveolar septum contain?
cards.a:
Type I and II cells on both faces
Dense capillary plexus (red cells, leukocytes)
Connective tissue: fibroblasts, elastic and reticular fibres, macrophages

cards.q: What is the difference between the interalveolar septum and the blood–air barrier?
cards.a:
Septum: the whole partition between two alveoli
Barrier: just the shortest path gas takes across it

cards.q: List the layers of the blood–air barrier, air to blood.
cards.a: Surfactant (counted by some sources) → type I cell → fused basal laminae → capillary endothelium

cards.q: What kind of capillary endothelium forms the blood–air barrier?
cards.a: Thin, continuous

cards.q: On TEM, what is a thin portion of the alveolar septum?
cards.a: Where the two basal laminae fuse — gas exchange happens here

cards.q: On TEM, what is a thick portion of the alveolar septum?
cards.a: Where connective-tissue cells (fibroblasts) and fibres sit between epithelium and endothelium

cards.q: What are the pores of Kohn?
cards.a: Small holes through the alveolar septa connecting neighbouring alveoli

cards.q: What do the pores of Kohn do?
cards.a: Equalize air pressure; let air arrive from the side when an alveolus's airway is blocked

cards.q: How do the pores of Kohn help lobar pneumonia spread?
cards.a: Let fluid and bacteria pass from alveolus to alveolus

cards.q: What is the pleura made of?
cards.a: Mesothelium (simple squamous) on thin connective tissue — visceral on lung, parietal on chest wall

cards.q: What causes hyaline membrane disease, and in whom?
cards.a: Surfactant deficiency from immature type II cells — premature infants
cards.more: It is the respiratory distress syndrome of premature infants.

cards.q: What happens to the lungs without surfactant in hyaline membrane disease?
cards.a: Alveoli collapse (atelectasis) → hypoxia

cards.q: What does hyaline membrane disease look like in section?
cards.a: Many collapsed alveoli; open airspaces lined by pink hyaline membranes

cards.q: What are hyaline membranes made of?
cards.a: Dead type II cell debris + fibrin

cards.q: What is emphysema?
cards.a: Destruction of alveolar walls with loss of elasticity — a form of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)

cards.q: How does smoking cause emphysema?
cards.a: Loss of antitrypsin activity → elastase from macrophages destroys elastin

cards.q: What does emphysema do to the alveoli, and what are the consequences?
cards.a: Many small alveoli → fewer, larger, floppy spaces → less surface for exchange, less recoil to push air out

cards.q: What is pulse aspiration pneumonia?
cards.a: Non-infectious granulomatous pneumonitis from inhaled legumes (e.g. lentils); images as small, poorly defined nodules

cards.q: On a slide, how do you name the parts of the respiratory portion?
cards.a:
Terminal bronchiole: complete cuboidal-and-muscle wall, no alveoli
Respiratory bronchiole: same lining broken by alveolar openings
Alveolar duct: only a row of alveolar mouths with muscle knobs
Alveolar sac: the cluster at the end

cards.q: At high power, how do you tell type I, type II and macrophage apart?
cards.a:
Flat dark nucleus hugging the wall → type I
Plump rounded cell bulging into lumen → type II
Large free cell with brown or black granules → macrophage
cards.more: On TEM, lamellar bodies mean type II.

lessons.t: Blood: what is actually in it

cards.q: What tissue type is blood classified as?
cards.a: Connective tissue

cards.q: Why is blood counted as a connective tissue?
cards.a: Cells suspended in an extracellular matrix — the matrix just happens to be liquid

cards.q: Spin anticoagulated blood: what three layers form, bottom to top?
cards.a:
Red cells
Buffy coat (white cells + platelets)
Plasma

cards.q: About what percentage of blood volume is red cells, and what is that figure called?
cards.a: ~45% — the haematocrit

cards.q: How much of spun blood's volume is plasma?
cards.a: Just over half

cards.q: What is the buffy coat, and how much of the blood volume does it make up?
cards.a: Thin pale layer of white cells and platelets, between red cells and plasma; <1%

cards.q: What is the one difference between plasma and serum?
cards.a: Plasma has clotting factors; serum does not
cards.more: The lesson flags this as asked constantly.

cards.q: How do you obtain serum from blood?
cards.a: Let it clot → fibrinogen is consumed → leftover fluid = serum

cards.q: How do you obtain plasma from blood?
cards.a: Prevent clotting → spin → the fluid = plasma

cards.q: Which organelles does a mature red cell contain?
cards.a: None — no nucleus, no mitochondria; just a bag of haemoglobin

cards.q: What shape is a red cell?
cards.a: Biconcave disc

cards.q: What two advantages does the red cell's biconcave-disc shape give?
cards.a:
Extra surface area for gas exchange
Deforms to squeeze through capillaries narrower than itself

cards.q: Why is it fitting that a red cell has no mitochondria?
cards.a: It cannot use the oxygen it carries — right for a courier

cards.q: How long does a red cell live?
cards.a: About 120 days
cards.more: The summary box at the bottom of the figure also gives the 120-day life span.

cards.q: Rank the white blood cells from most to least common in normal adult blood.
cards.a: Neutrophil → lymphocyte → monocyte → eosinophil → basophil
cards.more:
Neutrophil~60%
Lymphocyte~30%
Monocyte~5%
Eosinophil~3%
Basophil<1%

The order itself is testable; the clickers use it.

cards.q: Which is the most common white blood cell, and roughly what share?
cards.a: Neutrophil, ~60%

cards.q: Which is the rarest white blood cell?
cards.a: Basophil (<1%)

cards.q: What does a neutrophil's nucleus look like?
cards.a: Multilobed
cards.more: Its granules are pale.

cards.q: What is the neutrophil's main job?
cards.a: First responder to bacteria

cards.q: Which white cell is second most common, and roughly what share?
cards.a: Lymphocyte, ~30%

cards.q: What does a lymphocyte look like on a smear?
cards.a: Large round nucleus, almost no cytoplasm

cards.q: What is the lymphocyte's role?
cards.a: Adaptive immunity

cards.q: Which is the largest white blood cell?
cards.a: Monocyte

cards.q: What shape is a monocyte's nucleus, and what share of white cells are monocytes?
cards.a: Kidney-shaped; ~5%

cards.q: What does a monocyte become once it enters tissue?
cards.a: Macrophage

cards.q: What does an eosinophil look like on a smear?
cards.a: Bilobed nucleus; large, bright red-orange granules

cards.q: What share of white cells are eosinophils, and what do they fight?
cards.a: ~3%; parasites and allergy

cards.q: What does a basophil look like on a smear?
cards.a: Dark granules that obscure the nucleus
cards.more: Basophils look dark and are sparse.

cards.q: What mediator is the basophil known for?
cards.a: Histamine

cards.q: Are platelets cells?
cards.a: No — fragments shed from a megakaryocyte, with no nucleus

cards.q: What do platelets do?
cards.a: Plug damaged vessels

cards.q: Why do platelets appear as small specks on a smear?
cards.a: No nucleus — they are fragments, not cells with structure

cards.topic: The stem cell and two lines
cards.q: Which single cell do all blood cells descend from?
cards.a: Haematopoietic stem cell

cards.topic: The stem cell and two lines
cards.q: What two things can the haematopoietic stem cell do?
cards.a:
Renew itself
Commit to a lineage

cards.topic: The stem cell and two lines
cards.q: Which cells does the myeloid line produce?
cards.a:
Red cells
Platelets
Granulocytes
Monocytes

cards.topic: The stem cell and two lines
