cards.q: Which cells does the lymphoid line produce?
cards.a:
T cells
B cells
NK cells

cards.topic: Where blood is made, by age
cards.q: In the fetus, where is blood made, in order?
cards.a: Yolk sac → liver and spleen → (increasingly) bone marrow
cards.more: The lesson notes the age pattern gets asked directly.

cards.topic: Where blood is made, by age
cards.q: After birth, where is blood made?
cards.a: Bone marrow, entirely

cards.topic: Where blood is made, by age
cards.q: In a child, how much of the marrow is red and active?
cards.a: Essentially all of it

cards.topic: Where blood is made, by age
cards.q: What happens to red marrow with age?
cards.a: Replaced by fat (yellow marrow); red marrow retreats to the axial skeleton

cards.topic: Where blood is made, by age
cards.q: Where does red marrow remain in an adult?
cards.a:
Vertebrae
Sternum
Ribs
Pelvis
Ends of long bones

cards.topic: Where blood is made, by age
cards.q: Why is an adult bone marrow biopsy taken from the iliac crest?
cards.a: One of the few adult sites with plenty of red marrow

cards.topic: Where blood is made, by age
cards.q: Why can a child's marrow be sampled far more widely than an adult's?
cards.a: A child's marrow is essentially all red

cards.q: What two changes happen in parallel as blood cells mature in the marrow?
cards.a:
Cell gets smaller
Nucleus condenses and shrinks

cards.q: Why does the nucleus-to-cytoplasm ratio fall as marrow cells mature?
cards.a: Nucleus shrinks while cytoplasm accumulates

cards.q: How does cytoplasm colour change as a red cell precursor matures?
cards.a: Deep blue → muddy intermediate → pink-orange

cards.q: Why is early red cell precursor cytoplasm deep blue, and late cytoplasm pink-orange?
cards.a:
Blue = many ribosomes making protein
Pink-orange = full of haemoglobin

cards.q: What happens to the nucleus in the red cell line?
cards.a: Condenses → extruded

cards.q: What is a reticulocyte?
cards.a: The cell left once the nucleus is extruded, with a few remaining ribosomes → becomes a mature red cell

cards.q: How does nuclear shape change as a granulocyte matures?
cards.a: Round → indented → horseshoe (band cell) → segmented into lobes

cards.q: What is a band cell?
cards.a: Immature granulocyte with a horseshoe-shaped nucleus

cards.q: What is a "left shift"?
cards.a: A rise in band cells in the blood

cards.q: What does a left shift mean, and what usually causes it?
cards.a: Marrow pushing out immature cells to meet demand — usually infection

cards.q: What two jobs does the lymphatic system do?
cards.a:
Drains tissue fluid back to the bloodstream
Immune function — filters that fluid through immune tissue

cards.q: Where does the fluid that lymphatics collect come from?
cards.a: Fluid leaked from capillaries into the tissues with every pass

cards.q: How are lymphatic capillaries built, compared with blood capillaries?
cards.a: Blind-ended tubes; thinner-walled and far more permeable

cards.q: How do lymphatic capillaries keep flow one-way?
cards.a: Overlapping endothelial cells act as one-way flaps — fluid pushes in, cannot push out

cards.q: What separates primary from secondary lymphoid organs?
cards.a:
Primary: lymphocytes made and matured
Secondary: lymphocytes do their work

cards.q: Name the primary lymphoid organs.
cards.a:
Bone marrow
Thymus

cards.q: What lymphoid role does the bone marrow play?
cards.a: All lymphocytes originate there; B cells mature there

cards.q: Where do T cells mature?
cards.a: Thymus

cards.q: Do lymphocytes in primary lymphoid organs meet antigen?
cards.a: No — they become competent there before meeting any antigen

cards.q: Name the secondary lymphoid organs.
cards.a:
Lymph nodes
Spleen
Tonsils
Gut-associated lymphoid tissue
cards.more: Where mature lymphocytes encounter antigen and respond.

cards.q: How does lymph enter and leave a lymph node?
cards.a: Several afferent vessels (convex surface) in → single efferent vessel out at the hilum

cards.q: Why does a lymph node have several vessels in and only one out?
cards.a: Slows flow → gives immune cells time to sample the lymph

cards.q: What does the cortex of a lymph node contain?
cards.a: B cells in follicles

cards.q: What does a pale germinal centre in a lymph-node follicle mean?
cards.a: The follicle is actively responding

cards.q: What is the paracortex of a lymph node?
cards.a: T cell zone, just deeper than the cortex

cards.q: What happens in the medulla of a lymph node?
cards.a: Cells exit

cards.q: What is the organising idea of B versus T cell zones in lymphoid tissue?
cards.a: B cells in cortical follicles; T cells in the paracortex between
cards.more: The same split appears in the spleen, as white pulp.

cards.q: What does the spleen filter?
cards.a: Blood (not lymph)

cards.q: What is splenic white pulp, and its function?
cards.a: Lymphoid tissue around arterioles — immune function

cards.q: What is splenic red pulp, and its job?
cards.a: Blood and macrophages — removes worn-out red cells

cards.q: How does the thymus change with age?
cards.a: Large and active in childhood → progressively replaced by fat after puberty

cards.q: What is a Hassall corpuscle, and where is it found?
cards.a: Whorl of flattened epithelial cells in the thymic medulla — found nowhere else

cards.topic: Which organ am I looking at?
cards.q: Slide: a capsule, follicles around the outside, sinuses draining towards a hilum. Which organ?
cards.a: Lymph node (filters lymph)
cards.more: The three lymphoid organs are routinely asked as image questions.

cards.topic: Which organ am I looking at?
cards.q: Slide: islands of lymphocytes around small arteries in a sea of blood-filled tissue. Which organ?
cards.a: Spleen — white pulp in red pulp (filters blood)

cards.topic: Which organ am I looking at?
cards.q: Slide: lobules with dark cortex and pale medulla, whorled bodies in the medulla, no follicles. Which organ?
cards.a: Thymus

cards.topic: Which organ am I looking at?
cards.q: On a lymphoid slide, what do follicles with germinal centres tell you?
cards.a: Lymph node or spleen — reacting to something

cards.topic: Which organ am I looking at?
cards.q: Why does the thymus have no follicles?
cards.a: It trains T cells; it is not where they respond to antigen

lessons.t: Amino acids and how proteins fold

cards.q: How many amino acids are commonly built into proteins?
cards.a: 20 (of more than 300 in nature)

cards.q: What four things are attached to an amino acid's α-carbon?
cards.a:
Amino group
Carboxyl group
Hydrogen
Side chain (R group)

cards.q: Which amino acid has an α-carbon that is not chiral?
cards.a: Glycine

cards.q: Which stereoisomer of amino acids do mammalian proteins use?
cards.a: L form

cards.q: What sets an amino acid's class?
cards.a: Its side chain: hydrophobic ones hide from water, hydrophilic ones face it

cards.q: Which amino acids are hydrophobic and aliphatic?
cards.a: Gly (G), Ala (A), Cys (C), Val (V), Leu (L), Ile (I), Met (M)
cards.more:
Hydrophobic, aliphaticG A C V L I M
Hydrophobic, aromaticF Y W
IminoP
Polar, unchargedS T N Q
AcidicD E
BasicK R H

cards.q: Which amino acids are hydrophobic and aromatic?
cards.a: Phe (F), Tyr (Y), Trp (W)

cards.q: Is tyrosine hydrophobic or hydrophilic?
cards.a: Mainly hydrophobic — though its OH can hydrogen-bond

cards.q: Which amino acid is the imino acid, and what does its structure do?
cards.a: Proline (P) — rigid ring; sits in bends

cards.q: Which amino acids are polar and uncharged?
cards.a: Ser (S), Thr (T), Asn (N), Gln (Q)
cards.more: They form hydrogen bonds.

cards.q: Which amino acids are acidic, and what is their charge at pH 7.4?
cards.a: Asp (D), Glu (E) — negative

cards.q: Which amino acids are basic, and what is their charge at pH 7.4?
cards.a: Lys (K), Arg (R), His (H) — positive

cards.q: What is histidine's charge at pH 7.4?
cards.a: Mostly uncharged — only weakly basic

cards.q: Which two amino acids sit on the border between hydrophobic and polar uncharged?
cards.a: Cysteine and tyrosine
cards.more: Many charts call them polar uncharged.

cards.q: Name the seven amino acids whose side chains can ionise.
cards.a: Asp, Glu, Arg, His, Lys, Cys, Tyr

cards.q: Where do a soluble protein and a membrane protein put their nonpolar residues?
cards.a:
Soluble: buried inside
Membrane: turned outward into the lipid bilayer

cards.q: How does a G-protein-coupled receptor cross the membrane?
cards.a: Seven α-helices of mostly hydrophobic residues

cards.q: What sequence feature signals a membrane-spanning segment?
cards.a: A helix of ~20 residues rich in valine, leucine and isoleucine

cards.q: What are the approximate pK<sub>a</sub>s of an amino acid's α-carboxyl and α-amino groups?
cards.a:
α-carboxyl ~2.2
α-amino ~9.4

cards.q: At pH 7.4, what form are the α-carboxyl and α-amino groups in?
cards.a: COO<sup>−</sup> and NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup>

cards.q: What is a zwitterion?
cards.a: Molecule with equal positive and negative charges, net charge zero
cards.more: An amino acid with an uncharged side chain is a zwitterion at pH 7.4.

cards.q: What is the isoelectric point (pI)?
cards.a: The pH at which net charge is zero

cards.q: What is an amino acid's net charge below its pI, and above it?
cards.a:
Below pI: net positive
Above pI: net negative

cards.q: How do you calculate the pI of an amino acid with only two ionisable groups?
cards.a: Average the two pK<sub>a</sub>s

cards.q: What is the pI of alanine (pK<sub>a</sub>s 2.3 and 9.1)?
How do you calculate the pI of an amino acid with an ionisable side chain?
cards.a: Average the two nearest pK<sub>a</sub>s

cards.q: What is the pI of aspartate (pK<sub>a</sub>s 2.0, 4.0, 9.5)?
What is the pI of arginine (pK<sub>a</sub>s 2.1, 9.0, 12.5)?
What is a peptide bond?
cards.a: Amide link: α-carboxyl of one amino acid + α-amino group of the next

cards.q: What is released when a peptide bond forms, and what is needed to break it?
cards.a:
Forming releases water (condensation)
Breaking takes water back (hydrolysis)

cards.q: Why can't the peptide bond rotate?
cards.a: Partial double-bond character

cards.q: What is the peptide unit?
cards.a: Cα and C=O of one residue + N–H and Cα of the next, lying flat in one plane
cards.more: The R groups are trans.

cards.q: Are the R groups across a peptide bond cis or trans?
cards.a: Trans

cards.q: Around which bonds can a polypeptide chain bend, and what are the angles called?
cards.a:
N–Cα (Φ, phi)
Cα–C (Ψ, psi)

cards.q: In which direction is a peptide sequence written and read?
cards.a: N-terminus (left) → C-terminus (right)
cards.more: Tyr-Gly-Gly-Phe-Leu is tyrosylglycylglycylphenylalanylleucine.

cards.q: What is primary structure, and what holds it?
cards.a: The amino acid sequence — peptide bonds

cards.q: What is secondary structure, and what holds it?
cards.a: Local folding of the backbone — hydrogen bonds between backbone C=O and N–H

cards.q: What is tertiary structure, and what holds it?
cards.a: Whole fold of one chain — side-chain interactions (non-covalent and covalent)

cards.q: What is quaternary structure, and what holds it?
cards.a: Arrangement of several chains — non-covalent forces

cards.q: What handedness and how many residues per turn does an α-helix have?
cards.a: Right-handed; 3.6 residues per turn

cards.q: How long is an average α-helix?
cards.a: ~12 residues (range 5–45)

cards.q: How are the hydrogen bonds arranged in an α-helix?
cards.a: Each C=O bonds the N–H four residues along the same chain; bonds run inside, parallel to the axis

cards.q: Which way do the R groups point in an α-helix?
cards.a: Outward

cards.q: Where do the hydrogen bonds run in a β-sheet?
cards.a: Between neighbouring strands

cards.q: What two orientations can β-sheet strands have?
cards.a:
Parallel (same direction)
Antiparallel (opposite directions)

cards.q: Where do the R groups sit in a β-sheet?
cards.a: Above and below the sheet

cards.q: What are irregular stretches of a polypeptide called?
cards.a: Random coil

cards.q: Which small amino acid favours the α-helix?
cards.a: Alanine

cards.q: Which amino acid is the helix breaker, and why?
cards.a: Proline — its rigid ring kinks the chain

cards.q: Which amino acids are common in β-sheets, and why?
cards.a: Trp, Tyr, Phe (large rings) — sheets leave room for bulky side chains

cards.q: What is a β-turn, and which amino acids usually build it?
cards.a: A tight U-turn — glycine (smallest R group) and proline (the kink)

cards.q: Switching between β-sheet and α-helix rearranges which bonds?
cards.a: Hydrogen bonds, not peptide bonds — the sequence is unchanged
cards.more: That switch is what goes wrong in the misfolding diseases.

cards.q: What are domains, and give an all-α and a β-barrel example.
cards.a:
Packed secondary elements within a tertiary fold
All-α: myoglobin and haemoglobin chains
β-barrel: green fluorescent protein

cards.q: Name the five interactions that hold a tertiary fold.
cards.a:
Hydrophobic interactions
Hydrogen bonds
Ionic bonds
Disulfide bonds
Metal ions

cards.q: What is an example of an ionic bond in a folded protein?
cards.a: Electrostatic attraction, e.g. aspartate with lysine

cards.q: Which tertiary bond is covalent, between which residues, and in which named protein?
cards.a: Disulfide bond — between cysteines; e.g. insulin

cards.q: Give two examples of metal ions holding a protein fold.
cards.a:
Zinc in zinc fingers of steroid-hormone receptors
Copper site of plastocyanin

cards.q: Give two examples of quaternary structure.
cards.a:
Haemoglobin: 2α + 2β
Insulin: hexamer around zinc
cards.more: Subunits may be identical or different.

cards.q: How can quaternary subunits behave relative to each other?
cards.a: Independently, or cooperatively (as in haemoglobin)

cards.q: What determines a protein's tertiary structure?
cards.a: Its primary sequence — a chain folds itself

cards.q: What is the driving force of protein folding?
cards.a: Hydrophobic effect — nonpolar side chains gather in the core away from water
cards.more: Entropy-driven; the protein settles at its lowest free energy.

cards.q: At what energy state does a folded protein settle?
cards.a: Lowest free energy

cards.q: What are chaperones, and what do they use?
cards.a: Heat shock proteins (Hsp) that help folding — use ATP

cards.q: What does Hsp70 do?
cards.a: Binds exposed hydrophobic stretches that would clump

cards.q: What does Hsp60 do?
cards.a: Encloses the folding chain and acts as a template

cards.q: What two things can make a protein misfold?
cards.a:
A mutation
A folding fault

cards.q: What usually happens to a misfolded protein?
cards.a: Degraded (ubiquitin–proteasome)

cards.q: What structure do amyloid-forming proteins adopt, and what do they form?
cards.a: β-sheet → insoluble amyloid fibrils

cards.q: Which protein forms amyloid in Alzheimer disease?
cards.a: Amyloid β (Aβ)

cards.q: Which protein forms amyloid in Parkinson disease?
cards.a: α-Synuclein

cards.q: Which protein forms amyloid in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS)?
cards.a: TDP-43

cards.q: Which class of amyloid disease includes Huntington disease?
cards.a: Polyglutamine diseases

cards.q: How is Aβ made in Alzheimer disease?
cards.a: Amyloid precursor protein (APP) cut by β- and γ-secretase → Aβ (40/42) → aggregates into plaques

cards.q: What does α-secretase do to amyloid precursor protein?
cards.a: The usual cut — prevents Aβ forming

cards.q: Which gene is linked to sporadic Alzheimer disease?
cards.a: APOE

cards.q: How does PrP<sup>Sc</sup> differ from normal PrP<sup>C</sup>?
cards.a: Same sequence, different conformation

cards.q: What two properties make PrP<sup>Sc</sup> dangerous?
cards.a:
Forms protease-resistant fibrils
Templates more PrPC into PrPSc

cards.q: What are the three origins of prion disease, with examples?
cards.a:
Sporadic (most)
Inherited: familial Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease (autosomal dominant)
Acquired: mad cow disease, cadaveric growth hormone, kuru

cards.q: Name the prion disease in humans, sheep, cattle and deer.
cards.a:
Humans: Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease
Sheep: scrapie
Cattle: bovine spongiform encephalopathy
Deer: chronic wasting disease

cards.q: Fibrous vs globular proteins: shape and role?
cards.a:
Fibrous: long, narrow, structural
Globular: rounded, functional (catalysis, transport)
cards.more:
FibrousGlobular
Shape, roleLong, narrow; structuralRounded; functional
In waterGenerally insolubleGenerally soluble
SequenceRepetitiveIrregular
Heat, pHLess sensitiveMore sensitive

cards.q: Fibrous vs globular proteins: solubility in water?
cards.a:
Fibrous: generally insoluble
Globular: generally soluble

cards.q: Fibrous vs globular proteins: sequence?
cards.a:
Fibrous: repetitive
Globular: irregular

cards.q: Fibrous vs globular proteins: sensitivity to heat and pH?
cards.a:
Fibrous: less sensitive
Globular: more sensitive

cards.q: Give examples of fibrous proteins.
cards.a: Collagen, keratin, elastin, actin, myosin, fibrin

cards.q: Give examples of globular proteins.
cards.a: Haemoglobin, insulin, catalase, immunoglobulins

cards.q: Myoglobin and haemoglobin differ at which level of protein structure?
cards.a: Quaternary
cards.more: Both bind O2 with haem at the centre and have similar primary, secondary and tertiary structure; the quaternary difference drives everything else.

cards.q: What is myoglobin's structure?
cards.a: Monomer — one chain, one haem, one O<sub>2</sub>

cards.q: What is haemoglobin's structure?
cards.a: Tetramer — four chains (2α + 2β in adults), four haems, four O<sub>2</sub>

cards.q: Where is myoglobin found, and what does it do?
cards.a: Cardiac and skeletal muscle — stores O<sub>2</sub> for the muscle's own ATP production during contraction

cards.q: What are the approximate molecular masses of myoglobin and haemoglobin?
cards.a:
Myoglobin ~17 kDa
Haemoglobin ~64 kDa

cards.q: What share of the red cell's dry weight is haemoglobin?
cards.a: About 96%

cards.q: What is haemoglobin's job?
cards.a: Carry O<sub>2</sub> from lungs to tissues

cards.q: What is cooperativity in haemoglobin?
cards.a: One subunit binds O<sub>2</sub> → changes shape → next subunit binds more easily

cards.q: What shape is each oxygen-binding curve: haemoglobin vs myoglobin?
cards.a:
Haemoglobin: sigmoid (S-shaped)
Myoglobin: hyperbola

cards.q: Why does haemoglobin's curve have to be sigmoid?
cards.a: Loads fully in the lungs (high PO<sub>2</sub>) and unloads readily in the tissues (lower PO<sub>2</sub>)

cards.q: Why would a hyperbolic carrier like myoglobin be a poor O<sub>2</sub> transporter?
cards.a: It grips O<sub>2</sub> just as tightly in the tissues and won't let go — right for a store, wrong for a transporter

cards.q: How does the flat top of the haemoglobin curve protect loading, in numbers?
cards.a: Alveolar PO<sub>2</sub> 104 → 60 mm Hg drops saturation only ~97% → 89%
cards.more: As on a mountain.

cards.q: What is the P<sub>50</sub>?
cards.a: The PO<sub>2</sub> at which half the binding sites are full

cards.q: What are the P<sub>50</sub>s of myoglobin and haemoglobin?
cards.a:
Myoglobin ~1 mm Hg
Haemoglobin ~26 mm Hg

cards.q: Where is haemoglobin's curve steepest, and why does it matter?
cards.a: Across tissue PO<sub>2</sub> → a small fall in PO<sub>2</sub> releases a lot of O<sub>2</sub>
cards.more: In the lungs haemoglobin is fully saturated.

cards.q: In muscle, which way does O<sub>2</sub> pass between haemoglobin and myoglobin, and why?
cards.a: Haemoglobin → myoglobin — myoglobin stays almost full at tissue PO<sub>2</sub>; suits its storage role

cards.q: What is deoxyhaemoglobin's state, and its O<sub>2</sub> affinity?
cards.a: T (taut) — low affinity

cards.q: What is oxyhaemoglobin's state, and its O<sub>2</sub> affinity?
cards.a: R (relaxed) — high affinity

cards.q: How does every modifier change haemoglobin's grip on O<sub>2</sub>?
cards.a: By tipping the T ⇌ R equilibrium

cards.q: Which two molecules favour the R state, and which way do they shift the curve?
cards.a: O<sub>2</sub> and carbon monoxide → shift left (lower P<sub>50</sub>)
cards.more: O2 favouring R is the cooperativity itself.

cards.q: Which three things favour the T state, and which way do they shift the curve?
cards.a: H<sup>+</sup>, CO<sub>2</sub>, 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate (2,3-BPG) → shift right (higher P<sub>50</sub>)
cards.more: The lesson flags the shift directions as standard, tested material.

cards.q: Which three features of hard-working tissue make haemoglobin release O<sub>2</sub> more readily?
cards.a:
Acidic
Warm
High CO2

cards.q: What is the Bohr effect?
cards.a: Acid and CO<sub>2</sub> lowering haemoglobin's O<sub>2</sub> affinity
cards.more: Heat acts separately, in the same direction.

cards.q: Why is the Bohr effect self-targeting?
cards.a: Tissue signals its own need with its own metabolic waste

cards.q: How does carbonic anhydrase drive the Bohr effect?
cards.a: CO<sub>2</sub> → carbonic acid → H<sup>+</sup> binds ionisable groups on haemoglobin → stabilises T

cards.q: What is carbaminohaemoglobin?
cards.a: CO<sub>2</sub> bound to the terminal amino groups of the globin chains — stabilises T
cards.more: Hb–NH2 + CO2 ⇌ Hb–NH–COO− + H+

cards.q: What happens to the Bohr-effect chemistry in the lungs?
cards.a: Runs backwards: CO<sub>2</sub> breathed out → H<sup>+</sup> leaves → O<sub>2</sub> loads

cards.q: Where does 2,3-BPG come from?
cards.a: Red cells make it from a glycolytic intermediate — and can change how fast they make or break it down
cards.more: It acts like the Bohr effect but over a longer timescale.

cards.q: Where does 2,3-BPG bind haemoglobin, and with what effect?
cards.a: Positively charged pocket between the two β chains of deoxyhaemoglobin → stabilises T, lowers affinity

cards.q: When does 2,3-BPG rise?
cards.a:
Chronic hypoxia (altitude, anaemia, chronic lung disease)
Exercise

cards.q: At sea level, what saturations does haemoglobin load to and unload to, and how much is delivered?
cards.a: Loads 100% → leaves tissues 60% → 40% delivered

cards.q: At altitude before adaptation, how much O<sub>2</sub> does haemoglobin deliver?
cards.a: Loads 90% → leaves 60% → 30% delivered

cards.q: After altitude adaptation (more 2,3-BPG), how much O<sub>2</sub> does haemoglobin deliver?
cards.a: Loads 80% → unloads to 40% → 40% delivered

cards.q: Why does a right shift help at altitude?
cards.a: A small loss in loading buys a bigger gain in unloading

cards.q: How much more tightly than O<sub>2</sub> does carbon monoxide (CO) bind haem?
cards.a: About 220×

cards.q: Why does CO poisoning cut O<sub>2</sub> delivery twice over?
cards.a:
Takes binding sites from O2
Pushes Hb into R state → bound O2 not released
cards.more: CO binding is reversible.

cards.q: What is haem?
cards.a: Iron held in a protoporphyrin ring
cards.more: Other haem proteins include the cytochromes and catalase.

cards.q: Which form of iron binds O<sub>2</sub>?
cards.a: Ferrous (Fe<sup>2+</sup>)

cards.q: What is methaemoglobin?
cards.a: Haemoglobin with iron oxidised to Fe<sup>3+</sup> — cannot carry O<sub>2</sub>

cards.q: Which drugs and chemicals oxidise haemoglobin to methaemoglobin?
cards.a:
Nitrates and nitrites
Local anaesthetics (benzocaine)
Sodium nitroprusside
NO2
cards.more: The cell's own reactive oxygen species can also do it.

cards.q: Which enzyme reduces methaemoglobin back, and what happens when it is deficient?
cards.a: NADH–methaemoglobin reductase (NADH–cytochrome b<sub>5</sub> reductase) → methaemoglobin builds up

cards.q: What inherited haemoglobin variants cause methaemoglobinaemia?
cards.a: HbM

cards.q: What are the signs of methaemoglobinaemia?
cards.a:
Cyanosis with chocolate-brown blood
Anxiety, headache, dyspnoea (in proportion to the hypoxia)
cards.more: Nicknamed "blue baby syndrome".

cards.q: How is methaemoglobinaemia treated?
cards.a: Methylene blue — drives Fe<sup>3+</sup> back to Fe<sup>2+</sup>

cards.q: Define partial pressure, saturation and content of O<sub>2</sub>.
cards.a:
PO2: dissolved O2, pushing
Saturation: fraction of Hb sites occupied
Content: total O2 per unit blood

cards.q: What two things does O<sub>2</sub> content depend on?
cards.a:
Saturation
Amount of haemoglobin

cards.q: In anaemia, what happens to PO<sub>2</sub>, saturation and O<sub>2</sub> content?
cards.a:
PO2 normal
Saturation normal
Content low (less haemoglobin)

cards.q: In carbon monoxide poisoning, what happens to PO<sub>2</sub> and O<sub>2</sub> content, and why is delivery worse still?
cards.a:
PO2 normal; content low (sites taken by CO)
Remaining O2 held more tightly → less released
cards.more: Haemoglobin amount is normal. Two patients, normal PO2, badly low delivery, different mechanisms.

cards.q: Faced with an anaemia or CO question, what should you decide before reaching for the curve?
cards.a: Whether it asks for content, saturation or partial pressure

cards.q: Which chromosome carries the α-globin family, and which genes?
cards.a: Chromosome 16 — ζ (zeta), α1, α2

cards.q: Which chromosome carries the β-globin family, and which genes?
cards.a: Chromosome 11 — ε (epsilon), Gγ and Aγ (gamma), δ (delta), β

cards.q: What chain makeup does every haemoglobin share?
cards.a: Two α-like + two β-like chains

cards.q: Which haemoglobin does the embryo make in the first month, and where?
cards.a: Hb Gower, in the yolk sac (Gower 1 = ζ<sub>2</sub>ε<sub>2</sub>)

cards.q: Which haemoglobin takes over from around week 5, and where is it made?
cards.a: HbF (α<sub>2</sub>γ<sub>2</sub>) — liver, then marrow

cards.q: When does HbA (α<sub>2</sub>β<sub>2</sub>) synthesis rise, and when does it become the main haemoglobin?
cards.a: From ~8th month of pregnancy → main haemoglobin gradually after birth

cards.q: Why does HbF bind 2,3-BPG poorly?
cards.a: Its γ chains lack some of the positively charged amino acids lining the 2,3-BPG pocket

cards.q: What does weak 2,3-BPG binding do to HbF, and why does the fetus need it?
cards.a: Higher O<sub>2</sub> affinity → pulls O<sub>2</sub> across the placenta from the mother's blood

cards.q: What are HbA's chains and share of adult haemoglobin?
cards.a: α<sub>2</sub>β<sub>2</sub>, ~90%
cards.more:
HbAα2β2~90%
HbA2α2δ22–3%
HbFα2γ2<2%
HbA1cα2β2 + glucose4–6%

cards.q: What are HbA<sub>2</sub>'s chains and share of adult haemoglobin?
cards.a: α<sub>2</sub>δ<sub>2</sub>, 2–3%

cards.q: What are HbF's chains and share of adult haemoglobin?
cards.a: α<sub>2</sub>γ<sub>2</sub>, under 2%

cards.q: What is HbA<sub>1c</sub>, and what share of adult haemoglobin?
cards.a: HbA (α<sub>2</sub>β<sub>2</sub>) + glucose; 4–6%

cards.q: How does HbA<sub>1c</sub> form, and what does it reflect?
cards.a: Spontaneous glycation of HbA → average blood glucose over the previous 2–3 months

cards.q: What is a qualitative haemoglobin disorder, and the example?
cards.a: Normal amount of chain, structurally wrong — sickle cell

cards.q: What is a quantitative haemoglobin disorder, and the example?
cards.a: Structurally normal chain, not enough made — thalassaemias

cards.q: What is the sickle cell mutation?
cards.a: Glutamate → valine at position 6 of the β chain (E6V)
cards.more: Deoxygenated HbS polymerises.

cards.q: What are the thalassaemias (inheritance and cause)?
cards.a: Autosomal recessive haemolytic diseases from an imbalance in globin-chain synthesis

cards.q: Which are the most common single-gene disorders in humans?
cards.a: The thalassaemias

cards.q: Why does under-making one globin chain cause harm?
cards.a: α and β are normally made 1:1 → its partner chain is left in excess
cards.more: The shortfall can come from a point mutation, a deletion or another defect.

cards.q: How many β-globin genes are there, and what do β<sup>+</sup> and β<sup>0</sup> alleles make?
cards.a:
Two (one per chromosome 11)
β+: reduced amount
β0: none

cards.q: In β-thalassaemia, what kills the red cells early?
cards.a: Excess α chains aggregate and precipitate

cards.q: In β-thalassaemia, which haemoglobins rise?
cards.a: HbA<sub>2</sub> (α<sub>2</sub>δ<sub>2</sub>) and HbF (α<sub>2</sub>γ<sub>2</sub>)

cards.q: In which populations is β-thalassaemia most common?
cards.a: Asian, Mediterranean, Middle Eastern, Hispanic, West Indian

cards.q: β-thalassaemia minor: genotype and presentation?
cards.a: β<sup>+</sup>/β or β<sup>0</sup>/β — mild microcytic anaemia

cards.q: β-thalassaemia intermedia: genotype and presentation?
cards.a: β<sup>+</sup>/β<sup>+</sup> or β<sup>+</sup>/β<sup>0</sup> — microcytic anaemia; occasional transfusions

cards.q: β-thalassaemia major (Cooley anaemia): genotype and presentation?
cards.a: β<sup>0</sup>/β<sup>0</sup> — severe anaemia, splenomegaly, bone deformities; regular transfusions

cards.q: How many α-globin genes are there, and what sets α-thalassaemia severity?
cards.a: Four (two on each chromosome 16) — severity tracks how many are lost

cards.q: α-thalassaemia: one gene lost?
cards.a: Silent carrier — no symptoms

cards.q: α-thalassaemia: two genes lost?
cards.a: α-thalassaemia trait — mild anaemia

cards.q: α-thalassaemia: three genes lost?
cards.a: HbH disease — spare β chains form β<sub>4</sub> (HbH) → precipitates as Heinz bodies; variable anaemia

cards.q: α-thalassaemia: four genes lost?
cards.a: Hb Bart (γ<sub>4</sub>) → hydrops fetalis and fetal death

cards.q: In which populations is α-thalassaemia most common?
cards.a: Southeast Asian, West Indian, Mediterranean, African

cards.q: Why does the glutamate → valine swap make HbS stick to itself?
cards.a: Puts a hydrophobic protrusion on the surface that fits a hydrophobic pocket on a neighbouring molecule

cards.q: In which state does HbS polymerise, and with what result?
cards.a: Deoxy (T) state → long insoluble fibres → red cell bent into a sickle

cards.q: What general rule follows from HbS polymerising in the T state?
cards.a: Anything that favours the T state favours sickling

cards.q: What is a vaso-occlusive crisis?
cards.a: Rigid sickled cells block capillaries → ischaemia, microinfarction, tissue anoxia, severe pain

cards.q: Why do sickle cell patients have chronic anaemia and sometimes jaundice?
cards.a: Sickled cells are fragile → haemolyse and are removed by the spleen
cards.more: Jaundice may show as scleral icterus.

cards.q: How is sickle cell disease inherited, and how common is it in African Americans?
cards.a: Autosomal recessive; ~1 in 500

cards.topic: Sickle cell: triggers and a case
cards.q: By what four routes do triggers provoke sickling?
cards.a:
Push HbS to the T state
Concentrate HbS in the cell
Thicken the blood
Add oxidative stress

cards.topic: Sickle cell: triggers and a case
cards.q: Name the triggers of sickling.
cards.a:
Hypoxia (strenuous exercise, altitude, illness)
Acidosis
Dehydration
Extreme heat or cold
Alcohol, smoking
Infection, stress

cards.topic: Sickle cell: triggers and a case
cards.q: A woman with sickle cell disease flies to Denver, drinks heavily, and has severe back, abdominal and limb pain. Diagnosis?
cards.a: Acute vaso-occlusive pain episode
cards.more: She also had dehydration, tachypnoea and pale nail beds; haemoglobin 9 g/dL.

cards.topic: Sickle cell: triggers and a case
cards.q: How does altitude (Denver, ~5,300 ft) provoke sickling?
cards.a: PO<sub>2</sub> falls ~17–20% → more HbS in the deoxy state

cards.topic: Sickle cell: triggers and a case
cards.q: How does heavy drinking provoke sickling?
cards.a: Alcohol is a diuretic → dehydration → red cells shrink (HbS concentrated) + blood thickens and slows → cells stick and block capillaries

cards.topic: Sickle cell: triggers and a case
cards.q: The Denver sickle cell patient's anion gap is 147 − (110 + 16), with HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> 16. What is the gap, and what acid–base disorder is it?
cards.a: 21 → high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis
cards.more: pH 7.36, PCO2 29. Cause: alcohol-driven lactic acid, which itself favours deoxy-HbS.

cards.topic: Sickle cell: triggers and a case
cards.q: Why was the sickle cell patient in Denver breathing fast (PCO<sub>2</sub> 29)?
cards.a: Respiratory compensation for her metabolic acidosis

cards.topic: Sickle cell: triggers and a case
cards.q: What is the acute care for a vaso-occlusive pain episode?
cards.a:
IV opioids and saline
O2 if saturation <95%
Heparin to prevent clots, if admitted

cards.topic: Sickle cell: triggers and a case
cards.q: What long-term advice prevents sickle crises?
cards.a:
Avoid alcohol and smoking
Stay well hydrated
Avoid vigorous exercise
Take care at altitude

cards.q: What are the basic treatments for sickle cell disease?
cards.a:
Hydration
Analgesics
Packed red-cell transfusion

cards.q: How does hydroxyurea help in sickle cell disease?
cards.a: Raises HbF

cards.q: What is crizanlizumab and what does it do?
cards.a: Antibody against P-selectin (2019) — cuts vaso-occlusive crises

cards.q: What does L-glutamine (Endari, 2017) do in sickle cell disease?
cards.a: Reduces oxidative stress

cards.q: How does Casgevy work?
cards.a: CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing to raise HbF (2023; given with a stem-cell transplant)

cards.q: How does Lyfgenia work?
cards.a: Lentiviral vector → makes anti-sickling HbA (HbA<sup>T87Q</sup>) (2023; with a stem-cell transplant)

cards.q: What was voxelotor, and what happened to it?
cards.a: Blocked HbS polymerisation — approved, then withdrawn in 2024

cards.q: What does chronic transfusion target in sickle cell disease, and at what cost?
cards.a: Keeps HbS <50% → prevents stroke; cost: iron overload

cards.q: What is the HbC mutation?
cards.a: Glutamate → lysine at position 6 of the β chain (E6K)
cards.more: Sometimes printed "E6L", but L is leucine.

cards.q: What does HbC do inside red cells?
cards.a: Less soluble → forms crystals → cells less deformable

cards.q: What disease do HbC homozygotes and carriers have?
cards.a:
Homozygotes: mild chronic haemolytic anaemia, no pain crises
Carriers: silent

cards.q: What is HbSC disease?
cards.a: Compound heterozygote (one HbS + one HbC allele) — same kind of disease as sickle cell, milder

cards.q: Within what range is blood pH held?
What is the main defender of blood pH?
cards.a: The bicarbonate buffer system

cards.q: Why is the bicarbonate buffer called an open buffer system?
cards.a: Both ends are controlled: lungs → CO<sub>2</sub>; kidneys → HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>

cards.q: What is the definition of pH?
cards.a: pH = −log[H<sup>+</sup>]

cards.q: How much does [H<sup>+</sup>] change for a one-unit change in pH, and which way?
cards.a: Tenfold; lower pH = more H<sup>+</sup>

cards.q: Why is neutral pH 7?
cards.a: In pure water [H<sup>+</sup>] = [OH<sup>−</sup>] = 10<sup>−7</sup> M
cards.more: Their product is 10−14.

cards.q: How does [H<sup>+</sup>] at blood pH 7.1 compare with [H<sup>+</sup>] at pH 7.4?
cards.a: About twice as much
cards.more: Because pH is a log scale, blood’s narrow pH window still covers large changes in H+.

cards.q: What is an acid (proton definition)?
cards.a: A proton donor: HA → H<sup>+</sup> + A<sup>−</sup>
cards.more: A− is the acid’s conjugate base.

cards.q: What is a base (proton definition)?
cards.a: A proton acceptor: B + H<sup>+</sup> → BH<sup>+</sup>

cards.q: What makes an acid or base strong?
cards.a: Dissociates completely in water (e.g., HCl, NaOH)

cards.q: What makes an acid or base weak?
cards.a: Dissociates only partly; equilibrium set by its pK<sub>a</sub>
cards.more: Examples: acetic acid, lactic acid, ammonia.

cards.q: Lower pK<sub>a</sub> means what about an acid’s strength?
cards.a: Stronger acid

cards.q: What are the pK<sub>a</sub> values of lactic acid and acetic acid?
cards.a:
Lactic acid 3.9
Acetic acid 4.8
cards.more: Lactic acid has the lower pKa, so it is the stronger acid.

cards.q: State the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation.
cards.a: pH = pK<sub>a</sub> + log([A<sup>−</sup>]/[HA])
cards.more: It links pH to the ratio of a weak acid’s two forms.

cards.q: When pH = pK<sub>a</sub>, how do [A<sup>−</sup>] and [HA] compare?
cards.a: Equal

cards.q: Above its pK<sub>a</sub>, which form of a weak acid dominates, and how does it cross membranes?
cards.a: Charged A<sup>−</sup>; crosses poorly

cards.q: Below its pK<sub>a</sub>, which form of a weak acid dominates, and how does it cross membranes?
cards.a: Uncharged HA; crosses easily

cards.q: Does the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation apply to strong acids?
cards.a: No — weak acids and weak bases only
cards.more: Strong acids dissociate completely, so there is no equilibrium ratio to describe.

cards.q: What is the pK<sub>a</sub> of aspirin?
cards.a: 3.5 (a weak acid)

cards.q: Why is aspirin absorbed from the stomach?
cards.a: Stomach pH ≈ 2 < pK<sub>a</sub> 3.5 → mostly uncharged → crosses into blood
cards.more: This is why drug absorption depends on pH.

cards.q: What is a buffer?
cards.a: A weak acid mixed with its conjugate base

cards.q: How does a buffer keep pH from moving?
cards.a: Acid neutralises added base; conjugate base neutralises added acid

cards.q: At what pH is a buffer strongest, and why?
cards.a: pH = pK<sub>a</sub> — the two forms are equal

cards.q: Over what range is a buffer useful?
cards.a: Within about ±1 pH unit of its pK<sub>a</sub>
cards.more: The figure shows acetic acid (pKa 4.8) and its buffer region.

cards.q: What makes a buffer suited to hold a particular pH?
cards.a: Its pK<sub>a</sub> is close to that pH

cards.q: What is the main buffer in blood and its pK<sub>a</sub>?
cards.a: Bicarbonate/CO<sub>2</sub>, pK<sub>a</sub> 6.1
cards.more:
BufferWherepKa
Bicarbonate/CO2Blood6.1
PhosphateInside cells6.8
HaemoglobinBlood7.8

Plasma pH 7.4.

cards.q: What is the main buffer inside cells and its pK<sub>a</sub>?
cards.a: Phosphate, pK<sub>a</sub> 6.8
cards.more: Intracellular pH is about 6.9.

cards.q: What is the pK<sub>a</sub> of haemoglobin as a blood buffer?
Why is bicarbonate the main blood buffer even though its pK<sub>a</sub> (6.1) is more than a unit below blood pH?
cards.a: Lungs and kidneys keep resetting both of its halves

cards.q: Write the bicarbonate buffer reaction.
cards.a: CO<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O ↔ H<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> ↔ H<sup>+</sup> + HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>

cards.q: In the bicarbonate reaction, what does pushing it right vs pulling it left do?
cards.a:
Right → generates acid
Left → consumes acid

cards.q: Which organ controls the CO<sub>2</sub> side of the bicarbonate system, and how fast?
cards.a: Lungs; within minutes

cards.q: Which organ controls the HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> side of the bicarbonate system, and how fast?
cards.a: Kidneys; hours to days

cards.q: What does breathing faster do to blood pH?
cards.a: Blow off CO<sub>2</sub> → reaction pulled left → pH rises

cards.q: Write the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation for blood (bicarbonate system).
cards.a: pH = 6.1 + log([HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>] / (0.03 × PCO<sub>2</sub>))

cards.q: How is dissolved CO<sub>2</sub> calculated from PCO<sub>2</sub>?
cards.a: Dissolved CO<sub>2</sub> = 0.03 × PCO<sub>2</sub>

cards.q: Calculate normal blood pH from HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> 24 and PCO<sub>2</sub> 40.
cards.more: The acid-base map plots PCO2 against HCO3−; each line is one pH. The orange ellipse is the normal range (around 24 and 40).

cards.q: Which pK<sub>a</sub> should you use for the bicarbonate system in blood?
cards.more: Tables sometimes list 6.4 for carbonic acid/bicarbonate; use 6.1 for blood.

cards.q: What are the kidneys’ three acid-base jobs?
cards.a:
Reabsorb filtered HCO3−
Make new HCO3−
Excrete H+ as ammonium (NH4+)

cards.q: Which enzyme in the renal tubule cells is central to reabsorbing and making bicarbonate?
cards.a: Carbonic anhydrase

cards.q: How is an acid-base disorder named?
cards.a:
CO2 problem → respiratory; HCO3− problem → metabolic
pH low → acidosis; pH high → alkalosis
cards.more: Two questions, four answers.

cards.q: What is the basic problem in respiratory acidosis?
cards.a: CO<sub>2</sub> retained — not breathing enough

cards.q: What are the causes of respiratory acidosis?
cards.a:
COPD, opioid overdose, respiratory failure
Asthma, myasthenia gravis, restrictive lung disease
Excess CO2 in inspired air
Extra CO2 production (malignant hyperthermia)
cards.more: COPD = chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.

cards.q: Which acid-base disorder does malignant hyperthermia cause, and why?
cards.a: Respiratory acidosis — extra CO<sub>2</sub> production

cards.q: What is the basic problem in respiratory alkalosis?
cards.a: CO<sub>2</sub> blown off — breathing too much

cards.q: What are the causes of respiratory alkalosis?
cards.a:
Anxiety, high altitude, pain
Respiratory-centre stimulants (salicylates, analeptics)
Hypoxaemia (via peripheral chemoreceptors)
Pulmonary emboli
Excessive mechanical ventilation

cards.q: What is the basic problem in metabolic acidosis?
cards.a: Acid gained or bicarbonate lost

cards.q: What are the causes of metabolic acidosis?
cards.a:
Ketoacidosis, lactic acidosis, renal failure, diarrhoea
Toxins: methanol, ethylene glycol, salicylate

cards.q: What is the basic problem in metabolic alkalosis?
cards.a: Acid lost or bicarbonate gained

cards.q: What are the causes of metabolic alkalosis?
cards.a:
Vomiting
Diuretics
Bicarbonate (NaHCO3) infusion
Metabolism of ketoanions and other salts of metabolic acids

cards.q: What is the difference between acidaemia and acidosis?
cards.a:
Acidaemia = blood pH below 7.4
Acidosis = the process pushing it there
cards.more: Likewise alkalaemia (pH above 7.4) vs alkalosis. They usually travel together.

cards.q: Can an acidosis and an alkalosis be present with a normal pH?
cards.a: Yes — they can run at the same time

cards.q: What is the normal PCO<sub>2</sub>?
cards.a: 33–44 mm Hg (reference 40)
cards.more:
ValueRangeRef.
pH7.35–7.457.40
PCO233–44 mm Hg40
PO275–105 mm Hg
Na+135–145 mEq/L
HCO3−22–28 mEq/L24
Cl−98–106 mEq/L100
Anion gap8–16 mEq/L12

cards.q: What is the normal plasma HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>?
cards.a: 22–28 mEq/L (reference 24)

cards.q: What is the normal arterial PO<sub>2</sub>?
cards.a: 75–105 mm Hg

cards.q: What is the normal plasma Na<sup>+</sup>?
What is the normal plasma Cl<sup>−</sup>?
cards.a: 98–106 mEq/L (reference 100)

cards.q: What is the general rule for how the body compensates an acid-base disorder?
cards.a: Moves the other variable in the same direction

cards.q: How is a metabolic acidosis compensated?
cards.a: Breathing hard → blow off CO<sub>2</sub> (Kussmaul respiration)

cards.q: How is a respiratory acidosis compensated?
cards.a: Kidney retains HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> over days

cards.q: Is compensation ever complete?
cards.a: No — pulls pH towards normal, never past it
cards.more: So the pH still tells you which disorder is primary.

cards.q: Which compensation is fast and which is slow?
cards.a:
Respiratory (breathing) = fast, minutes
Renal = slow, a day or more

cards.q: Why does a respiratory disorder have an acute phase and a chronic phase?
cards.a: Kidney compensation takes a day+ → acute: almost none; chronic: substantial
cards.more: That is why an acute respiratory problem can look uncompensated. On the map, each respiratory disorder has two shaded bands: acute and chronic.

cards.q: What is the expected compensation for a respiratory acidosis?
cards.a: HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> up: acute +1–2, chronic +3–4 mEq/L per 10 mm Hg rise in PCO<sub>2</sub>

cards.q: What is the expected compensation for a respiratory alkalosis?
cards.a: HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> down: acute −1–2, chronic −4–5 mEq/L per 10 mm Hg fall in PCO<sub>2</sub>

cards.q: What is the expected compensation for a metabolic acidosis?
cards.a: Hyperventilation: PCO<sub>2</sub> −1.2 mm Hg per 1 mEq/L fall in HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>

cards.q: What is the expected compensation for a metabolic alkalosis?
cards.a: Hypoventilation: PCO<sub>2</sub> +0.6–0.75 mm Hg per 1 mEq/L rise in HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>; not past 55

cards.q: What does it mean if the compensation is bigger or smaller than expected?
cards.a: A second disorder is present
cards.more: The expected size also tells you whether a respiratory disorder is acute or chronic.

cards.q: What is the diagnostic sequence for a blood gas?
cards.a: Primary problem from pH and HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> → check compensation is expected size → split metabolic acidosis by anion gap

cards.q: Emphysema, 3 hours breathless: pH 7.18, PCO<sub>2</sub> 58, HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> 26. Diagnosis?
cards.a: Acute respiratory acidosis
cards.more: PCO2 is up 18 but bicarbonate only 2: the kidney has not caught up.

cards.q: COPD: pH 7.37, PCO<sub>2</sub> 52, HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> 29. Diagnosis?
cards.a: Respiratory acidosis with renal compensation

cards.q: Large aspirin dose, full rapid breathing: pH 7.57, PCO<sub>2</sub> 25, HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> 23. Diagnosis?
cards.a: Acute respiratory alkalosis

cards.q: Bulimia: pH 7.52, HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> 39, PCO<sub>2</sub> 49, K<sup>+</sup> 2.6. Diagnosis?
cards.a: Metabolic alkalosis with partial respiratory compensation
cards.more: Cause: lost stomach acid.

cards.q: What acid-base disorder does hyperventilation syndrome (anxiety/panic) cause, and what symptoms?
cards.a: Respiratory alkalosis; dizziness, tingling of lips and fingertips

cards.q: Why does breathing into a paper bag help hyperventilation syndrome?
cards.a: Rebreathing exhaled air raises PCO<sub>2</sub> back to normal

cards.q: What is the anion gap formula?
cards.a: [Na<sup>+</sup>] − ([Cl<sup>−</sup>] + [HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>])

cards.q: What is the normal anion gap?
What does the anion gap actually represent?
cards.a: Unmeasured anions minus unmeasured cations
cards.more: Na+ is the main measured cation; Cl− and HCO3− the main measured anions.

cards.q: Which unmeasured anions make up the anion gap?
cards.a: Lactate, phosphate, sulfate, ketones, albumin, any poison

cards.q: Which unmeasured cations are subtracted in the anion gap?
cards.a: K<sup>+</sup>, Ca<sup>2+</sup>, Mg<sup>2+</sup>, γ-globulin

cards.q: Which disorder does the anion gap split in two, and what question does it answer?
cards.a: Metabolic acidosis — was acid gained or base lost?

cards.q: Why does adding an acid (ketones, lactate) widen the anion gap?
cards.a: Its anions are new unmeasured anions

cards.q: Why does losing bicarbonate (diarrhoea) leave the anion gap normal?
cards.a: Cl<sup>−</sup> rises to replace the lost HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>

cards.q: What chloride terms go with high-gap and normal-gap metabolic acidosis?
cards.a:
High gap = normochloraemic
Normal gap = hyperchloraemic

cards.q: What causes a high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis?
cards.a:
Ketoacidosis, lactic acidosis, renal failure
Methanol, ethylene glycol, salicylate

cards.q: What causes a normal-anion-gap metabolic acidosis?
cards.a: Bicarbonate loss from the gut (diarrhoea) or kidney

cards.q: What does GOLD MARK stand for (high-gap causes)?
cards.a:
Glycols (ethylene, propylene)
5-Oxoproline
L-lactate
D-lactate
Methanol
Aspirin
Renal failure
Ketoacidosis
cards.more: The newer mnemonic.

cards.q: In GOLD MARK, what causes 5-oxoproline and D-lactate acidosis?
cards.a:
5-Oxoproline: chronic acetaminophen use
D-lactate: short bowel

cards.q: What does MUDPILES stand for (high-gap causes)?
cards.a:
Methanol
Uraemia
Diabetic ketoacidosis
Paraldehyde
Iron, isoniazid
Lactic acid
Ethanol, ethylene glycol
Salicylates
cards.more: The older mnemonic.

cards.q: Diarrhoea: pH 7.31, PCO<sub>2</sub> 31, HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> 16, Na<sup>+</sup> 134, Cl<sup>−</sup> 110. Gap and diagnosis?
cards.a: Gap 8 → normal-gap metabolic acidosis with expected respiratory compensation
cards.more: 134 − (110 + 16) = 8. PCO2 is down about 10, as expected.

cards.q: 6 days of diarrhoea: pH 7.12, PCO<sub>2</sub> 16, HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> 5, Na<sup>+</sup> 137, Cl<sup>−</sup> 118. Gap and diagnosis?
cards.a: Gap 14 → hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis

cards.q: Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), stopped insulin: pH 7.26, PCO<sub>2</sub> 19, HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> 8, Na<sup>+</sup> 136, Cl<sup>−</sup> 101. Gap and diagnosis?
cards.a: Gap 27 → high-gap metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation

cards.q: Depressed 16-year-old, possible ingestion, vomited ×3: pH 7.40, PCO<sub>2</sub> 40, HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> 24, Na<sup>+</sup> 144, Cl<sup>−</sup> 100. What does the gap show?
cards.a: Gap 20 → hidden high-gap metabolic acidosis

cards.q: In that 16-year-old with a gap of 20, why is the pH normal?
cards.a: Vomiting added a metabolic alkalosis → mixed disorder
cards.more: It is a second disorder, not compensation, because compensation never brings pH all the way back.

cards.q: Should you calculate the anion gap when pH, PCO<sub>2</sub> and bicarbonate are all normal?
cards.a: Yes — a normal blood gas does not rule out a disorder
cards.more: A high gap with a normal pH means a metabolic acidosis is being cancelled by a second process.

cards.q: What acid-base disorders does aspirin (salicylate) poisoning cause?
cards.a: Respiratory alkalosis + high-gap metabolic acidosis

cards.q: Why does salicylate cause a respiratory alkalosis?
cards.a: Stimulates the respiratory centre directly

cards.q: What three acids create the high gap in salicylate poisoning?
cards.a:
Salicylic acid
Lactic acid (uncouples oxidative phosphorylation → anaerobic metabolism)
Ketones (fatty-acid breakdown rises)

cards.q: How is salicylate poisoning treated?
cards.a: Activated charcoal + alkalinise urine with sodium bicarbonate
cards.more: Alkalinising the urine speeds salicylate excretion.

cards.q: How is ethylene glycol metabolised?
cards.a: Alcohol dehydrogenase → glycolaldehyde → glycolic → glyoxylic → oxalic acid

cards.q: What lab findings does ethylene glycol poisoning give?
cards.a:
High anion gap
Calcium oxalate crystals in urine
Low serum calcium
cards.more: Glycolate can read falsely as lactate.

cards.q: How is ethylene glycol poisoning treated?
cards.a: Fomepizole (blocks alcohol dehydrogenase)
cards.more: Ethanol, which competes for the enzyme, was used before fomepizole.

cards.q: Which tests tell aspirin poisoning from ethylene glycol poisoning?
cards.a: Serum salicylate level, serum calcium, urine crystals

cards.q: What property defines lipids as a group?
cards.a: Insoluble in water; soluble in nonpolar solvents (chloroform, ether)

cards.q: What are the four jobs of lipids?
cards.a:
Store energy
Build membranes
Carry signals
Insulate

cards.q: What is the difference between a nonpolar and a polar molecule?
cards.a:
Nonpolar: electrons shared equally, no charged poles
Polar: electrons shared unequally

cards.q: What is the structure of a fatty acid?
cards.a: Long hydrocarbon tail + acid (carboxyl) group at one end
cards.more: The tail is greasy and hates water; the acid end tolerates it. Almost every lipid in this block is built from fatty acids.

cards.q: How long are natural fatty acid chains, and what two features do almost all share?
cards.a: 4–36 carbons; unbranched, even number of carbons

cards.q: What is a saturated fatty acid, and what are its properties?
cards.a: No double bonds → straight, packs tightly, solid at room temperature (butter)

cards.q: What is an unsaturated fatty acid?
cards.a: One or more double bonds in the chain

cards.q: Which form of double bond is natural in fatty acids, and what does it do to the chain?
cards.a: Cis; puts a kink in it

cards.q: Why are unsaturated fats (e.g., olive oil) liquid at room temperature?
cards.a: Cis double bonds → kinks → can’t pack → liquid

cards.q: What does a trans double bond do to a fatty acid chain?
cards.a: Leaves it almost straight, like a saturated one

cards.q: How does melting point vary with chain length and unsaturation?
cards.a: Rises with chain length; falls with unsaturation
cards.more: More cis bonds mean more kinks.

cards.q: Which fats are risk factors for coronary artery disease?
cards.a: Saturated and trans fats

cards.q: How are fatty acid carbons numbered and named?
cards.a:
C1 = carboxyl carbon
C2 = α-carbon
C3 = β-carbon
Far methyl carbon = ω-carbon

cards.q: What does fatty acid shorthand such as 16:0 mean?
cards.a: Number of carbons : number of double bonds
cards.more: Palmitic acid is 16:0.

cards.q: How is the position of a double bond written, using oleic acid as the example?
cards.a: Δ counted from the carboxyl end: oleic = 18:1Δ9

cards.q: Name two saturated fatty acids with their shorthand.
cards.a:
Palmitic 16:0
Stearic 18:0

cards.q: What is a monounsaturated fatty acid? Give two examples.
cards.a: One double bond: palmitoleic 16:1, oleic 18:1

cards.q: What is a polyunsaturated fatty acid (PUFA)? Give three examples.
cards.a: Two or more double bonds: linoleic 18:2, linolenic 18:3, arachidonic 20:4
cards.more:
TypeDouble bondsExamples
Saturatednonepalmitic 16:0, stearic 18:0
Monounsaturatedonepalmitoleic 16:1, oleic 18:1
PUFAtwo or morelinoleic 18:2, linolenic 18:3, arachidonic 20:4

cards.q: How are fatty acids classified by length?
cards.a:
Short <6 C
Medium 6–12
Long 14–22
Very long >22
cards.more: In fatty acid oxidation, “very long” is usually drawn at over 20 carbons.

cards.q: Which tissue makes medium-chain fatty acids, and why does it matter?
cards.a: Lactating breast; infants digest them easily

cards.q: Where do fatty acid chains of up to 34 carbons occur?
cards.a: Central nervous system, especially myelin

cards.q: What is a triacylglycerol (TAG)?
cards.a: Three fatty acids on a glycerol backbone
cards.more: Simply fat as you would recognise it.

cards.q: What is the role of triacylglycerol?
cards.a: Body’s storage form of fat; holds most fatty acids

cards.q: Why is fat a better energy store than glycogen?
cards.a: >2× energy per gram vs carbohydrate/protein; stored dry (glycogen carries water)

cards.q: What bond joins each fatty acid to glycerol in TAG, and how is it broken?
cards.a: Ester bond; hydrolysis by a lipase

cards.q: Why is TAG even less water-soluble than free fatty acids?
cards.a: Charged carboxyl groups are used up in the ester bonds

cards.q: Why do fats and oils float?
cards.a: TAG is less dense than water

cards.q: How does a phospholipid differ from a TAG?
cards.a: One fatty acid replaced by a phosphate-containing head group
cards.more: Now one end loves water and the other hates it.

cards.q: What do phospholipids form in water, and how are they arranged?
cards.a: A bilayer: tails inward, heads outward → every membrane

cards.q: What is the structure of a glycerophospholipid?
cards.a: Two fatty acids ester-linked to C1 and C2 of L-glycerol 3-phosphate; C3 phosphate carries polar head group

cards.q: In a glycerophospholipid, which carbon usually holds the unsaturated fatty acid?
cards.a: C2

cards.q: What is the charge of a glycerophospholipid head group at body pH?
cards.a: Charged

cards.q: What is phosphatidic acid?
cards.a: Glycerophospholipid with no head group; parent of all the others

cards.q: What are the three most abundant phospholipids in humans?
cards.a:
Phosphatidylcholine (PC)
Phosphatidylethanolamine (PE)
Phosphatidylserine (PS)

cards.q: What is lecithin?
cards.a: Phosphatidylcholine (PC)

cards.q: What is the structure of cardiolipin?
cards.a: Two phosphatidic acids joined through a glycerol

cards.q: Where is cardiolipin found?
cards.a: Inner mitochondrial membrane (and bacteria)
cards.more: It is an acidic phospholipid.

cards.q: In which diseases do anti-cardiolipin antibodies appear?
cards.a:
Antiphospholipid syndrome
Syphilis
Systemic lupus erythematosus

cards.q: What is phosphatidylinositol and what does it do?
cards.a: Inositol head group; membrane lipid that also works in cell signalling

cards.q: What is the structure of platelet-activating factor (PAF)?
cards.a:
C1: ether-linked saturated chain
C2: acetyl ester
C3: phosphocholine

cards.q: What does platelet-activating factor (PAF) do?
cards.a:
Activates inflammatory cells
Mediates hypersensitivity, acute inflammation, anaphylaxis
Platelets aggregate and release serotonin

cards.q: What backbone do sphingolipids use instead of glycerol?
cards.a: Sphingosine, a long-chain amino alcohol

cards.q: What bond joins a fatty acid to sphingosine, and what does it form?
cards.a: Amide bond → ceramide

cards.q: What is ceramide?
cards.a: Sphingosine + fatty acid (amide); parent of every sphingolipid

cards.q: How does a polar head group attach to ceramide?
cards.a: Glycosidic or phosphodiester bond

cards.q: What is sphingomyelin?
cards.a: Ceramide + phosphocholine head; the only significant sphingophospholipid in humans

cards.q: Where is sphingomyelin important?
cards.a: Myelin sheath (key lipid); sits alongside cholesterol in membranes

cards.q: What is myelin made of?
cards.a: 76% lipid, 18% protein

cards.q: Which three bond types keep lipid classes apart (glycerol, sphingosine, PAF C1)?
cards.a:
Ester → glycerol (TAG, glycerophospholipids)
Amide → sphingosine (ceramide, all sphingolipids)
Ether → C1 of PAF

cards.q: What is the structure of cholesterol?
cards.a: Rigid four-ring structure (not a chain)

cards.q: What does cholesterol do in membranes?
cards.a: Wedges between phospholipids; regulates fluidity

cards.q: What is cholesterol the starting material for?
cards.a: Steroid hormones and bile salts

cards.q: Which lipids are storage lipids, and what are their properties?
cards.a: TAG and cholesteryl esters; neutral, in lipid droplets (above all adipose)

cards.q: Which lipids are membrane lipids, and what property do they share?
cards.a: Phospholipids, cholesterol, glycolipids; amphipathic

cards.q: What does amphipathic mean, and why does it matter for membranes?
cards.a: Both polar and nonpolar parts → lets them form a bilayer

cards.q: Why is fat hard to digest?
cards.a: Lipases are water-soluble, fat is not → enzyme works only at droplet surface
cards.more: One big droplet has very little surface.

cards.q: How much fat does an adult eat daily, and what is most of it?
cards.a: 60–150 g/day; >90% triacylglycerol (TAG)

cards.q: Besides TAG, what lipids are in the diet?
cards.a: Phospholipid, cholesterol, cholesteryl ester, free fatty acid

cards.q: Which enzymes digest each dietary lipid class?
cards.a:
TAG → lipases
Phospholipids → phospholipases A1, A2, C, D
Cholesteryl esters → cholesterol esterase

cards.q: How much energy does fat hold per gram, and what share of stored energy?
cards.a: 9.3 kcal/g; about 84% of the body’s stored energy

cards.q: Which lipases digest a little fat before the duodenum?
cards.a:
Lingual lipase (mouth)
Gastric lipase (stomach)

cards.q: At what pH do lingual and gastric lipase work?
cards.a: pH 4–6 (acid-stable)

cards.q: What substrate do lingual and gastric lipase prefer?
cards.a: TAG with short- and medium-chain fatty acids (<12 C: milk, butter, coconut oil)

cards.q: What do lingual and gastric lipase produce from TAG?
cards.a: Diacylglycerol + fatty acid
cards.more: They also remove a long unsaturated fatty acid from position 3.

cards.q: When do lingual and gastric lipase matter most?
cards.a:
Newborns (milk fat)
Cystic fibrosis (pancreatic lipase lacking)

cards.q: Where does digestion of the bulk of dietary fat begin?
cards.a: Duodenum

cards.q: Where are bile salts made and stored?
cards.a: Made by liver; stored in gallbladder

cards.q: How do bile salts act on fat?
cards.a: Detergents → break one large droplet into thousands of tiny ones (emulsification)
cards.more: One end greasy, one end water-friendly.

cards.q: Where does emulsification happen, and what helps it?
cards.a: Duodenum; mechanical mixing of peristalsis

cards.q: Do bile salts digest fat? What does emulsification achieve?
cards.a: No — multiplies surface area so the enzyme can work

cards.q: Which enzyme actually digests dietary fat?
cards.a: Pancreatic lipase

cards.q: What triggers cholecystokinin (CCK) release?
cards.a: Lipids and partly digested protein reaching lower duodenum and jejunum

cards.q: What does cholecystokinin (CCK) do?
cards.a:
Gallbladder contracts → releases bile
Pancreas releases digestive enzymes

cards.q: What triggers secretin release?
cards.a: Acid chyme entering the intestine

cards.q: What does secretin do?
cards.a: Pancreas and liver release a bicarbonate-rich fluid

cards.q: Which fatty acids does pancreatic lipase remove, and what is left?
cards.a: Positions 1 and 3 → 2-monoacylglycerol

cards.q: What happens to some 2-monoacylglycerol after pancreatic lipase?
cards.a: Isomerase → 1-monoacylglycerol → lipase finishes it to glycerol

cards.q: What partner protein does pancreatic lipase need?
cards.a: Colipase

cards.q: How is colipase activated?
cards.a: Secreted as procolipase; activated by trypsin

cards.q: What does colipase do for pancreatic lipase?
cards.a: Keeps the pH right and stops lipase denaturing
cards.more: Textbooks add that it anchors lipase to the droplet surface, where bile salts would otherwise block it.

cards.q: What does phospholipase A2 do, and what activates it?
cards.a: Removes fatty acid from C2 → lysophospholipid; activated by trypsin

cards.q: What does cholesterol esterase do?
cards.a: Cholesteryl ester → cholesterol + fatty acid

cards.q: How does orlistat work?
cards.a: Irreversibly binds pancreatic lipase active site (also inhibits gastric lipase)
cards.more: Because so much rides on lipase, blocking it causes weight loss.

cards.q: What fraction of dietary fat is lost in stool on orlistat?
cards.a: About a third

cards.q: What is olestra, and why does it give no calories?
cards.a: 6–8 fatty acids on sucrose; cannot be hydrolysed

cards.q: What is Salatrim (Benefat)?
cards.a: Designer fat of mixed long and short chains; about half the calories of ordinary fat

cards.q: What goes into mixed micelles?
cards.a:
Free fatty acids, monoacylglycerol, lysophospholipid, cholesterol
+ bile salts + fat-soluble vitamins

cards.q: How are mixed micelles organised, and why does it matter?
cards.a: Hydrophobic parts inside, water-loving parts outside → dissolve in lumen

cards.q: What job do micelles do?
cards.a: Ferry digestion products across the watery layer to the brush border

cards.q: Where is the main site of fat absorption?
cards.a: Jejunum

cards.q: How are short- and medium-chain fatty acids absorbed?
cards.a: Without micelles → straight into blood → portal circulation → liver (not chylomicrons)

cards.q: Why are medium-chain fats used to feed patients with fat malabsorption?
cards.a: They are absorbed without micelles, straight into portal blood

cards.q: How well is cholesterol absorbed, and which drug reduces it?
cards.a: Poorly, even from micelles; ezetimibe

cards.q: Where in the intestinal cell are absorbed lipids reassembled?
cards.a: Endoplasmic reticulum

cards.q: How is a long-chain fatty acid activated in the intestinal cell?
cards.a: Fatty acid + ATP + CoA → fatty acyl-CoA + AMP

cards.q: How is TAG rebuilt from 2-monoacylglycerol?
cards.a: Adds two acyl-CoAs

cards.q: What happens to lysophospholipid in the intestinal cell?
cards.a: Re-esterified to phospholipid

cards.q: Which enzyme esterifies cholesterol in the intestinal cell?
cards.a: Acyl-CoA:cholesterol acyltransferase (ACAT)

cards.q: Into what particle is rebuilt TAG packaged, and with which main protein?
cards.a: Chylomicron; apolipoprotein B-48 (apo B-48)

cards.q: Why do chylomicrons enter lymph rather than blood capillaries?
cards.a: Too big for blood capillaries

cards.q: What route do chylomicrons take to reach the blood?
cards.a: Lacteals → lymphatics → thoracic duct → bloodstream

cards.q: Which apolipoproteins does a nascent chylomicron pick up in blood to mature?
cards.a: Apo C-II and apo E

cards.q: Which enzyme releases chylomicron fatty acids to the tissues?
cards.a: Lipoprotein lipase

cards.q: Why does serum look milky after a fatty meal?
cards.a: Lipaemia (chylomicrons); clears within a few hours

cards.q: What happens to fat when bile is blocked (gallstones, biliary obstruction)?
cards.a: Poorly emulsified → passes undigested → steatorrhoea

cards.q: Which vitamins are lost when fat absorption is blocked, and why?
cards.a: A, D, E, K — they ride along with dietary fat

cards.q: What is steatorrhoea?
cards.a: Frothy, foul-smelling, floating stool with too much fat (normal <6%)

cards.q: What causes maldigestion steatorrhoea, and what fat is in the stool?
cards.a: Too little bile (liver disease, blocked flow) or pancreatic insufficiency; triacylglycerol

cards.q: What causes malabsorption steatorrhoea, and what fat is in the stool?
cards.a: Bacterial/parasitic infection, Crohn’s, coeliac disease; fatty acids

cards.q: In cholestasis, which fat-soluble vitamin is singled out as poorly absorbed?
cards.a: Vitamin K (with the other fat-soluble vitamins)
cards.more: Cholestasis = bile flow blocked, e.g., by a gallstone.

cards.q: In cholestasis, is octanoic acid (C8) still absorbed? Why?
cards.a: Yes — medium-chain, doesn’t need micelles

cards.q: Who secretes bile, and how much does the gallbladder concentrate it?
cards.a: Hepatocytes; gallbladder concentrates 10–20-fold

cards.q: What are the main components of bile?
cards.a:
Bile salts 85%
Free cholesterol 10%
Phospholipid 5% (mainly lecithin)
cards.more: Textbooks name bile salts and lecithin as the two main organic components.

cards.q: Besides cholesterol, what is excreted through bile?
cards.a: Bilirubin, steroids, many drugs

cards.q: From what, and where, are bile acids made?
cards.a: From cholesterol, in the liver

cards.q: What are the primary bile acids?
cards.a:
Cholic acid
Chenodeoxycholic acid

cards.q: What are bile acids conjugated with?
cards.a: Glycine or taurine

cards.q: Why are conjugated bile acids present as bile salts in the gut?
cards.a: pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 2–4 → deprotonated, paired with Na<sup>+</sup>/K<sup>+</sup>
cards.more: Bile salts are better detergents than the acids.

cards.q: What are the secondary bile acids, and how are they made?
cards.a: Deoxycholic and lithocholic acid; gut bacteria deconjugate and remove a hydroxyl

cards.q: What are the four jobs of bile salts?
cards.a:
Excrete excess cholesterol
Keep cholesterol dissolved in bile (with phospholipid)
Emulsify dietary TAG
Absorb fat-soluble vitamins

cards.q: What is the enterohepatic circulation?
cards.a: Bile salts reabsorbed in ileum → portal blood → liver → bile again

cards.q: What fraction of bile salts is reabsorbed, where, and how?
cards.a: 95–98%; ileum; Na<sup>+</sup>-coupled cotransporter

cards.q: How many times a day does each bile salt molecule recycle?
cards.a: About 10

cards.q: How much new bile acid does the liver make daily, and to replace what?
cards.a: 3–5 g/day, replacing the 2–5% lost in stool
cards.more: Textbooks put daily synthesis nearer 0.5 g.

cards.q: What is cholestyramine?
cards.a: Positively charged, unabsorbed resin that binds bile acids in the gut → excreted

cards.q: How does cholestyramine lower LDL?
cards.a: Less feedback inhibition → liver turns more cholesterol into bile acid → less hepatic cholesterol → more LDL receptors → serum LDL falls
cards.more: LDL = low-density lipoprotein. Used to treat high cholesterol.

cards.q: Why do cholesterol gallstones (cholelithiasis) form?
cards.a: More cholesterol enters bile than bile salts + phospholipid can keep dissolved

cards.q: What causes too few bile acids, leading to gallstones?
cards.a:
Severe ileal disease (not reabsorbed)
Biliary obstruction (loop broken)
Severe liver disease (not made)
Excessive feedback inhibition of synthesis

cards.q: What causes too much biliary cholesterol, leading to gallstones?
cards.a:
Obesity, acute high calorie/fat intake
Oral contraceptives, steroids, pregnancy
Diabetes mellitus
Fibrates (gemfibrozil)

cards.q: What are most gallstones made of?
cards.a: Cholesterol (about 10% are pigment stones)

cards.q: What are pigment gallstones, and what is their main risk factor?
cards.a: Bile pigment + some cholesterol and calcium salts; chronic haemolysis

cards.q: Which imaging finds gallstones best?
cards.a: Ultrasound

cards.q: What are the “5 F’s” of the classic gallstone patient?
cards.a: Fat, forty, fertile, female, flatulent

cards.q: What are the symptoms of gallstones?
cards.a: Steady upper abdominal pain → between shoulder blades or under right shoulder; nausea, vomiting

cards.q: Why are women affected by gallstones more often?
cards.a: Oestrogen raises biliary cholesterol; progesterone causes bile stasis

cards.q: What is the treatment for gallstones, and what is its consequence?
cards.a: Cholecystectomy; bile no longer released with meals → fatty food tolerated less well

cards.q: Which oral drugs can dissolve gallstones, and what is the side effect?
cards.a: Chenodeoxycholic or ursodeoxycholic acid (mostly-cholesterol stones); diarrhoea

cards.q: In what metabolic state, and under which hormone, does fatty acid synthesis run?
cards.a: Fed state; high insulin
cards.more: After a meal there is more fuel than needed, so the surplus is stored. Knowing it is a fed, high-insulin process predicts most of its regulation.

cards.q: In which cell compartment are fatty acids synthesised?
cards.a: Cytosol

cards.q: In which tissues does fatty acid synthesis mainly occur?
cards.a: Liver and lactating mammary gland (less in adipose tissue)

cards.q: What two-carbon unit are fatty acids built from?
cards.a: Acetyl-CoA

cards.q: Why do natural fatty acids have an even number of carbons?
cards.a: The chain is assembled two carbons at a time

cards.q: From what fuel, and from what precursor, is the acetyl-CoA for fat synthesis made?
cards.a: Carbohydrate; from pyruvate inside the mitochondrion

cards.q: Why must acetyl-CoA leave the mitochondrion as citrate for fat synthesis?
cards.a: Acetyl-CoA cannot cross the inner mitochondrial membrane; fat is built in the cytosol

cards.q: How is acetyl-CoA moved from the mitochondrion to the cytosol for fat synthesis?
cards.a: Citrate synthase (acetyl-CoA + OAA → citrate) → citrate exported → ATP-citrate lyase splits it back to acetyl-CoA + OAA
cards.more: Oxaloacetate = OAA. The cytosolic split by ATP-citrate lyase spends an ATP.

cards.q: Which cytosolic enzyme splits exported citrate back into acetyl-CoA and oxaloacetate, and what does it spend?
cards.a: ATP-citrate lyase; one ATP

cards.q: Why does citrate leave the mitochondrion only when the cell is well fuelled?
cards.a: High ATP and NADH inhibit isocitrate dehydrogenase → citric acid cycle backs up → citrate accumulates and spills into the cytosol

cards.q: How does insulin feed the citrate route to fat synthesis "from the top"?
cards.a: Activates PFK-2 → fructose 2,6-bisphosphate → speeds glycolysis at PFK-1
cards.more: PFK = phosphofructokinase. More glycolysis → more pyruvate → more acetyl-CoA and citrate.

cards.q: Besides fatty acids, what can acetyl-CoA become?
cards.a:
Citric acid cycle fuel
Cholesterol (→ bile acids, vitamin D, steroid hormones)
Ketone bodies (when insulin is low)

cards.q: What is the rate-limiting (first committed) step of fatty acid synthesis?
cards.a: Acetyl-CoA → malonyl-CoA, by acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC)

cards.q: What prosthetic group does acetyl-CoA carboxylase use, and what does it add?
cards.a: Biotin; adds CO<sub>2</sub>

cards.q: What are the two steps of the acetyl-CoA carboxylase reaction, and what energy does it spend?
cards.a: CO<sub>2</sub> attached to biotin → handed on to acetyl-CoA; spends 1 ATP

cards.q: Name the two other biotin-dependent carboxylases worth remembering.
cards.a:
Pyruvate carboxylase
Propionyl-CoA carboxylase
cards.more: Biotin is a water-soluble vitamin that carries CO2 for carboxylases.

cards.q: What two jobs make malonyl-CoA the hinge of fat metabolism?
cards.a:
Building block for fat synthesis
Blocks the enzyme that lets fat be burned
cards.more: One molecule says "store, do not burn" — exactly what you want after a meal.

cards.q: Which hormone activates acetyl-CoA carboxylase, and why does that make sense?
cards.a: Insulin; fuel is plentiful, so store it

cards.q: Which hormones inhibit acetyl-CoA carboxylase?
cards.a: Glucagon and adrenaline (fuel scarce → stop storing)

cards.q: Which metabolite allosterically activates acetyl-CoA carboxylase?
cards.a: Citrate (accumulates when energy is plentiful)

cards.q: Which end product inhibits acetyl-CoA carboxylase by feedback?
cards.a: Palmitoyl-CoA

cards.q: Besides hormones and palmitoyl-CoA, what else inhibits acetyl-CoA carboxylase?
cards.a:
High AMP (low energy)
Polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFA)

cards.q: A question set a couple of hours after a big sugary meal is testing which enzyme and activator?
cards.a: Acetyl-CoA carboxylase, activated by citrate (and insulin)
cards.more: Glucagon, adrenaline, AMP acting through AMPK, palmitoyl-CoA and PUFA all switch it off.

cards.q: What is the structure of inactive acetyl-CoA carboxylase?
cards.a: Small four-subunit protomer

cards.q: How does citrate activate acetyl-CoA carboxylase structurally?
cards.a: Polymerises protomers into active filaments

cards.q: How does palmitoyl-CoA inhibit acetyl-CoA carboxylase structurally?
cards.a: Promotes depolymerisation of the filaments

cards.q: Which kinase phosphorylates and inactivates acetyl-CoA carboxylase?
cards.a: AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK)
cards.more: Phosphorylation depolymerises the enzyme. AMPK is switched on by high AMP and, through its own upstream kinases, by glucagon and adrenaline.

cards.q: How does insulin reactivate phosphorylated acetyl-CoA carboxylase?
cards.a: Lowers cAMP and activates a protein phosphatase → dephosphorylation

cards.q: Besides dephosphorylating rate-limiting enzymes, what does insulin induce or raise (and via which signalling)?
cards.a: Induces glucokinase; raises GLUT4 in muscle and fat — via PI3-kinase and protein kinase B

cards.q: Which diets increase vs decrease the amount of acetyl-CoA carboxylase over days?
cards.a:
↑ High-calorie, high-carbohydrate, low-fat diet
↓ Fasting or high-fat diet

cards.q: What induces and what represses fatty acid synthase?
cards.a:
Induced: insulin, feeding
Repressed: PUFA, fasting

cards.q: What induces ATP-citrate lyase?
cards.a: Glucose and insulin

cards.q: What is the product of fatty acid synthase?
cards.a: Palmitate (16:0)

cards.q: What reducing power does fatty acid synthase use?
cards.a: NADPH

cards.q: What is the quaternary structure of fatty acid synthase?
cards.a: Dimer of identical chains lying head to tail

cards.q: How many enzyme activities does each fatty acid synthase chain carry, plus what carrier?
cards.a: Seven activities + an acyl carrier protein (ACP)

cards.q: Name the seven enzyme activities of fatty acid synthase.
cards.a:
Acetyl transacylase
Malonyl transacylase
3-Ketoacyl synthase
3-Ketoacyl reductase
Dehydratase
Enoyl reductase
Thioesterase

cards.q: What does the acyl carrier protein's phosphopantetheine arm do?
cards.a: Swings the growing chain from one active site to the next

cards.q: Why does only the fatty acid synthase dimer work?
cards.a: Each cycle needs the ACP of one chain and the ketoacyl synthase cysteine of the other

cards.q: How does fatty acid synthase make the first 4-carbon unit?
cards.a: Loads acetyl + malonyl → transfers 2 carbons from malonyl to acetyl, releasing CO<sub>2</sub>
cards.more: The CO2 released is the one acetyl-CoA carboxylase added.

cards.q: After condensation, what three steps complete each fatty acid synthase cycle?
cards.a: Reduce → dehydrate → reduce
cards.more: Then it repeats with a fresh malonyl-CoA.

cards.q: How many cycles does fatty acid synthase run to make palmitate?
In which direction is the palmitate chain built?
cards.a: From the ω-end toward the carboxyl end

cards.q: Which activity cuts the finished palmitate off fatty acid synthase?
cards.a: Thioesterase

cards.q: What does thioesterase II do in the lactating breast?
cards.a: Releases shorter 8–12-carbon fatty acids, easier for infants to digest

cards.q: What is the overall equation for palmitate synthesis?
cards.a: Acetyl-CoA + 7 malonyl-CoA + 14 NADPH + 14 H<sup>+</sup> → palmitate + 7 CO<sub>2</sub> + 6 H<sub>2</sub>O + 8 CoA + 14 NADP<sup>+</sup>

cards.q: How many NADPH does one palmitate cost?
cards.more: 2 per cycle × 7 cycles (the two reductions in each cycle).

cards.q: What is the chief source of NADPH for fatty acid synthesis?
cards.a: Pentose phosphate pathway

cards.q: Which enzyme supplies roughly half the NADPH for fat synthesis?
cards.a: Malic enzyme

cards.q: How is the oxaloacetate left by ATP-citrate lyase recycled while making NADPH?
cards.a: OAA → malate (cytosolic malate dehydrogenase, uses NADH) → pyruvate + CO<sub>2</sub> (malic enzyme, makes NADPH)

cards.q: Besides fatty acid synthesis, what else uses NADPH?
cards.a:
Steroid synthesis
Cytochrome P450 system
Detoxifying reactive oxygen species

cards.q: From which fatty acid are all other fatty acids made, and in what form?
cards.a: Palmitate, activated to palmitoyl-CoA

cards.q: Where does fatty acid elongation occur, and what is the two-carbon donor at each site?
cards.a:
Smooth ER: malonyl-CoA
Mitochondria: acetyl-CoA
cards.more: Both add two carbons at a time and use NADPH.

cards.q: Where does fatty acid desaturation occur?
cards.a: Endoplasmic reticulum

cards.q: Where does the first double bond almost always go, and which enzyme places it?
cards.a: Δ9 (between C9 and C10); stearoyl-CoA (Δ9) desaturase

cards.q: What does Δ9 desaturase make from stearic acid?
cards.a: Stearic acid (18:0) → oleic acid (18:1Δ9)

cards.q: At which positions can human desaturases insert double bonds?
cards.a: Δ4, Δ5, Δ6, Δ9 — never beyond C9 toward the ω-end

cards.q: Name the two essential fatty acids and their ω family.
cards.a:
Linoleic acid: ω-6
α-Linolenic acid: ω-3

cards.q: Why are linoleic and α-linolenic acid essential?
cards.a: Their double bonds lie beyond C9 toward the ω-end, where human desaturases cannot work
cards.more: Linoleic (18:2Δ9,12): bond nearest the ω-end is 6 carbons in → ω-6. α-Linolenic (18:3Δ9,12,15): 3 carbons in → ω-3. Both come from the diet (plant oils, fish).

cards.q: Which ω fatty acid family can humans make themselves, and from what?
cards.a: ω-9, starting from oleic acid

cards.q: How is arachidonic acid made from linoleic acid?
cards.a: Linoleic → (Δ6 desaturase) γ-linolenic → (elongase) 20:3 → (Δ5 desaturase) arachidonic acid (20:4Δ5,8,11,14)

cards.q: How is eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) made from α-linolenic acid?
cards.a: α-Linolenic → (Δ6) 18:4 → (elongase) 20:4 → (Δ5) EPA (20:5)

cards.q: How is docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) made from EPA?
cards.a: EPA → elongation to 24:5 → (Δ6) 24:6 → one round of β-oxidation → DHA (22:6)

cards.q: What is a triacylglycerol (TAG) built from?
cards.a: Three fatty acyl-CoA added one at a time to a glycerol 3-phosphate backbone

cards.q: Where does liver TAG go vs adipose TAG?
cards.a:
Liver: exported as VLDL
Adipose: stored as depot fat

cards.q: What fatty acids typically sit on C1, C2 and C3 of stored TAG?
cards.a:
C1 saturated
C2 unsaturated
C3 variable

cards.q: Where is most of the body's lipid stored, and as what?
cards.a: >95% as TAG in adipose tissue (small amounts in liver and muscle)

cards.q: Where do adipose tissue and muscle get most of their fatty acids?
cards.a: Plasma: FFA on albumin, or TAG of chylomicrons (after a meal) and VLDL (post-absorptive, 6–12 h later)

cards.q: Which enzyme frees fatty acids from lipoprotein TAG for adipose and muscle, and when is it most active?
cards.a: Lipoprotein lipase (LPL); fed state, especially high-carbohydrate diet; stimulated by insulin

cards.q: From what glycolytic intermediate can both liver and adipose make glycerol 3-phosphate, and with which enzyme?
cards.a: Dihydroxyacetone phosphate (DHAP); glycerol 3-phosphate dehydrogenase

cards.q: Which tissue has glycerol kinase to use free glycerol: liver or adipose?
cards.a: Liver only — adipose lacks glycerol kinase

cards.q: How does glucose enter liver vs adipose cells?
cards.a:
Liver: GLUT2
Adipose: GLUT4, insulin-dependent
