Carriercitratecarnitine
CoenzymeNADPHNAD+, FAD
ControlACCCPT-I
Productpalmitateacetyl-CoA

cards.q: What does each cycle of β-oxidation release?
cards.a: 1 acetyl-CoA + 1 NADH + 1 FADH<sub>2</sub>; chain 2 carbons shorter

cards.q: Where do the products of β-oxidation go?
cards.a:
Acetyl-CoA → citric acid cycle
NADH, FADH2 → electron transport chain

cards.q: What are the four reaction types of a β-oxidation turn, in order?
cards.a: Oxidation → hydration → oxidation → thiolysis

cards.q: What does acyl-CoA dehydrogenase do in β-oxidation, and what does it produce?
cards.a: Trans double bond between α- and β-carbons; FADH<sub>2</sub>

cards.q: What does enoyl-CoA hydratase do?
cards.a: Adds water across the double bond

cards.q: What does 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase do, and what does it produce?
cards.a: Oxidises the β-carbon; NADH

cards.q: What does β-ketoacyl-CoA thiolase do?
cards.a: Uses fresh CoA to cut off acetyl-CoA → acyl-CoA two carbons shorter

cards.q: Name the four chain-length versions of acyl-CoA dehydrogenase and their ranges.
cards.a:
SCAD: under C6
MCAD: C6–C12
LCAD: C14–C18
VLCAD: over C20

cards.q: How many ATP does one palmitate yield (older values) vs one glucose?
cards.a: Palmitate 129; glucose 36–38

cards.q: Why is fat the fuel of prolonged fasting?
cards.a: Huge ATP yield: ~2.5× the energy of the same mass of carbohydrate or protein

cards.q: How many turns of β-oxidation does palmitate need, and what do they yield?
cards.a: 7 turns → 7 FADH<sub>2</sub>, 7 NADH, 8 acetyl-CoA

cards.q: Show the calculation of 129 ATP from palmitate.
cards.a: 7 FADH<sub>2</sub> × 2 + 7 NADH × 3 + 8 acetyl-CoA × 12 = 131; − 2 activation = 129

cards.q: What are the older ATP conversion values per NADH, FADH<sub>2</sub> and acetyl-CoA?
cards.a:
NADH 3
FADH2 2
Acetyl-CoA 12

cards.q: What are the newer ATP conversion values, and the resulting yields per palmitate and glucose?
cards.a: NADH 2.5, FADH<sub>2</sub> 1.5, acetyl-CoA 10 → palmitate 106; glucose ~30–32
cards.more: Expect to see either 129 or 106 on exams.

cards.q: Which fatty acids does mitochondrial β-oxidation handle?
cards.a: Most — those under 20 carbons

cards.q: Which pathway handles very-long-chain fatty acids (VLCFA, over C20), and what is its drawback?
cards.a: Peroxisomal β-oxidation; less ATP than mitochondria

cards.q: Why does peroxisomal β-oxidation make less ATP?
cards.a: Acyl-CoA oxidase passes electrons straight to O<sub>2</sub> (→ H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>) instead of the electron transport chain

cards.q: What happens to a VLCFA once peroxisomes shorten it below 20 carbons?
cards.a: Exported to mitochondria

cards.q: Which fatty acid does α-oxidation handle, where, and with what energy yield?
cards.a: Branched phytanic acid; peroxisome; no energy yield

cards.q: Why can't phytanic acid enter β-oxidation directly?
cards.a: Methyl group on its β-carbon blocks it

cards.q: Where does phytanic acid come from?
cards.a: Chlorophyll; found in dairy products and some fish
cards.more: Chemically 3,7,11,15-tetramethylhexadecanoic acid.

cards.q: What does α-oxidation do to phytanic acid?
cards.a: Removes one carbon from the carboxyl end → pristanic acid, which β-oxidation can handle

cards.q: Where does ω-oxidation occur, what enzyme does it use, and what does it make?
cards.a: Endoplasmic reticulum; cytochrome P450 oxidises the ω-carbon → dicarboxylic acids (e.g. adipic acid)

cards.q: When does ω-oxidation rise above its normally minor role?
cards.a: When β-oxidation fails, e.g. MCAD deficiency

cards.q: What does the last turn of odd-chain fatty acid β-oxidation leave?
cards.a: Propionyl-CoA (3 carbons) instead of acetyl-CoA

cards.q: Besides odd-chain fatty acids, which amino acids feed into propionyl-CoA?
cards.a: Valine, isoleucine, methionine, threonine

cards.q: How is propionyl-CoA converted to succinyl-CoA?
cards.a: Propionyl-CoA carboxylase (biotin, ATP) → D-methylmalonyl-CoA → racemase → L-methylmalonyl-CoA → methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (B12) → succinyl-CoA
cards.more: Succinyl-CoA can go on to make glucose.

cards.q: Which vitamin coenzyme does methylmalonyl-CoA mutase need?
cards.a: Vitamin B12 (deoxyadenosylcobalamin)

cards.q: What does a defective methylmalonyl-CoA mutase or B12 lack cause?
cards.a: Methylmalonic aciduria: metabolic acidosis, intellectual disability

cards.q: What does a block at propionyl-CoA carboxylase cause?
cards.a: ↑ Propionyl-CoA and metabolic acidosis

cards.q: Which two extra enzymes does β-oxidation of unsaturated fatty acids need?
cards.a:
Enoyl-CoA isomerase
NADPH-dependent enoyl-CoA reductase
cards.more: They fix double bonds sitting in the wrong place for the cycle.

cards.q: Do unsaturated fatty acids yield more or fewer ATP than saturated ones of the same length?
cards.a: Fewer

cards.q: When does the liver make ketone bodies?
cards.a: Fat burned faster than the citric acid cycle can handle the acetyl-CoA (prolonged fasting, uncontrolled diabetes)

cards.q: Name the three ketone bodies.
cards.a:
Acetoacetate
D-β-hydroxybutyrate
Acetone

cards.q: Why do ketone bodies add acid to the blood?
cards.a: Acetoacetate and β-hydroxybutyrate are acids (pK<sub>a</sub> 3.5) → almost fully dissociated at blood pH

cards.q: Where are ketone bodies made?
cards.a: Only in liver mitochondria

cards.q: What are the four steps of ketone body synthesis?
cards.a:
Thiolase: 2 acetyl-CoA → acetoacetyl-CoA
HMG-CoA synthase: + acetyl-CoA → HMG-CoA
HMG-CoA lyase: → acetoacetate + acetyl-CoA
3-Hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase (NADH): → β-hydroxybutyrate
cards.more: HMG-CoA = 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA.

cards.q: Which enzyme reduces acetoacetate to β-hydroxybutyrate, and with what cofactor?
cards.a: 3-Hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase; NADH

cards.q: How is acetone formed, and what is its fate?
cards.a: Spontaneous loss of CO<sub>2</sub> from acetoacetate; dead end, breathed out (fruity breath)

cards.q: How do extrahepatic tissues use acetoacetate?
cards.a: Thiophorase (succinyl-CoA:acetoacetate CoA transferase) → acetoacetyl-CoA → thiolase → 2 acetyl-CoA

cards.q: Why can't the liver use the ketones it makes?
cards.a: Lacks thiophorase

cards.q: Which tissues use ketones, and which cannot?
cards.a:
Use: muscle, brain (in starvation)
Cannot: liver, red cells

cards.q: How many ATP do acetoacetate and β-hydroxybutyrate each yield?
cards.a:
Acetoacetate 23
β-Hydroxybutyrate 26

cards.q: Why does β-hydroxybutyrate yield more ATP than acetoacetate?
cards.a: Converting it back to acetoacetate makes an extra NADH

cards.q: How do blood glucose and ketones change over prolonged fasting?
cards.a: Ketones climb for weeks while glucose levels off

cards.q: Well fed vs 5 weeks starvation: blood glucose and fatty acids?
cards.a:
Glucose ~6.1 → 3.6 mM
Fatty acids 0.14 → 1.4 mM

cards.q: Well fed vs 5 weeks starvation: acetoacetate and β-hydroxybutyrate?
cards.a:
Acetoacetate 0.04 → 1.3 mM
β-Hydroxybutyrate 0.03 → ~6 mM

cards.q: Which fuel rises most in prolonged starvation?
cards.a: β-Hydroxybutyrate (to ~6 mM)

cards.q: What is diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), in one line?
cards.a: The fasting programme running unchecked: little insulin, much glucagon

cards.q: In DKA, why does β-oxidation make a surplus of acetyl-CoA?
cards.a: HSL floods liver with fatty acids; ACC off → malonyl-CoA falls → CPT-I runs freely

cards.q: In DKA, why can't the citric acid cycle take up the acetyl-CoA?
cards.a: Gluconeogenesis (↑ pyruvate carboxylase, PEPCK) pulls away oxaloacetate; high NADH slows the cycle too
cards.more: PEPCK = phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase. The acetyl-CoA's one exit is ketone bodies, and the ketoacids overwhelm the buffers.

cards.q: In poorly controlled type 1 diabetes, which fat-metabolism enzyme is more active than normal?
cards.a: Hormone-sensitive lipase (HSL)

cards.q: In poorly controlled type 1 diabetes, which insulin-driven proteins are less active?
cards.a:
Lipoprotein lipase
Acetyl-CoA carboxylase
Fatty acid synthase
GLUT4

cards.q: What is the classic fatty acid oxidation defect?
cards.a: Medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (MCAD) deficiency

cards.q: What is the typical story of MCAD deficiency?
cards.a: Child fine while eating, then fasts (illness, missed meal) and cannot switch to burning fat

cards.q: What lab combination is the fingerprint of MCAD deficiency?
cards.a: Hypoglycaemia with inappropriately low ketones

cards.q: In MCAD deficiency, why does gluconeogenesis fail during a fast?
cards.a: Liver lacks ATP and acetyl-CoA; acetyl-CoA is the obligatory activator of pyruvate carboxylase

cards.q: In MCAD deficiency, why are few ketones made?
cards.a: Little acetyl-CoA

cards.q: In what form do stranded medium chains leave mitochondria in MCAD deficiency?
cards.a: C6–C10 acylcarnitines (C8 and C10 build up in blood and urine)

cards.q: In MCAD deficiency, which pathway turns medium chains into dicarboxylic acids, and how are they excreted?
cards.a: ω-Oxidation; with their carnitine and glycine conjugates

cards.q: What is the incidence of MCAD deficiency?
Classic MCAD case: what is the presentation?
cards.a: 6-month-old breast-fed girl, unrousable for feed after 3 days of cold with vomiting
cards.more: Irritable/lethargic before feeds since 2 months; older sibling died of a "Reye-like" illness; tachypnoeic, opens eyes only to pain, large fatty liver. Parents German.

cards.q: MCAD case: why is glucose 2.5 mmol/L (normal 5)?
cards.a: Fasting + infection empty liver glycogen; gluconeogenesis cannot run without acetyl-CoA and ATP

cards.q: MCAD case: why is ammonia 100 µmol/L (normal under 20)?
cards.a: Fat-laden liver works poorly; octanoate (C8) uncouples mitochondria → less ATP → less urea made

cards.q: MCAD case: which acylcarnitines are high, and why?
cards.a: Hexanoyl- (C6) and octanoylcarnitine (C8) — trapped medium chains leave mitochondria

cards.q: MCAD case: what are hexanoylglycine and suberylglycine in the urine?
cards.a:
Hexanoylglycine: C6 β-oxidation product
Suberylglycine: C8 dicarboxylic ω-oxidation product

cards.q: MCAD case: why is urine acetoacetate only a trace?
cards.a: Little acetyl-CoA, so few ketones

cards.q: MCAD case: why is the anion gap 20 (normal 8–16)?
cards.a: Extra mono- and dicarboxylic acids

cards.q: List the differential of hypoketotic hypoglycaemia.
cards.a:
Carnitine deficiency
CPT deficiency
LCAD deficiency
MCAD deficiency
Congenital hyperinsulinism

cards.q: How does congenital hyperinsulinism differ from MCAD deficiency?
cards.a: Usually at birth, often large for gestational age; free fatty acids also suppressed
cards.more: Insulin blocks both lipolysis and ketogenesis, so FFA and ketones are both low.

cards.q: Which gene is sequenced to confirm MCAD deficiency, and on which chromosome?
cards.a: ACADM; chromosome 1

cards.q: What is the commonest MCAD mutation in people of European descent, and its effect?
cards.a: Lys304Glu (985A→G); enzyme cannot assemble into its homotetramer

cards.q: Besides gene sequencing, how else can MCAD deficiency be confirmed?
cards.a: MCAD activity in leukocytes or fibroblasts; C6–C10 acylcarnitines in cultured fibroblasts

cards.q: How is MCAD deficiency treated in infancy?
cards.a: Never fast: feeds every 3–4 h with complex carbohydrate; no medium-chain-TAG formula

cards.q: Why must MCAD-deficient infants avoid formula based on medium-chain triacylglycerol?
cards.a: It is the very fat they cannot burn

cards.q: How is MCAD deficiency managed in toddlers?
cards.a: Lower-fat diet (<30% calories) + uncooked cornstarch 2 g/kg at bedtime (slow-release overnight glucose)

cards.q: What causes primary carnitine deficiency, and how does it present?
cards.a: Too little carnitine (vegan diet, transporter, liver synthesis or renal reabsorption defects); muscle cramps and weakness

cards.q: What causes secondary carnitine deficiency?
cards.a: Acylcarnitines from CPT-II or CACT defects block renal carnitine reabsorption

cards.q: What is the outcome of liver CPT-I or CACT deficiency?
cards.a: Lethal at a young age

cards.q: Which carnitine-shuttle defect causes cardiomyopathy and rhabdomyolysis?
cards.a: CPT-II deficiency (muscle form)

cards.q: What is the defect in Zellweger syndrome, and its consequence?
cards.a: Peroxisome biogenesis (peroxins); VLCFA not oxidised

cards.q: Which disease lies on the Zellweger spectrum, and what are its features?
cards.a: Infantile Refsum disease: poor cerebral myelination, loss of hearing and vision

cards.q: What is the defect in X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy?
cards.a: ABCD1, which carries VLCFA-CoA into peroxisomes → VLCFA not oxidised

cards.q: What is the enzyme defect in adult Refsum disease?
cards.a: Phytanoyl-CoA hydroxylase (α-oxidation)

cards.q: What are the features of adult Refsum disease?
cards.a:
Cerebellar ataxia
Peripheral polyneuropathy
Retinitis pigmentosa
Hearing loss

cards.q: How are carnitine-shuttle defects managed?
cards.a:
High-carbohydrate, low long-chain-fat diet
Extra medium-chain fat
Limited physical activity
Carnitine supplements

cards.q: Why is medium-chain fat given in carnitine-shuttle defects?
cards.a: It enters mitochondria without carnitine

cards.q: What causes Jamaican vomiting sickness?
cards.a: Hypoglycin A in unripe ackee fruit

cards.q: How does hypoglycin A block β-oxidation?
cards.a: Its metabolites tie up carnitine and CoA

cards.q: What is the clinical course of Jamaican vomiting sickness?
cards.a: Vomiting within 2–6 h → severe hypoglycaemia, weakness, altered consciousness, sometimes death

cards.q: Match: infant, fasting, hypoketotic hypoglycaemia, C8 acylcarnitines, dicarboxylic aciduria → ?
cards.a: MCAD deficiency

lessons.t: The thoracic cage and intercostal space

cards.q: What two contradictory jobs must the chest wall do?
cards.a:
Protect the heart and lungs
Move constantly for breathing
cards.more: Its structure is a compromise between the two.

cards.q: What is the sternal angle?
cards.a: The ridge where the manubrium meets the body of the sternum

cards.q: Which rib does the sternal angle mark?
cards.a: The 2nd rib (2nd costal cartilage)
cards.more: Counting ribs starts here. It is the single most useful landmark in the thorax.

cards.q: Why does rib counting start at the sternal angle instead of the 1st rib?
cards.a: The 1st rib is hidden behind the clavicle and cannot be felt

cards.q: At what vertebral level does the sternal angle lie?
cards.a: T4/T5 intervertebral disc

cards.q: What three thoracic events happen at the level of the sternal angle?
cards.a:
Aortic arch begins and ends (descending aorta starts)
Trachea bifurcates
Azygos vein joins the superior vena cava (SVC)

cards.q: Where is the jugular (suprasternal) notch, and at what vertebral level does it lie?
cards.a: Top of the sternum, between the medial ends of the clavicles → lower border of T2

cards.q: How far below the jugular notch is the sternal angle, and why?
cards.a: About 4 cm → the manubrium is about 4 cm long

cards.q: At what vertebral level does the xiphisternal joint lie?
cards.a: T9

cards.q: What four things does the xiphisternal joint mark or guide?
cards.a:
Hand position in cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR)
Upper limit of the liver
Central tendon of the diaphragm
Inferior border of the heart

cards.q: At what level is the tip of the xiphoid process, and when does it become easier to feel?
cards.a: About T10 → easier to feel after about age 40

cards.q: What forms the costal margin?
cards.a: Costal cartilages of ribs 7–10

cards.q: What is the angle where the two costal margins meet?
cards.a: Infrasternal (subcostal) angle

cards.q: Over which intercostal space does the nipple usually lie in men?
cards.a: 4th intercostal space
cards.more: In women the shape and size of the breast make the nipple an unreliable landmark.

cards.q: What forms the anterior axillary fold?
cards.a: Lower border of pectoralis major

cards.q: What forms the posterior axillary fold?
cards.a: Latissimus dorsi and teres major

cards.q: What vertical lines are drawn on the thoracic wall to describe location?
cards.a:
Anterior and posterior median lines
Midclavicular line (MCL)
Anterior and posterior axillary lines
Midaxillary line (MAL)
Scapular lines

cards.q: Through what point does the midclavicular line (MCL) run?
cards.a: Midpoint of the clavicle

cards.q: From where does the midaxillary line (MAL) run down?
cards.a: Apex of the axilla
cards.more: The anterior and posterior axillary lines run along the anterior and posterior axillary folds.

cards.q: Through what do the scapular lines run?
cards.a: Inferior angles of the scapulae

cards.q: What three components make up the thoracic cage?
cards.a:
Sternum + costal cartilages (front)
12 pairs of ribs (sides)
12 thoracic vertebrae (behind)

cards.q: What are the functions of the thoracic cage?
cards.a:
Protects heart, great vessels, lungs and trachea
Passage between neck and abdomen
Supports the upper limbs

cards.q: What are the three parts of the sternum, top to bottom?
cards.a: Manubrium → body → xiphoid process

cards.q: What notches and articulations does the manubrium carry?
cards.a:
Jugular and clavicular notches
Takes the clavicle and the 1st rib

cards.q: Opposite which vertebrae does the body of the sternum lie?
cards.a: T5–T9

cards.q: Which ribs attach directly to the body of the sternum?
cards.a: Ribs 3–6

cards.q: Where do the 2nd and 7th ribs attach to the sternum?
cards.a:
2nd → sternal angle
7th → xiphisternal joint

cards.q: What feature defines a thoracic vertebra?
cards.a: Costal facets (on the bodies and transverse processes)

cards.q: Besides costal facets, what three features mark a thoracic vertebra?
cards.a:
Heart-shaped body
Small vertebral foramen
Long spine sloping downward

cards.q: Which thoracic vertebrae are typical, and what facets do their bodies carry?
cards.a: T2–T9 → a demifacet (half-facet) above and below on each body

cards.q: Why do typical thoracic vertebrae have demifacets?
cards.a: A typical rib head touches two vertebrae

cards.q: What costal facets do T10–T12 have?
cards.a: One whole facet each

cards.q: What costal facets does T1 have?
cards.a: Whole facet for the 1st rib + inferior demifacet for the 2nd rib

cards.q: Which are the true ribs, and how do they reach the sternum?
cards.a: Ribs 1–7 → directly, through their own costal cartilages

cards.q: Which are the false ribs, and how do they reach the sternum?
cards.a: Ribs 8–10 → indirectly; their cartilages join the cartilage of the rib above

cards.q: Which are the floating ribs, and where do they end?
cards.a: Ribs 11 and 12 → in the muscles of the posterior abdominal wall (do not reach the sternum)

cards.q: Why is the 7th rib usually counted as a true rib?
cards.a: Its cartilage meets the sternum (at the xiphisternal joint)
cards.more: You may also see the split given as true 1–6 and false 7–9, with the 10th sometimes floating.

cards.q: By shape, which ribs are typical and which are atypical?
cards.a:
Typical: 3–9
Atypical: 1, 2, 10, 11, 12

cards.q: What are the parts of a typical rib, from medial to lateral?
cards.a: Head → neck → tubercle → body (with angle and costal groove)

cards.q: What does the head of a typical rib look like?
cards.a: Wedge-shaped, with two facets separated by a crest

cards.q: Which vertebrae do the two facets on a typical rib head meet?
cards.a:
Inferior facet → its own vertebra
Superior facet → the vertebra above

cards.q: What does the facet on a rib tubercle articulate with?
cards.a: Transverse process of its own vertebra

cards.q: What is the angle of a rib, and what does it mark?
cards.a: Where the body turns forward → lateral limit of the deep back muscles

cards.q: Where is the costal groove, and what does it shelter?
cards.a: Inner lower edge of the rib body → intercostal vessels and nerve

cards.q: How does the shape of the 1st rib compare with the other true ribs?
cards.a: Broadest, shortest and most sharply curved

cards.q: Why does the head of the 1st rib have only one facet?
cards.a: It meets only T1

cards.q: What grooves lie on the upper surface of the 1st rib?
cards.a: Grooves for the subclavian artery and subclavian vein

cards.q: What marks the 2nd rib?
cards.a: A rough area for serratus anterior
cards.more: It is also thinner, less curved and longer than the 1st rib.

cards.q: What is atypical about the 10th rib?
cards.a: A single facet on its head

cards.q: What is atypical about the 11th and 12th ribs?
cards.a: Shortest ribs; one facet; no neck or tubercle

cards.q: What two joints does each typical rib make posteriorly, and what type are they?
cards.a: Costovertebral + costotransverse → both synovial plane joints

cards.q: What does the costovertebral joint connect?
cards.a: Rib head → two vertebral bodies and the disc between them

cards.q: Which vertebrae does the head of the 5th rib meet?
cards.a: T5 (below) and T4 (above)

cards.q: What does the costotransverse joint connect?
cards.a: Rib tubercle → transverse process of its own vertebra

cards.q: What type of joint is formed by the intervertebral discs between thoracic vertebral bodies?
cards.a: Symphyses

cards.q: What joint attaches the 1st costal cartilage to the sternum?
cards.a: Primary cartilaginous joint (synchondrosis)

cards.q: What joints do costal cartilages 2–7 form with the sternum?
cards.a: Synovial plane sternocostal (chondrosternal) joints

cards.q: What are interchondral joints, and what type are they?
cards.a: Joints between the cartilages of the false ribs → synovial plane

cards.q: What is a costochondral joint?
cards.a: Where a rib joins its costal cartilage

cards.q: What type of joint are the manubriosternal and xiphisternal joints?
cards.a: Symphyses

cards.q: What type of joint is the sternoclavicular joint, and why does it matter?
cards.a: Saddle-shaped → the main joint between the upper limb and the thorax

cards.q: How is the vertical diameter of the thorax increased in inspiration?
cards.a: Diaphragm contracts → presses abdominal viscera down

cards.q: What is the pump-handle movement?
cards.a: Upper six ribs swing up about an axis through their necks → push the sternum forward

cards.q: Which thoracic diameter does the pump-handle movement increase?
cards.a: Anteroposterior

cards.q: What is the bucket-handle movement?
cards.a: Ribs 7–10 rise at their middles and swing outward

cards.q: Which thoracic diameter does the bucket-handle movement increase?
cards.a: Transverse

cards.q: Which thoracic diameters must every inspiration enlarge?
cards.a: All three at once: vertical, anteroposterior and transverse

cards.q: What happens in expiration?
cards.a: Diaphragm relaxes → intra-abdominal pressure falls → lungs recoil and expel the air

cards.q: What does a 1st-rib fracture signal, and why?
cards.a: Severe trauma → the 1st rib is rarely fractured

cards.q: Which ribs break most often?
cards.a: The middle ribs

cards.q: Where is a rib weakest?
cards.a: Just in front of its angle

cards.q: What can broken lower ribs damage?
cards.a:
Tear the diaphragm
Pierce the lung or heart

cards.q: What is a flail chest?
cards.a: Several rib fractures leave a loose segment of chest wall → impairs ventilation

cards.q: How does a flail segment move during breathing?
cards.a: The wrong way: in on inspiration, out on expiration

cards.q: What does notching of the ribs usually indicate?
cards.a: Coarctation of the aorta

cards.q: Why does coarctation of the aorta notch the ribs?
cards.a: Blood rerouted around the narrowing enlarges the intercostal arteries

cards.q: Which bone is used for bone marrow biopsy and marrow harvest for transplantation, and why?
cards.a: Body of the sternum → broad and just under the skin

cards.q: What are the boundaries of the thoracic inlet (superior thoracic aperture)?
cards.a:
Behind: T1
Sides: 1st ribs and their cartilages
Front: upper border of the manubrium
cards.more: The inlet is small and kidney-shaped, and connects the thorax with the neck and upper limbs.

cards.q: Besides vessels and nerves, what passes through the thoracic inlet?
cards.a:
Trachea
Oesophagus
Apices of the lungs
Thoracic duct

cards.q: Which blood vessels pass through the thoracic inlet?
cards.a:
Subclavian artery and vein
Brachiocephalic artery
Costocervical trunk
Internal thoracic artery

cards.q: Which nerves pass through the thoracic inlet?
cards.a:
Phrenic and vagus nerves
Sympathetic chain
Anterior ramus of T1

cards.q: What are the boundaries of the thoracic outlet (inferior thoracic aperture)?
cards.a:
Behind: T12
Posterolaterally: ribs 11 and 12
Anterolaterally: costal margins
Front: xiphisternal joint
cards.more: Much larger than the inlet.

cards.q: What almost closes off the thoracic outlet?
cards.a: The diaphragm

cards.q: What passes through or behind the diaphragm into the abdomen?
cards.a:
Aorta
Oesophagus
Inferior vena cava (IVC)
Azygos vein
Thoracic duct
Nerves

cards.q: Which anatomical aperture does thoracic outlet syndrome actually involve?
cards.a: The thoracic inlet (superior thoracic aperture)
cards.more: The naming trap: it is named for the vessels and nerves “coming out” of the thorax to supply the head, neck and arm.

cards.q: What causes thoracic outlet syndrome?
cards.a: Extra cervical rib or abnormal anterior scalene attachment → compresses subclavian vessels and/or T1 nerve

cards.q: What does the T1 nerve feed, making it relevant in thoracic outlet syndrome?
cards.a: Lower trunk of the brachial plexus

cards.q: What are the signs of thoracic outlet syndrome?
cards.a:
Diminished radial pulse
Poor blood flow to the arm
Pain along medial forearm and hand
Wasting of the small muscles of the hand

cards.q: What three muscle layers lie in each intercostal space, superficial to deep?
cards.a: External intercostal → internal intercostal → innermost intercostal
cards.more: They are arranged like the abdominal wall in miniature.

cards.q: Which way do the fibres of the external intercostals run?
cards.a: Downward and forward

cards.q: What is the extent of the external intercostals, and what replaces them anteriorly?
cards.a: Rib tubercles (behind) → costochondral junctions (front) → then a membrane

cards.q: Below the thorax, the external intercostals are continuous with which muscle?
cards.a: External oblique

cards.q: Which way do the fibres of the internal intercostals run?
cards.a: Downward and backward (at right angles to the externals)

cards.q: What is the extent of the internal intercostals, and what replaces them posteriorly?
cards.a: Sternum → rib angles → then a membrane

cards.q: Below the thorax, the internal intercostals are continuous with which muscle?
cards.a: Internal oblique

cards.q: How do the internal intercostals compare with the externals in strength and timing?
cards.a: Weaker → most active in expiration

cards.q: What are the innermost intercostals?
cards.a: Deepest fibres of the internal layer, split off by the neurovascular bundle

cards.q: What is the action of the innermost intercostals?
cards.a: Probably like the internals → not established

cards.q: Which accessory muscles of respiration join in forced inspiration?
cards.a:
Pectoralis major and minor
Serratus anterior
Scalenes

cards.q: Which small thoracic wall muscles are thought to work mainly as proprioceptors?
cards.a:
Serratus posterior muscles
Levatores costarum
cards.more: Serratus posterior is implicated in myofascial pain; levatores costarum also help move the vertebrae.

cards.q: What are the attachments of serratus posterior superior?
cards.a: Nuchal ligament + spines C7–T3 → ribs 2–4
cards.more: Action: proprioception (elevates ribs).

cards.q: What nerves supply serratus posterior superior?
cards.a: Intercostal nerves 2–5

cards.q: What are the attachments of serratus posterior inferior?
cards.a: Spines T11–L2 → ribs 8–12
cards.more: Action: proprioception (depresses ribs).

cards.q: What nerves supply serratus posterior inferior?
cards.a: Anterior rami T9–T12

cards.q: What are the attachments and action of levatores costarum?
cards.a: Transverse processes → rib below → elevate ribs

cards.q: What nerves supply levatores costarum?
cards.a: Posterior rami C8–T11

cards.q: What are the attachments of the intercostal muscles?
cards.a: Lower border of a rib → upper border of the rib below

cards.q: What is the action of the external intercostals?
cards.a: Elevate the ribs (inspiration)

cards.q: What is the action of the internal and innermost intercostals?
cards.a: Depress the ribs → but the part between the cartilages elevates them

cards.q: What are the attachments of the subcostal muscles?
cards.a: Inner surface of lower ribs near the angles → 2nd or 3rd rib below
cards.more: Best developed low in the thorax; they run like the internal intercostals and probably act like them.

cards.q: What are the attachments and action of transversus thoracis?
cards.a: Back of lower sternum → costal cartilages 2–6 → weakly depresses ribs
cards.more: Continuous below with transversus abdominis; the internal thoracic vessels lie just in front of it.

cards.q: What nerves supply the intercostals, subcostals and transversus thoracis?
cards.a: Intercostal nerves
cards.more:
MuscleFrom → toNerveAction
Serratus posterior superiorNuchal ligament, C7–T3 → ribs 2–4Intercostal 2–5Proprioception (elevates)
Serratus posterior inferiorT11–L2 → ribs 8–12Anterior rami T9–T12Proprioception (depresses)
Levatores costarumTransverse processes → rib belowPosterior rami C8–T11Elevate
IntercostalsRib → rib belowIntercostalExternal elevate; internal/innermost depress
SubcostalsLower ribs → 2nd/3rd rib belowIntercostalAs internals
Transversus thoracisLower sternum → cartilages 2–6IntercostalWeakly depresses

cards.q: Where does the intercostal neurovascular bundle run?
cards.a: In the costal groove on the inferior border of each rib, between the internal and innermost intercostals

cards.q: What is the order of structures in the intercostal neurovascular bundle, top to bottom?
cards.a: Vein → artery → nerve
cards.more: Tucked up under the lower border of the rib in the costal groove.

cards.q: Which intercostal structure is most often injured, and why?
cards.a: The nerve → it is the lowest and least protected of the three
cards.more: This is also why pain follows the intercostal distribution.

cards.q: Where do the collateral branches of the intercostal bundle run?
cards.a: Along the upper border of the rib below, between the internal and innermost layers

cards.q: What is the order of structures in the collateral branches, top to bottom?
cards.a: Nerve → artery → vein (reverse of the main bundle)

cards.q: Where in the intercostal space is a needle or chest drain inserted?
cards.a: Just above the rib below (lower part of the space)

cards.q: Why is a chest needle placed just above the rib below, but not right on it?
cards.a: Avoids the main bundle under the rib above → yet clears the collateral branches on the rib below

cards.q: How many intercostal spaces are there, and how are they numbered?
cards.a: 11 → each numbered for the rib above
cards.more: The 4th space lies between ribs 4 and 5. These numbers are how you name where to put a stethoscope or a needle.

cards.q: What is the space below the 12th rib called?
cards.a: Subcostal space

cards.q: What are the intercostal nerves?
cards.a: Anterior rami of thoracic spinal nerves T1–T11

cards.q: What is the anterior ramus of T12 called?
cards.a: Subcostal nerve

cards.q: What do the posterior rami of the thoracic spinal nerves supply?
cards.a: Deep back muscles and the skin over them

cards.q: Which intercostal nerves are typical?
cards.a: T3–T6

cards.q: Between which muscle layers does a typical intercostal nerve run?
cards.a: Internal and innermost intercostals

cards.q: What branches does a typical intercostal nerve give, in order?
cards.a: Collateral branch (near rib angle) → lateral cutaneous branch (midaxillary line) → anterior cutaneous branch (beside sternum)
cards.more: The lateral cutaneous branch splits into anterior and posterior branches.

cards.q: Besides skin, what does a typical intercostal nerve supply along its course?
cards.a:
Intercostal muscles
Parietal pleura

cards.q: Which intercostal nerves are atypical?
cards.a: T1–T2 and T7–T11

cards.q: How does the anterior ramus of T1 divide?
cards.a:
Large upper part → brachial plexus
Small lower part → 1st intercostal nerve
cards.more: The 1st intercostal nerve usually has no anterior cutaneous branch.

cards.q: How does the course of the 1st and 2nd intercostal nerves differ from typical ones?
cards.a: They run on the inner surface of their ribs, not along the lower border

cards.q: What is the intercostobrachial nerve?
cards.a: Lateral cutaneous branch of the 2nd intercostal nerve → supplies the floor of the axilla
cards.more: It comes through serratus anterior at the midaxillary line.

cards.q: What are the thoracoabdominal nerves?
cards.a: Intercostal nerves 7–11 → continue into the abdominal wall, supplying its skin and muscles
cards.more: Their anterior cutaneous branches pierce rectus abdominis near the midline.

cards.q: What is a dermatome?
cards.a: The strip of skin supplied by one spinal nerve

cards.q: Which dermatome lies at the clavicles?
cards.a: C5 (many charts put C4 there)

cards.q: Which dermatome lies at the nipple?
cards.a: T4

cards.q: Which dermatome lies at the umbilicus?
Which dermatome lies at the inguinal region?
cards.a: L1

cards.q: Why is loss of all feeling over one whole dermatome rare?
cards.a: Neighbouring dermatomes overlap

cards.q: Why does the herpes zoster (shingles) rash stay in one dermatome?
cards.a: The virus invades one spinal ganglion and travels out along its axons

cards.q: Why must an intercostal nerve block numb several nerves?
cards.a: Dermatomes overlap → neighbouring nerves also supply the area
cards.more: Care is taken not to puncture the neurovascular bundle.

cards.q: How is a thoracotomy incision placed to spare the intercostal bundles?
cards.a: Midway between ribs, or (for wider access) through the periosteum of a removed piece of rib
cards.more: A thoracotomy is an opening into the pleural cavity.

cards.q: From which two directions do the intercostal spaces get their blood supply?
cards.a:
Posterior intercostals from behind (mostly aorta)
Anterior intercostals from the internal thoracic artery in front
cards.more: The two meet in the middle.

cards.q: What is the internal thoracic artery a branch of, and where does it run?
cards.a: Subclavian artery → runs down just lateral to the sternum

cards.q: Which spaces get anterior intercostal arteries from the internal thoracic artery directly?
cards.a: Spaces 1–6

cards.q: What are the two terminal branches of the internal thoracic artery?
cards.a:
Superior epigastric artery
Musculophrenic artery

cards.q: Where does the superior epigastric artery go, and what does it anastomose with?
cards.a: Descends in the rectus sheath → inferior epigastric artery (from external iliac)

cards.q: What is the course of the musculophrenic artery, and which spaces does it supply?
cards.a: Follows the costal margin → anterior intercostals of spaces 7–9

cards.q: Why do intercostal spaces 10 and 11 have no anterior intercostal arteries?
cards.a: The cage is open in front at that level

cards.q: How much of each intercostal space do the posterior intercostal arteries supply?
cards.a: About two-thirds

cards.q: Where do the posterior intercostal arteries of spaces 1 and 2 come from?
cards.a: Superior (supreme) intercostal artery ← costocervical trunk

cards.q: Where do the posterior intercostal arteries of spaces 3–11 come from?
cards.a: Thoracic aorta

cards.q: Why are the right posterior intercostal arteries longer than the left?
cards.a: The aorta lies to the left → right arteries must cross the vertebral bodies

cards.q: In which intercostal spaces do anterior and posterior intercostal arteries anastomose?
cards.a: Spaces 1–9

cards.q: Into which venous system do the intercostal veins mainly drain?
cards.a: Azygos system
cards.more: A set of channels parallel to the venae cavae that drains the thoracic and posterior abdominal walls.

cards.q: How does the azygos system begin?
cards.a: Ascending lumbar vein + subcostal vein → azygos vein (right) / hemiazygos vein (left)

cards.q: Where do the 1st posterior intercostal veins drain?
cards.a: Brachiocephalic vein of the same side

cards.q: Where do the right 2nd–4th posterior intercostal veins drain?
cards.a: Right superior intercostal vein → azygos or right brachiocephalic vein

cards.q: Where do the left 2nd–4th posterior intercostal veins drain?
cards.a: Left superior intercostal vein → left brachiocephalic or accessory hemiazygos vein

cards.q: Where do the 5th–8th posterior intercostal veins drain on each side?
cards.a:
Right → azygos
Left → accessory hemiazygos → crosses to azygos

cards.q: Where do the 9th–11th posterior intercostal, subcostal and lumbar veins drain on each side?
cards.a:
Right → azygos
Left → hemiazygos → crosses to azygos
cards.more:
VeinsRightLeft
1stRight brachiocephalicLeft brachiocephalic
2nd–4thRight superior intercostal → azygos or right brachiocephalicLeft superior intercostal → left brachiocephalic or accessory hemiazygos
5th–8thAzygosAccessory hemiazygos → azygos
9th–11th, subcostal, lumbarAzygosHemiazygos → azygos

cards.q: Where does the azygos vein end?
cards.a: Arches over the root of the right lung → superior vena cava

cards.q: What nerve supplies the diaphragm, and from which spinal levels?
cards.a: Phrenic nerve → C3, C4, C5

cards.q: Why does the phrenic nerve arise so high, in the neck?
cards.a: The diaphragm develops in the neck and migrates down, dragging its nerve with it

cards.q: What does the phrenic nerve supply in the diaphragm?
cards.a:
Motor to the whole diaphragm
Sensory to its central part

cards.q: What carries sensation from the periphery of the diaphragm?
cards.a: Lower five intercostal nerves
cards.more: Texts give the lower six or seven intercostals plus the subcostal nerve.

cards.q: Where is pain referred from irritation of the central vs. peripheral diaphragm?
cards.a:
Central → shoulder
Periphery → skin over the costal margin
cards.more: Central sensation travels in the phrenic nerve (C3–C5); peripheral sensation in the lower intercostal nerves.

cards.q: What is the structure of the diaphragm?
cards.a: Musculotendinous dome between the thoracic and abdominal cavities

cards.q: Which dome of the diaphragm sits higher, and why?
cards.a: Right → pushed up by the liver

cards.q: In expiration, what levels do the right and left domes of the diaphragm reach?
cards.a:
Right → 5th rib
Left → 5th intercostal space

cards.q: What are the three muscular parts of the diaphragm and their origins?
cards.a:
Sternal → xiphoid (not always present)
Costal → lower six costal cartilages
Lumbar → arcuate ligaments + upper three lumbar vertebrae

cards.q: Where do all three muscular parts of the diaphragm insert?
cards.a: Central tendon

cards.q: What is the central tendon of the diaphragm fused to?
cards.a: Underside of the fibrous pericardium

cards.q: What happens to the central tendon when the diaphragm contracts?
cards.a: The peripheral muscle pulls it down

cards.q: Which part of the diaphragm forms the crura, and which crus is larger?
cards.a: Lumbar part → right crus is larger and longer

cards.q: What unites the two crura, and what does it arch in front of?
cards.a: Median arcuate ligament → arches in front of the aorta

cards.q: Where is the caval opening of the diaphragm, and at what level?
cards.a: In the central tendon → T8

cards.q: What passes through the caval opening?
cards.a:
Inferior vena cava
Right phrenic nerve
Lymphatics

cards.q: Where is the oesophageal hiatus, and at what level?
cards.a: In the right crus → T10

cards.q: What passes through the oesophageal hiatus?
cards.a:
Oesophagus
Anterior and posterior vagal trunks
Oesophageal branches of the left gastric vessels

cards.q: Where is the aortic hiatus, and at what level?
cards.a: Behind the diaphragm → T12

cards.q: What passes through the aortic hiatus?
cards.a:
Aorta
Azygos vein
Thoracic duct
cards.more:
OpeningLevelPasses
Caval (central tendon)T8IVC, right phrenic nerve, lymphatics
Oesophageal (right crus)T10Oesophagus, vagal trunks, oesophageal branches of left gastric vessels
Aortic (behind)T12Aorta, azygos vein, thoracic duct

cards.q: Why does diaphragm contraction constrict the oesophagus but not the aorta?
cards.a: Right crus muscle surrounds the oesophageal hiatus → the aorta passes behind the diaphragm, not through it

cards.q: What happens to the diaphragm if one phrenic nerve is cut?
cards.a: That half is paralysed → dome stays permanently elevated on chest X-ray; muscle atrophies

cards.q: How can the diaphragm herniate?
cards.a: Congenitally, or through a rupture (most after major trauma)

cards.q: On which side do most traumatic diaphragmatic ruptures occur, and why?
cards.a: Left → the liver shields the right

cards.q: Which organs can pass into the thorax through a diaphragmatic hernia?
cards.a:
Stomach
Small intestine
Transverse colon
Spleen

cards.q: Which muscles act in quiet inspiration?
cards.a: Diaphragm and external intercostals

cards.q: What produces quiet expiration?
cards.a: Passive lung recoil and diaphragm relaxation, with the internal intercostals
cards.more: Many texts treat quiet expiration as purely passive and bring in the internal intercostals only for forced breathing.

cards.q: Which muscles drive forced expiration?
cards.a: Muscles of the abdominal wall
cards.more:
InspirationExpiration
QuietDiaphragm + external intercostalsPassive recoil + diaphragm relaxation, with internal intercostals
ForcedAdds pectoralis major and minor, serratus anterior, scalenesAbdominal wall muscles

cards.q: In what layer does the breast sit?
cards.a: Superficial fascia of the anterior chest wall → on top of pectoralis major, not within it

cards.q: What is the retromammary space, and what does it allow?
cards.a: Loose plane between the breast and pectoralis major → lets the breast move freely over the chest wall

cards.q: What does a breast lump fixed to the chest wall indicate?
cards.a: Invasion through the retromammary space into the muscle → changes the staging
cards.more: A lump that moves freely is confined to the breast.

cards.q: Over which muscles does the mammary gland develop?
cards.a: Pectoralis major and serratus anterior (superficial to their fascia)
cards.more: The gland is well developed in women and rudimentary in men.

cards.q: What is the extent of the breast bed?
cards.a:
Lateral border of sternum → midaxillary line
2nd → 6th rib

cards.q: What forms the bed of the breast, and in what proportion?
cards.a:
~2/3 pectoralis major and its fascia
~1/3 serratus anterior and its fascia

cards.q: What is the axillary process (tail) of the breast?
cards.a: An extension of the breast toward the axilla

cards.q: How many lobes of glandular tissue does the breast contain?
How does each breast lobe drain to the nipple?
cards.a: Lactiferous duct → lactiferous sinus → opens separately onto the nipple

cards.q: What kind of gland is the breast?
cards.a: A modified sweat gland, with no capsule

cards.q: What makes up most of the breast's size, and what grows in pregnancy?
cards.a: Fat (laid down at puberty) → in pregnancy the glandular tissue itself grows

cards.q: What are the suspensory ligaments of Cooper?
cards.a: Fibrous bands from the skin to the deep fascia, separating the lobes

cards.q: What do the suspensory ligaments do, and where are they strongest?
cards.a: Bind the gland firmly to the overlying skin → strongest in the upper breast

cards.q: What glands make the areola rich, and what do they do?
cards.a: Sebaceous glands → keep the areola and nipple from cracking during breastfeeding

cards.q: Where can supernumerary nipples appear?
cards.a: Anywhere along a line from the axilla to the groin (above or below the normal breasts)
cards.more: They are usually rudimentary.

cards.q: How does a breast tumour cause skin dimpling?
cards.a: Tethers and shortens the suspensory ligaments → pulls the overlying skin inward

cards.q: What causes the peau d'orange appearance of the breast?
cards.a: Blocked superficial lymphatics → oedematous, puffy, pitted skin

cards.q: What causes nipple retraction in breast cancer?
cards.a: A cancer under the areola shortens the lactiferous ducts → pulls the nipple in
cards.more: The nipple can also deviate and the breast's contour change.

cards.q: What are the four arterial sources of the breast?
cards.a:
Internal thoracic (medial mammary + anterior intercostal branches)
Lateral thoracic artery
Thoracoacromial trunk
Posterior intercostal arteries

cards.q: Where does venous blood from the breast drain?
cards.a:
Mostly → axillary vein
Smaller part → internal thoracic vein

cards.q: Which nerves supply the breast?
cards.a: 4th–6th intercostal nerves

cards.q: What do the intercostal nerves carry to and from the breast?
cards.a:
Sensation from the overlying skin
Sympathetic fibres to blood vessels and smooth muscle of skin and nipple
cards.more: They pass through the pectoral fascia.

cards.q: How is the breast divided to describe a lump?
cards.a: Four quadrants around the nipple, read like a clock face

cards.q: Why do breast quadrants matter clinically?
cards.a:
They drain to different nodes
Cancers are not spread evenly among them

cards.q: Which breast quadrant is the site of most cancers, and what share?
cards.a: Superolateral → about 60%

cards.q: Why does the superolateral quadrant get the most breast cancers?
cards.a: It has the most glandular tissue (includes the axillary tail)

cards.q: What share of breast cancers arise in the other three quadrants?
cards.a:
Superomedial ~15%
Inferolateral ~10%
Inferomedial ~5%

cards.q: Why is the breast's lymphatic drainage worth knowing precisely?
cards.a: It determines where cancer spreads

cards.q: Where does most of the breast's lymph drain, and how much?
cards.a: Axillary nodes → more than 75% (mainly from the lateral quadrants)
cards.more: That is why the axilla is examined and sampled in breast cancer.

cards.q: Which group of axillary nodes receives breast lymph first?
cards.a: Pectoral group

cards.q: Where does lymph from the medial part of the breast drain?
cards.a: Parasternal (internal thoracic) nodes → can cross to the opposite side

cards.q: Where can lymph from the lower and upper quadrants of the breast drain?
cards.a:
Lower quadrants → abdominal nodes
Upper quadrants → supraclavicular nodes

cards.q: What is the most common cancer in women, and what type is it usually?
cards.a: Breast cancer → adenocarcinoma of the lactiferous duct epithelium

cards.q: Where does breast cancer spread?
cards.a:
Most often axillary nodes
Also supraclavicular nodes, opposite breast, abdomen
cards.more: It spreads along the lymph routes, so the drainage map is the map of spread.

cards.q: What is the main screening test for breast cancer?
cards.a: Mammography

cards.q: What is ultrasound used for in breast imaging?
cards.a:
Where mammograms see poorly (dense breasts)
Telling a fluid-filled cyst from a solid mass

cards.q: What is magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) used for in breast cancer?
cards.a:
Examining a known tumour
Ruling out false positives
Planning treatment

cards.q: What share of breast cancer cases occur in men?
cards.a: About 4.5% (anatomy texts give about 1.5%)

cards.q: How does breast cancer in men typically behave?
cards.a: Invades pectoral fascia, pectoralis major and axillary nodes → often found only after wide spread

cards.q: What share of males with Klinefelter syndrome develop gynaecomastia, and when?
cards.a: About 40% → at puberty
cards.more: Gynaecomastia = enlarged breast tissue.

cards.q: What does a simple mastectomy remove?
cards.a: The breast, down to the retromammary space

cards.q: What does a radical mastectomy remove beyond a simple mastectomy?
cards.a: Pectoral muscles, fat, fascia, and as many axillary and pectoral nodes as needed

cards.q: What breast cancer surgery is more common today?
cards.a: Lumpectomy or quadrantectomy → followed by radiation

cards.q: Which nerve is at risk in surgery on the lateral breast quadrants, and what does its injury cause?
cards.a: Long thoracic nerve → winged scapula

cards.q: Why is lymphoedema of the arm common after breast cancer treatment?
cards.a: Removing or irradiating axillary nodes destroys the arm's drainage route → fluid accumulates in the limb

cards.q: What is the visceral pleura?
cards.a: The pleura clinging tightly to the lung surface
cards.more: The pleura is one continuous membrane folded back on itself.

cards.q: What does the parietal pleura line?
cards.a: Inside of the chest wall, the diaphragm and the mediastinum

cards.q: Where do the visceral and parietal pleura become continuous?
cards.a: Where the root of the lung enters

cards.q: What is the pleural cavity?
cards.a: A potential space between visceral and parietal pleura, holding a thin film of fluid

cards.q: What two jobs does the pleural fluid do?
cards.a:
Lets the layers slide
Holds the lung against the chest wall by surface tension
cards.more: Because the lung is held to the wall, the lung expands when the chest does.

cards.q: How many pleural sacs does the thoracic cavity hold, and what lies between them?
cards.a: Two (one per lung); the mediastinum between them
cards.more: The heart has its own equivalent of a pleural sac: the pericardium.

cards.q: In the “fist pushed into a balloon” model of the pleura, what does each part represent?
cards.a:
Fist = lung
Balloon wall touching fist = visceral pleura
Rest of balloon = parietal pleura
Flattened space between = pleural cavity

cards.q: Why does the lung collapse when the chest wall is punctured?
cards.a: Air enters pleural cavity → surface-tension link broken → elastic lung recoils from the wall
cards.more: That is a pneumothorax, and it follows entirely from the pleura being a potential space.

cards.q: Name the four parts of the parietal pleura (named by what they line).
cards.a:
Cervical
Costal
Diaphragmatic
Mediastinal

cards.q: What is the cupula?
cards.a: Cervical parietal pleura, rising into the root of the neck over the apex of the lung

cards.q: What layer separates the parietal pleura from the chest wall?
cards.a: Endothoracic fascia

cards.q: What are the lines of pleural reflection?
cards.a: Lines where one part of the parietal pleura turns into the next

cards.q: At the sternal and vertebral lines of pleural reflection, what does costal pleura turn into?
cards.a: Mediastinal pleura
cards.more: Sternal line in front, vertebral line behind.

cards.q: At the costal line of pleural reflection, what does costal pleura turn into?
cards.a: Diaphragmatic pleura (the line runs below)

cards.q: What is the pulmonary ligament?
cards.a: Loose double fold of mediastinal pleura below the lung root, running from hilum toward the diaphragmatic surface

cards.q: What is the function of the pulmonary ligament?
cards.a: Gives the root structures room to expand
cards.more: For example when venous return rises in exercise.

cards.q: How does the visceral pleura differ in texture and extent from the parietal pleura?
cards.a: Shiny, inseparable from the lung; covers all lung surfaces, fissures included, except the hilum

cards.q: What is a pleural recess?
cards.a: Where two layers of parietal pleura lie against each other with no lung between
cards.more: They exist because the lungs do not fill their pleural sacs completely.

cards.q: Where is the costomediastinal recess?
cards.a: Behind the sternum, where costal pleura meets mediastinal pleura

cards.q: Where is the costodiaphragmatic recess?
cards.a: Below the inferior border of the lung, between costal and diaphragmatic pleura
cards.more: It is the larger of the two recesses. The pleural cavity extends further down than the lung does.

cards.q: Which ribs does the costodiaphragmatic recess span in the midaxillary line?
cards.a: Roughly 8th → 10th ribs

cards.q: When does the lung fill the costodiaphragmatic recess?
cards.a: Only during a deep breath in

cards.q: Which part of the pleural cavity fills first with a pleural effusion, and why?
cards.a: Costodiaphragmatic recess: the lowest point of the cavity (in someone sitting up)
cards.more: Because fluid collects there first, it is also where fluid is drained from.

cards.q: What nerves supply the parietal pleura, and how pain-sensitive is it?
cards.a: Somatic (intercostal and phrenic nerves) → exquisitely pain-sensitive
cards.more: Pain from its costal part localises well.

cards.q: What is the nerve supply of the visceral pleura, and is it pain-sensitive?
cards.a: Autonomic only → insensitive to pain

cards.q: Pleuritic chest pain comes from which layer of pleura?
cards.a: Parietal pleura

cards.q: Which nerves supply the costal pleura and the periphery of the diaphragmatic pleura?
cards.a: Intercostal nerves

cards.q: Which nerve supplies the mediastinal pleura and the central diaphragmatic pleura?
cards.a: Phrenic nerve

cards.q: Which arteries supply the parietal pleura?
cards.a: Internal thoracic and posterior intercostal arteries
cards.more: The parietal pleura shares the blood supply of the chest wall.

cards.q: Where do the veins of the parietal pleura drain?
cards.a: Azygos and internal thoracic veins

cards.q: Where does lymph from the parietal pleura drain?
cards.a: Parasternal, mediastinal and intercostal nodes

cards.q: What blood vessels supply and drain the visceral pleura?
cards.a: The lung’s own bronchial vessels: bronchial arteries; bronchial veins → azygos system or left superior intercostal vein

cards.q: Where does lymph from the visceral pleura drain?
cards.a: Bronchopulmonary nodes

cards.q: What can be heard with a stethoscope in pleuritis, and why?
cards.a: Friction rub: the inflamed pleural layers rub together

cards.q: What collects in the pleural cavity in pneumothorax, haemothorax, hydrothorax and chylothorax?
cards.a:
Pneumothorax = air
Haemothorax = blood
Hydrothorax = fluid
Chylothorax = lymph

cards.topic: Lobes and surfaces of the lungs
cards.q: How many lobes and which fissures does the right lung have?
cards.a: 3 lobes; oblique + horizontal fissures

cards.topic: Lobes and surfaces of the lungs
cards.q: How many lobes and which fissures does the left lung have?
cards.a: 2 lobes; oblique fissure only

cards.topic: Lobes and surfaces of the lungs
cards.q: Which two features of the left lung give up space to the heart?
cards.a:
Cardiac notch
Lingula (tongue-like)

cards.topic: Lobes and surfaces of the lungs
cards.q: Compare the size and shape of the right and left lungs.
cards.a:
Right: larger, heavier, short and wide, shallow cardiac impression
Left: long and narrow, deep cardiac impression
cards.more: Lobes and fissures do vary between people.

cards.topic: Lobes and surfaces of the lungs
cards.q: How high does the apex of the lung rise, and what artery lies against it?
cards.a: About an inch into the root of the neck, under the cervical pleura; against the subclavian artery
cards.more: Each lung is a cone; the apex is its top.

cards.topic: Lobes and surfaces of the lungs
cards.q: What marks the costal surface of the lung?
cards.a: Impressions of the ribs

cards.topic: Lobes and surfaces of the lungs
cards.q: What does the diaphragmatic surface of the right lung sit over?
cards.a: Right lobe of the liver
cards.more: The diaphragmatic surface is concave.

cards.topic: Lobes and surfaces of the lungs
cards.q: What does the diaphragmatic surface of the left lung sit over?
cards.a:
Left lobe of the liver
Stomach
Spleen

cards.topic: Lobes and surfaces of the lungs
cards.q: What does the mediastinal surface of the lung face, and what lies in its middle?
cards.a: Vertebrae behind, mediastinum in front; hilum in the middle

cards.topic: Lobes and surfaces of the lungs
cards.q: Compare the anterior and posterior borders of the lung.
cards.a:
Anterior: thin, shorter
Posterior: thick, beside the spine from C7 to T10

cards.topic: Lobes and surfaces of the lungs
cards.q: Why does healthy lung float in water while a stillborn baby’s lungs sink?
cards.a: Healthy lung is spongy and air-filled; a stillborn’s lungs were never aerated

cards.topic: Lobes and surfaces of the lungs
cards.q: How does the colour of the lung change with age?
cards.a: Pink at birth → grey from years of inhaled carbon

cards.q: What structures make up the root of each lung?
cards.a:
1 main bronchus
1 pulmonary artery
2 pulmonary veins

cards.q: Which structures are the most anterior and inferior at the hilum of both lungs?
cards.a: Pulmonary veins

cards.q: At the right hilum, which structure is most posterior, and what does “eparterial” mean?
cards.a: Main bronchus; one bronchial branch passes above the pulmonary artery (eparterial)
cards.more: The figure labels this branch the bronchus to the superior lobe.

cards.q: At the right hilum, where does the pulmonary artery lie relative to the bronchus?
cards.a: Anterior

cards.q: Which structure is highest at the left hilum?
cards.a: Pulmonary artery

cards.q: Which nerve passes in front of the lung root, and which behind it?
cards.a:
Phrenic nerve in front
Vagus nerve behind

cards.q: Name the impressions on the mediastinal surface of the right lung.
cards.a:
Right brachiocephalic vein
Superior vena cava
Azygos vein and its arch
Oesophagus
Trachea
Inferior vena cava

cards.q: Which vein hooks over the root of the right lung?
cards.a: Arch of the azygos vein

cards.q: Name the impressions on the mediastinal surface of the left lung.
cards.a:
Aortic arch and descending aorta
Left subclavian artery
Left brachiocephalic vein
Oesophagus
Trachea
Heart (apex, left ventricle, auricle)

cards.q: What is the surface marking of the oblique fissure?
cards.a: Spine of T2 behind → 6th costal cartilage in front

cards.q: What is the surface marking of the horizontal fissure?
cards.a: Forward from the oblique fissure along the 4th rib and costal cartilage

cards.q: How does the inferior border of the lung relate to the inferior border of the pleura?
cards.a: Lung lies two levels above the pleura all the way round
cards.more:
LineLungPleura
Midclavicular6th rib8th rib
Midaxillary8th rib10th rib
Beside the spineT10T12

cards.q: In the midclavicular line, where are the inferior borders of the lung and the pleura?
cards.a:
Lung: 6th rib
Pleura: 8th rib

cards.q: In the midaxillary line, where are the inferior borders of the lung and the pleura?
cards.a:
Lung: 8th rib
Pleura: 10th rib

cards.q: Beside the spine, where are the inferior borders of the lung and the pleura?
cards.a:
Lung: T10
Pleura: T12

cards.q: Why is there a zone where a needle can enter the pleural cavity without touching lung?
cards.a: The pleura reaches lower than the lung at every point (the costodiaphragmatic recess)
cards.more: That mismatch between lung border and pleural border is the anatomy behind chest drainage.

cards.q: What is thoracentesis?
cards.a: Draining fluid, blood or pus from the costodiaphragmatic recess

cards.q: Where is the needle inserted for thoracentesis?
cards.a: 9th intercostal space, midaxillary line
cards.more: Below the lung but inside the pleura.

cards.q: Why does the thoracentesis needle pass just above the rib below the space?
cards.a: High enough to miss the collateral branches

cards.q: Why is the thoracentesis needle angled upward?
cards.a: So it does not go through the diaphragm into the liver

cards.q: At what level does the trachea divide into the two main bronchi?
cards.a: Sternal angle

cards.q: What is the carina?
cards.a: The internal ridge between the openings of the two main bronchi

cards.q: What course does the left main bronchus take to reach its hilum?
cards.a: Below the aortic arch, in front of the oesophagus and thoracic aorta

cards.q: How does the right main bronchus differ from the left?
cards.a: Wider, shorter, more vertical

cards.q: Into which side do inhaled foreign bodies and aspirated material usually go, and why?
cards.a: Right: its main bronchus is wider, shorter and more vertical
cards.more: There it can be seen through a bronchoscope.

cards.q: In what order does the bronchial tree branch?
cards.a: Main bronchus → lobar (secondary) bronchi → segmental (tertiary) bronchi → terminal bronchioles → respiratory bronchioles → alveolar ducts → alveolar sacs

cards.q: How many lobar (secondary) bronchi are there on each side?
cards.a:
Right: 3
Left: 2

cards.q: What does each segmental (tertiary) bronchus supply?
cards.a: One bronchopulmonary segment

cards.q: What shape is a bronchopulmonary segment?
cards.a: A pyramid, apex toward the root of the lung

cards.q: How many bronchopulmonary segments are there?
cards.a: Usually 18–20: 10 right, 8–10 left

cards.q: Why can a surgeon remove a single bronchopulmonary segment?
cards.a: Each segment is an independent respiratory unit
cards.more: So the segment containing a lung cancer can be removed and the rest of the lung keeps working.

cards.topic: Blood, lymph and nerves of the lung
cards.q: What are the two circulations of the lung, and the job of each?
cards.a:
Pulmonary: gas exchange
Bronchial: feeds the lung’s supporting tissue and the visceral pleura

cards.topic: Blood, lymph and nerves of the lung
cards.q: Trace the pulmonary circulation through the lung.
cards.a: Right ventricle → pulmonary trunk → right/left pulmonary arteries → lobar → segmental arteries → capillaries → intersegmental veins → superior/inferior pulmonary veins → left atrium
cards.more: The pulmonary arteries carry poorly oxygenated blood and branch alongside the airways.

cards.topic: Blood, lymph and nerves of the lung
cards.q: How many bronchial arteries supply the right lung, and where do they arise?
cards.a: One: from a left superior bronchial artery, the thoracic aorta or a posterior intercostal artery

cards.topic: Blood, lymph and nerves of the lung
cards.q: How many bronchial arteries supply the left lung, and where do they arise?
cards.a: Two: from the thoracic aorta

cards.topic: Blood, lymph and nerves of the lung
cards.q: Where does the right bronchial vein drain?
cards.a: Azygos vein

cards.topic: Blood, lymph and nerves of the lung
cards.q: Where do the left bronchial veins drain?
cards.a: Left superior intercostal vein or hemiazygos vein
cards.more: Texts name the accessory hemiazygos vein.

cards.topic: Blood, lymph and nerves of the lung
cards.q: Trace the lymph drainage of the lung and visceral pleura.
cards.a: Bronchopulmonary (hilar) nodes → superior and inferior (carinal) tracheobronchial nodes → bronchomediastinal trunks → lymphatic duct of own side or venous angle

cards.topic: Blood, lymph and nerves of the lung
cards.q: What is the venous angle?
cards.a: Where the internal jugular and subclavian veins meet

cards.topic: Blood, lymph and nerves of the lung
cards.q: Through which plexuses do nerves reach the lung?
cards.a: Anterior and posterior pulmonary plexuses
cards.more: Autonomic plexuses whose fibres follow the bronchial tree as it branches.

cards.topic: Blood, lymph and nerves of the lung
cards.q: What is the source of the parasympathetic supply to the lung, and its effects?
cards.a: Vagus nerve → bronchoconstriction, vasodilation, bronchial gland secretion
cards.more: Parasympathetic fibres also take part in the cough reflex and in monitoring blood gases.

cards.topic: Blood, lymph and nerves of the lung
cards.q: What is the source of the sympathetic supply to the lung, and its effects?
cards.a: Sympathetic chain T2–T5 → bronchodilation, vasoconstriction, inhibition of alveolar glands

cards.q: What is the usual source of a pulmonary embolus?
cards.a: A clot from a leg vein, lodging in the pulmonary arterial tree

cards.q: What happens if a pulmonary embolus blocks the pulmonary artery itself versus a segmental artery?
cards.a:
Pulmonary artery → acute respiratory distress
Segmental artery → that segment can die (pulmonary infarct)

cards.q: What are the usual symptoms of a pulmonary embolus?
cards.a: Chest pain; sudden shortness of breath (dyspnoea)

cards.q: Where does a Pancoast tumour sit, and what does it press on?
cards.a: Apex of the lung → lower trunk of the brachial plexus + sympathetic chain

cards.q: What arm and hand signs does a Pancoast tumour cause?
cards.a:
Severe pain down the medial arm
Wasting of forearm and hand muscles
cards.more: From pressure on the lower trunk of the brachial plexus.

cards.q: What facial signs does a Pancoast tumour cause?
cards.a:
Small pupil (miosis)
Drooping eyelid (ptosis)
Loss of sweating (anhidrosis)
cards.more: From pressure on the sympathetic chain.

cards.q: What does pneumonia do to the alveoli, and how does it show on a chest X-ray?
cards.a: Inflamed alveoli fill with fluid → localised radiodense area
cards.more: It can bring up blood-stained sputum.

cards.q: What percussion note is heard over air, fluid and solid tissue?
cards.a:
Air: resonant
Fluid: dull
Solid: flat

cards.q: What percussion note do you expect over the liver and spleen, and over the scapula and thick muscle?
cards.a:
Liver/spleen: dull to flat
Scapula/thick muscle: flat

cards.q: From what does the respiratory system begin?
cards.a: An outpouching from the foregut (respiratory diverticulum)
cards.more: It grows downward and branches repeatedly.

cards.q: When and from where does the laryngotracheal diverticulum appear?
cards.a: Day 28 (week 4), from the ventral wall of the primordial pharynx
cards.more: Also called the respiratory diverticulum or lung bud; it is the first sign of the respiratory system.

cards.q: What is the laryngotracheal groove, and what does it become?
cards.a: Opening of the laryngotracheal diverticulum → laryngeal inlet

cards.q: Which germ layer forms the lining of the respiratory tract, and what does it give?
cards.a: Endoderm → lung epithelium + glands of larynx, trachea and bronchi

cards.q: What forms the cartilage, muscle and connective tissue around the airway?
cards.a: Splanchnic mesoderm

cards.q: What do the laryngeal muscles and cartilages develop from, and what nerve does that give the larynx?
cards.a: Mesoderm of pharyngeal arches 4 and 6 → vagus nerve (cranial nerve X)
cards.more: The larynx is the exception: its walls come from the arches, not from splanchnic mesoderm.

cards.q: Why must a septum grow between the developing airway and the oesophagus?
cards.a: The airway buds off the gut tube (foregut)

cards.q: How does the tracheo-oesophageal septum form?
cards.a: Tracheo-oesophageal folds grow in from the sides and fuse

cards.q: What does the tracheo-oesophageal septum divide the foregut into?
cards.a:
Ventral laryngotracheal tube
Dorsal oesophagus

cards.q: What causes a tracheo-oesophageal fistula?
cards.a: Incomplete separation by the tracheo-oesophageal septum → persistent trachea–oesophagus connection
cards.more: Often occurs with oesophageal atresia.

cards.q: Why does a pregnancy with tracheo-oesophageal fistula often show polyhydramnios?
cards.a: The fetus cannot swallow amniotic fluid normally

cards.q: How common is tracheo-oesophageal fistula, and which sex is more affected?
cards.a: About 1 in 3000–4500 live births; boys more often

cards.q: What is the commonest variety of tracheo-oesophageal fistula (about 85%)?
cards.a: Oesophageal atresia (blind upper pouch) + fistula between trachea and lower oesophagus

cards.q: Name the other three varieties of tracheo-oesophageal fistula.
cards.a:
H-type fistula, no atresia
Atresia + fistula from the upper pouch
Atresia + fistulas at both ends

cards.q: What is seen in the mouth and nose of a newborn with oesophageal atresia and fistula?
cards.a: Excess saliva: fine white frothy mucus that returns after suctioning

cards.q: What happens at feeds in a newborn with oesophageal atresia and fistula?
cards.a: Chokes, gags and turns cyanotic; regurgitates milk (because of the atresia)

cards.q: How can tracheo-oesophageal fistula cause aspiration pneumonia or pneumonitis?
cards.a: Stomach contents reflux into the lungs

cards.q: What prenatal findings suggest tracheo-oesophageal fistula with atresia?
cards.a:
Polyhydramnios
Small or absent stomach bubble on ultrasound
Low fetal weight
cards.more: The stomach bubble is the fluid-filled fetal stomach.

cards.q: How is tracheo-oesophageal fistula with atresia usually diagnosed after birth?
cards.a: A catheter cannot be passed from the mouth into the stomach
cards.more: Most cases are diagnosed after birth, between birth and about 12 days.

cards.q: How is tracheo-oesophageal fistula treated?
cards.a: Surgery; postponed if the baby is very small or has complications such as pneumonia

cards.q: What does the distal end of the laryngotracheal tube swell into?
cards.a: The respiratory bud

cards.q: By week 5, what has the respiratory bud split into?
cards.a: Two bronchial buds

cards.q: Why does the right lung have three lobes and the left two?
cards.a: Bronchial buds branch into 3 secondary (lobar) bronchi on the right, 2 on the left

cards.q: Into which canals do the growing lung buds push, and what do they become?
cards.a: Pericardioperitoneal canals → pleural cavities

cards.q: What does the visceral pleura develop from?
cards.a: Splanchnic mesoderm carried as a coat on the growing lung buds

cards.q: What does the parietal pleura develop from?
cards.a: Somatic mesoderm lining the body wall

cards.q: Name the four stages of lung maturation in order, with timing.
cards.a: Pseudoglandular 6–16 wk → canalicular 16–26 wk → terminal sac 26 wk–birth → alveolar 32 wk–8 yr
cards.more: Some newer textbooks give overlapping windows: about 5–17 weeks, 16–25 weeks, 24 weeks to late fetal life, and late fetal life to 8 years.

cards.q: What forms in the pseudoglandular stage (6–16 weeks)?
cards.a: Branching airways: simple columnar endodermal tubes → about 15–25 terminal bronchioles; few capillaries
cards.more: The lung looks like a gland.

cards.q: Why is no gas exchange possible in the pseudoglandular stage?
cards.a: There are ducts but no alveoli

cards.q: What changes in the canalicular stage (16–26 weeks)?
cards.a: Airways widen, tissue vascularised; terminal bronchiole → ≥3 respiratory bronchioles → 3–6 alveolar ducts (simple cuboidal)

cards.q: When does respiration first become (just about) possible?
cards.a: At the very end of the canalicular stage
cards.more: Babies born before 20 weeks usually do not survive.

cards.q: What happens to the terminal sacs in the terminal sac stage (26 weeks to birth)?
cards.a: They bud from alveolar ducts and thin out; capillaries bulge into them

cards.q: In the terminal sac stage, what does the cuboidal lining become, and what do those cells form?
cards.a: Type I pneumocytes → with capillaries, the blood–air barrier

cards.q: In which stage do type II cells appear and surfactant production begin?
cards.a: Terminal sac stage (26 weeks to birth)

cards.q: At what gestational age can babies survive with intensive care?
cards.a: 25–28 weeks

cards.q: How many alveoli are there at birth versus age 8, and how are new ones made?
cards.a: 20–70 million → 300–400 million; by septation and branching of existing alveoli
cards.more: This is the alveolar stage (32 weeks to 8 years), running from late fetal life well into childhood.

cards.q: Which two things must arrive together for a premature baby to be viable?
cards.a:
Thin enough blood–air barrier
Enough surfactant to stop alveoli collapsing
cards.more: Delivery before surfactant is adequate causes neonatal respiratory distress syndrome.

cards.q: Which cells make surfactant, and what does it do?
cards.a: Type II pneumocytes; reduces surface tension in the alveolus

cards.q: Why do the smallest alveoli collapse without surfactant?
cards.a: Law of Laplace: smaller radius → higher collapsing pressure

cards.q: How can surfactant production be accelerated before a preterm delivery?
cards.a: Steroids given to the mother

cards.q: What is respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) of the newborn, its other name, and how common is it?
cards.a: Surfactant deficiency in a premature baby; hyaline membrane disease; about 2% of live newborns

cards.q: What are the signs of neonatal respiratory distress syndrome?
cards.a:
Effortful or abnormal breathing
Cyanosis
Episodes of apnoea
Less urine

cards.q: How is neonatal respiratory distress syndrome treated?
cards.a: Artificial surfactant, oxygen, continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP)
cards.more: Mechanical ventilation is kept for severe cases and avoided when possible.

cards.q: What do fetal breathing movements do?
cards.a: Draw in amniotic fluid → condition breathing muscles and stimulate lung maturation

cards.q: How full of fluid are the lungs at birth?
cards.a: About half full

cards.q: By which three routes is lung fluid cleared at birth?
cards.a:
Out through mouth and nose (chest squeezed in vaginal delivery)
Into pulmonary capillaries, arteries and veins
Into lymphatics

cards.q: What changes in the lungs and circulation at birth?
cards.a:
Lungs: secretory → gas-exchanging; surfactant released into alveolar sacs
Pulmonary and systemic circulations become separate circuits

cards.q: Name the four sources of the diaphragm.
cards.a:
Septum transversum
Pleuroperitoneal folds (membranes)
Muscular ingrowth from the body wall
Dorsal mesentery of the oesophagus

cards.q: What does the septum transversum become in the diaphragm?
cards.a: Central tendon

cards.q: What does the dorsal mesentery of the oesophagus form in the diaphragm?
cards.a: Crura

cards.q: What happens if the components of the diaphragm fail to fuse?
cards.a: Abdominal contents herniate into the chest (congenital diaphragmatic hernia)

cards.q: Why is a congenital diaphragmatic hernia dangerous for the lung?
cards.a: It compresses the developing lung → pulmonary hypoplasia
cards.more: The lung never gets room to grow; the problem is as much the lung as the hole.

cards.q: On which side, and where, does congenital diaphragmatic hernia usually occur?
cards.a: Left, posterolateral (Bochdalek type)

cards.q: Why is congenital diaphragmatic hernia usually on the left?
cards.a: Left pleuroperitoneal membrane lags in development and never fully fuses

cards.q: In a left posterolateral diaphragmatic hernia, what herniates and what does it do to the heart?
cards.a: Small intestine, colon, spleen, stomach → push the heart across
cards.more: About half of these babies survive.

cards.q: What nerve supplies the diaphragm, and why that nerve?
cards.a: Phrenic nerve (C3–C5): picked up where the diaphragm first formed, in the neck

cards.q: What is pulmonary hypoplasia, and is it usually primary or secondary?
cards.a: Incomplete development of lung tissue; usually secondary to something else

cards.q: Which two things does normal lung growth need?
cards.a:
The right transcription factors
Enough amniotic fluid

cards.q: Besides diaphragmatic hernia, what is the classic cause of pulmonary hypoplasia?
cards.a: Bilateral renal agenesis

cards.q: How does bilateral renal agenesis cause pulmonary hypoplasia?
cards.a: No fetal urine → oligohydramnios → small thorax squeezed by the uterine wall

cards.q: What is the clinical range and mortality of pulmonary hypoplasia?
cards.a: No symptoms → severe respiratory distress; mortality about 71–95%

cards.q: In pulmonary hypoplasia, which way does the mediastinum shift, and what happens to breath sounds?
cards.a: Toward the affected side; breath sounds reduced on that side

cards.q: Why can right-sided pulmonary hypoplasia be mistaken for dextrocardia?
cards.a: The mediastinum shifts toward the affected side, moving the heart to the right

cards.q: How is pulmonary hypoplasia managed?
cards.a: Fetal surgery sometimes (e.g. relieving urinary obstruction so amniotic fluid recovers); otherwise ventilate until lungs cope
cards.more: The condition may be fatal.

cards.q: What three things must the heart tube do to become a four-chambered double pump?
cards.a:
Loop
Divide by septa
Split its outflow in two
cards.more: Nearly every congenital heart defect is one of those three going wrong.

cards.q: In looping, which way does the heart tube bend, and where does that put the chambers?
cards.a: To the right → atria up and behind, ventricles down and in front

cards.q: What happens if the heart tube loops the wrong way?
cards.a: The chambers end up mirror-imaged

cards.q: Why must the fetal atrial septum still let blood cross from right to left?
cards.a: The fetal lungs are not working, so blood must bypass them

cards.q: How does the atrial septum divide the atria yet allow right-to-left flow?
cards.a: Two overlapping septa with a gap (the foramen ovale) acting as a one-way flap
cards.more: In the figure the two septa are the septum primum and septum secundum.

cards.q: Why does the foramen ovale close at birth?
cards.a: Lungs open → left atrial pressure rises → flap pressed shut

cards.q: What results if the foramen ovale fails to seal?
cards.a: Atrial septal defect

cards.q: How does the ventricular septum form?
cards.a: Grows up from the floor and meets tissue growing down from the outflow region

cards.q: What is the most common ventricular septal defect (VSD), and why?
cards.a: Membranous VSD: the membranous portion is the last part to close

cards.q: What divides the single outflow tract into aorta and pulmonary trunk?
cards.a: A spiral ridge of tissue (septum)

cards.q: Why do the aorta and pulmonary trunk wrap around each other?
cards.a: The septum that divides them spirals

cards.q: What defect results if the spiral septum fails to form at all?
cards.a: Persistent truncus arteriosus: aorta and pulmonary trunk stay one vessel

cards.q: What defect results if the outflow septum forms but does not spiral?
cards.a: Transposition of the great arteries: vessels come off the wrong ventricles

cards.q: What outflow septum error causes tetralogy of Fallot?
cards.a: Uneven division: septum sits too far forward → pulmonary side too narrow

cards.q: What are the four features of tetralogy of Fallot?
cards.a:
Pulmonary stenosis
Ventricular septal defect
Overriding aorta
Right ventricular hypertrophy
cards.more: All are consequences of one septum sitting too far forward.

cards.q: How many shunts does the fetal circulation have, and what does each do in general?
cards.a: Three; each bypasses something not yet in use

cards.q: What does the ductus venosus bypass?
cards.a: The liver

cards.q: What does the foramen ovale connect in fetal circulation, and what does it bypass?
cards.a: Right atrium → left atrium; bypasses the lungs

cards.q: What does the ductus arteriosus connect, and what does it bypass?
cards.a: Pulmonary trunk → aorta; bypasses the lungs

cards.q: Why do the three fetal shunts close at birth?
cards.a: The lungs inflate and pressures reverse
cards.more:
Each shunt leaves a remnant:

  • Ductus venosus → ligamentum venosum
  • Foramen ovale → fossa ovalis
  • Ductus arteriosus → ligamentum arteriosum
